parts.title: Part 1: A new neighbor
parts.intro: Mia sees a new person on her street.
paragraphs: Mia is a young woman. She lives in a small flat on Green Street. The street is quiet and there is a big tree in front of her window. She works in a bookshop, and she likes her job.
Today is Saturday. Mia is at home. She hears a loud noise outside. A big truck is in front of the house next door.
A man gets out of the truck. He is tall and he has short black hair. A small brown dog is with him. The dog has a red ball in its mouth.
"Hello!" says Mia. "Are you my new neighbor?"
"Yes, I am," says the man. "My name is Leo. This is my dog, Max."
"Nice to meet you, Leo," says Mia. "Can I help you?"
"Yes, please! I have many boxes," says Leo. He smiles.

parts.title: Part 2: Where is Max?
parts.intro: Leo has a problem on Sunday morning.
paragraphs: It is Sunday morning. Mia is in her kitchen. She has a cup of tea and a piece of bread. Suddenly, someone knocks on the door.
It is Leo. He looks very sad and tired.
"Mia, please help me!" he says. "Max is not at home. I can't find him!"
"Oh no!" says Mia. "Is the back door open?"
"Yes, it is," says Leo. "I think Max is outside. He has no collar, and he doesn't know this street."
Mia puts her cup on the table. "Don't worry," she says. "There is a park near here. Dogs like parks. Let's look there."
Mia takes her coat and her phone. Leo takes Max's red ball. "Max loves this ball," he says. "Maybe he can smell it."
They walk down Green Street together.

parts.title: Part 3: Looking in the park
parts.intro: Mia and Leo look for Max in different places.
paragraphs: The park is big and green. There are many trees, a small lake and a playground. Some children play on the swings. An old man sits on a bench and reads a newspaper.
"Excuse me," says Leo. "Do you see a small brown dog?"
The old man shakes his head. "No, I don't," he says. "But I see a dog near the lake. It is white."
"That is not Max," says Leo sadly.
Mia and Leo walk around the lake. They look under the trees. They look behind the bench. They call, "Max! Max!" but there is no dog.
Then Mia sees a woman with a small bag. She is outside the bakery next to the park.
"Hello," says Mia. "Is there a little brown dog here?"
The woman smiles. "Yes! A dog is behind the bakery. He is eating a piece of bread."
Leo runs to the bakery.

parts.title: Part 4: A happy ending
parts.intro: Leo and Mia finish their morning together.
paragraphs: Leo ran behind the bakery. Max was there! He was happy and he had a piece of bread in his mouth. His tail moved fast.
"Max!" said Leo. He sat on the ground and Max jumped into his arms. Leo laughed and his eyes were wet.
"Thank you, Mia," he said. "You are a very good neighbor."
"You are welcome," said Mia. "I was happy to help."
The baker came out of the shop. She gave Max some water. Then she gave Mia and Leo two warm rolls.
They sat on the bench in the park and ate. Max played with his red ball. The sun was warm.
"Come to my flat for dinner tonight," said Leo. "I can make pasta."
"Yes, I would love that," said Mia. She smiled. It was a good start to a new friendship.

parts.title: Part 1: A morning at home
parts.intro: Meet Nora and see her morning.
paragraphs: Nora Diaz is thirty years old. She lives in a small flat in the city. Her flat has two rooms, a kitchen and a bathroom. There is a big window in the kitchen.

Nora gets up at six o'clock every day. She takes a shower and puts on her clothes. Then she goes to the kitchen. She makes coffee and eats bread with cheese. There is a small radio on the table. She listens to music in the morning.
"I like my flat," Nora says. "It is not big, but it is warm and bright."
At seven fifteen, Nora takes her bag and her keys. She closes the door and goes down the stairs. Today is Monday. A new week starts.

parts.intro: Nora goes to work by bus.
paragraphs: Nora walks to the bus stop. It is five minutes from her flat. The bus is number twelve. Today the bus is late, and many people wait on the street.
The bus comes at seven forty. It is full. Nora stands near the door. A young man gives her his seat, and she says, "Thank you!"
Nora takes out a book from her bag. She reads for twenty minutes. The story is about a girl and a big city. Nora likes it very much.
The bus stops near a park, and a lot of people get off. Nora walks to a tall white building. Her office is on the third floor. She works for a travel company. She starts work at eight thirty.

parts.title: Part 3: A new colleague
parts.intro: There is a new person at the office.
paragraphs: At the office, Mrs. Reyes, the boss, says, "Good morning, everyone. This is Paul. He is our new colleague."
Paul is tall and thin. He has brown eyes and a kind smile. He is from Canada, but he lives in the city now. He can speak a little Spanish.
"Hello, Nora," says Paul. "I do not know the office. Can you help me?"
"Of course," says Nora. "Come with me." She shows him the kitchen, the printer and the meeting room. There is a coffee machine in the kitchen.
"Do you like coffee?" asks Nora.
"Yes, I love it," says Paul. "I drink three cups every day!"
Nora laughs. Paul has a desk next to hers. She thinks, "He is nice."

parts.intro: Nora has lunch with her friend.
paragraphs: At one o'clock, Nora goes out for lunch. Her friend Eva is outside the building. Eva is a teacher, and her school is near the park.
They go to a small restaurant on the corner. It is not expensive, and the food is good. Nora orders soup and a salad. Eva orders chicken with rice.
"How is your new colleague?" asks Eva.
"He is very nice," says Nora. "He drinks a lot of coffee!"
Eva smiles. Then she says, "Nora, my birthday is on Saturday. There is a party at my house at seven. Can you come?"
"Yes, I can!" says Nora. "I love parties."
"Great," says Eva. "You can bring a friend. Paul can come too."
They pay and walk back to the office.

parts.intro: Nora has a problem after work.
paragraphs: It is six o'clock. Nora is at her building. She is tired, and she wants to go home. She looks in her bag for her keys, but they are not there.
"Oh no!" she says. "Where are my keys?"
She looks again. There is a phone, a book, a pen and a small purse, but there are no keys. She is a little afraid.
Her neighbor, Mr. Lopez, comes down the stairs. He is an old man with white hair.
"Good evening, Nora. Is there a problem?" he asks.
"I cannot find my keys," says Nora.
"I have a key to your flat," says Mr. Lopez. "You can use it."
Nora opens the door. In the kitchen, she takes off her coat. There is something in the pocket. It is her keys! She laughs and says, "Thank you, Mr. Lopez!"

parts.title: Part 6: At the market
parts.intro: Nora goes shopping after work.
paragraphs: On Wednesday, Nora does not go home after work. She goes to the market near her flat. The market is open from four to eight.
It is a busy place. There are many small shops. A woman sells fruit, and a man sells flowers. The tomatoes are red and fresh. The bananas are yellow.
Nora buys tomatoes, onions, milk and eggs. Then she sees a man with a big bag of oranges. It is Paul!
"Hello, Nora!" he says. "I live near here. I come to this market every week."
"Really? I come here every Wednesday," says Nora.
"Then we can shop together next time," says Paul. He smiles.
They walk to the end of the street. Paul gives Nora two oranges. "They are for you," he says.
"Thank you," says Nora. "See you tomorrow at work!"

paragraphs: On Sunday, Nora wakes up at ten. She is tired, but she is very happy. She makes tea and sits by the kitchen window. The street is quiet.
At eleven, she calls her mother. Her mother lives in another city.
"Hi, Mom," says Nora. "I have a new colleague. His name is Paul. He is from Canada."
"Is he nice?" asks her mother.
"Yes, he is," says Nora. "We go to the market together, and we have fun at the party."
"I am happy for you," says her mother. "Come and see us next month."
"I can come in December," says Nora.
After the call, Nora has a sandwich and reads her book. In the afternoon, she writes a message to Paul: "Do you want to go to the market on Wednesday?"
Paul writes back: "Yes! See you at four." Nora smiles. Tomorrow is Monday, and she likes her life.

parts.title: Elephants
parts.intro: Learn about the biggest animals on land.
paragraphs: Elephants are the biggest animals on land. They live in Africa and Asia. An elephant is very tall and heavy. It can weigh 5,000 kilos.

Elephants live in families. The oldest female is the leader. Baby elephants stay close to their mothers. Elephants are kind to each other.
Elephants have big ears. The ears help them stay cool on hot days. People love elephants, and we must keep them safe.

parts.title: Football
parts.intro: Football is the most popular sport in the world.
paragraphs: Football is the most popular sport in the world. Millions of people play it. In the United States, people call it soccer.
There are two teams. Each team has eleven players. Players kick the ball and try to score a goal. They can not touch the ball with their hands. Only the goalkeeper can use his hands.
A game is ninety minutes long. It has two halves of forty-five minutes. The team with more goals wins the game.
You only need a ball to play. Children play football in the street, in the park and on the beach.
Every four years, there is a big World Cup. Teams from many countries play, and people watch the games on TV. Football is fun, and it is good for your health.

parts.intro: People in every country have special days.
paragraphs: People in every country have special days. Here are some festivals.
On New Year's Eve, people say goodbye to the old year. At midnight, they say "Happy New Year!" Many people watch fireworks.

In Mexico, people celebrate the Day of the Dead on November 1 and 2. Families remember people they love. They put flowers, food and photos on a table.
In China, the Spring Festival is a big holiday. Families eat a big dinner together. Children get red envelopes with money.
Festivals are happy days. People are together, and they enjoy music and food.

parts.title: A Healthy Life
parts.intro: Simple ways to take care of your body.
paragraphs: Your body needs care. Here are some simple ways to stay healthy.
First, eat good food. Eat fruit and vegetables every day. Do not eat too much sugar. Drink water. Your body needs about six to eight glasses of water a day.
Second, move your body. Walk, run, dance or play a sport. Try to do some exercise for thirty minutes every day.
Third, sleep well. Most adults need seven or eight hours of sleep each night. Sleep gives your body and your mind a rest.
Finally, wash your hands with soap before you eat. It stops germs. Also, see the doctor if you feel ill.
Small things every day make a big difference.

collections.title: The Tale of Peter Rabbit
collections.author: Beatrix Potter

parts.title: Part 1: Mother Rabbit's warning
parts.intro: Mother Rabbit warns her four children not to go into Mr. McGregor's garden, but one of them does not obey.
paragraphs: Once upon a time there were four little Rabbits, and their names were—
Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter.
They lived with their Mother in a sand-bank, underneath the root of a very big fir-tree.

'Now my dears,' said old Mrs. Rabbit one morning, 'you may go into the fields or down the lane, but don't go into Mr. McGregor's garden: your Father had an accident there; he was put in a pie by Mrs. McGregor.'
'Now run along, and don't get into mischief. I am going out.'
Then old Mrs. Rabbit took a basket and her umbrella, and went through the wood to the baker's. She bought a loaf of brown bread and five currant buns.
Flopsy, Mopsy, and Cotton-tail, who were good little bunnies, went down the lane to gather blackberries:
But Peter, who was very naughty, ran straight away to Mr. McGregor's garden, and squeezed under the gate!
First he ate some lettuces and some French beans; and then he ate some radishes;
And then, feeling rather sick, he went to look for some parsley.

parts.title: Part 2: Peter in the garden
parts.intro: Peter eats the vegetables in the garden, but Mr. McGregor finds him and starts a chase.
paragraphs: But round the end of a cucumber frame, whom should he meet but Mr. McGregor!
Mr. McGregor was on his hands and knees planting out young cabbages, but he jumped up and ran after Peter, waving a rake and calling out, 'Stop thief!'
Peter was most dreadfully frightened; he rushed all over the garden, for he had forgotten the way back to the gate.
He lost one of his shoes among the cabbages, and the other shoe amongst the potatoes.

After losing them, he ran on four legs and went faster, so that I think he might have got away altogether if he had not unfortunately run into a gooseberry net, and got caught by the large buttons on his jacket. It was a blue jacket with brass buttons, quite new.
Peter gave himself up for lost, and shed big tears; but his sobs were overheard by some friendly sparrows, who flew to him in great excitement, and implored him to exert himself.
Mr. McGregor came up with a sieve, which he intended to pop upon the top of Peter; but Peter wriggled out just in time, leaving his jacket behind him.
And rushed into the tool-shed, and jumped into a can. It would have been a beautiful thing to hide in, if it had not had so much water in it.

parts.title: Part 3: Lost among the plants
parts.intro: Peter hides, sneezes and escapes through a window, but he still cannot find the way out.
paragraphs: Mr. McGregor was quite sure that Peter was somewhere in the tool-shed, perhaps hidden underneath a flower-pot. He began to turn them over carefully, looking under each.
Presently Peter sneezed—'Kertyschoo!' Mr. McGregor was after him in no time.
And tried to put his foot upon Peter, who jumped out of a window, upsetting three plants. The window was too small for Mr. McGregor, and he was tired of running after Peter. He went back to his work.
Peter sat down to rest; he was out of breath and trembling with fright, and he had not the least idea which way to go. Also he was very damp with sitting in that can.
After a time he began to wander about, going lippity—lippity—not very fast, and looking all round.
He found a door in a wall; but it was locked, and there was no room for a fat little rabbit to squeeze underneath.

An old mouse was running in and out over the stone doorstep, carrying peas and beans to her family in the wood. Peter asked her the way to the gate, but she had such a large pea in her mouth that she could not answer. She only shook her head at him. Peter began to cry.

Then he tried to find his way straight across the garden, but he became more and more puzzled. Presently, he came to a pond where Mr. McGregor filled his water-cans. A white cat was staring at some gold-fish, she sat very, very still, but now and then the tip of her tail twitched as if it were alive. Peter thought it best to go away without speaking to her; he had heard about cats from his cousin, little Benjamin Bunny.

parts.title: Part 1: The wrong suitcase
parts.intro: Lena arrives in a small town by the sea for a short holiday.
paragraphs: Lena got off the train in Marbella Bay at four o'clock. The town was small and quiet, and the sea was bluer than in her photos. She was very happy. She had a week of holiday, and she was going to swim, read and do nothing.
At the station, a lot of people were waiting for their bags. Lena saw her suitcase at once. It was blue, and it had a yellow ribbon on the handle. She took it and walked to the hotel.

The Hotel Mar was old but friendly. Mr. Costa, the owner, gave her the key to Room 12. "Breakfast is at eight," he said. "The room is on the second floor. You can take the stairs, because the lift is broken."
Lena carried the heavy suitcase up the stairs. It was heavier than usual, but she did not think about it. In her room, she put the suitcase on the bed and opened it.
She looked inside and stopped. There were no summer clothes. There was no hat and no book. There was an old brown coat, a small metal box, and a yellow notebook.
"This is not my suitcase!" she said. She looked at the ribbon again. It was the same colour, but it was a different ribbon. It was longer and dirtier than hers.
Lena sat down on the bed. "What am I going to do now?" she thought.

"What key?" Lena asked. She opened the metal box. Inside there was a small silver key and an old photo of a young man in front of a lighthouse.
Lena went downstairs to speak to Mr. Costa. "Excuse me," she said. "Do you know a woman called Rosa Almeida?"
Mr. Costa looked surprised. "Rosa? Of course. She is a very old friend. But she doesn't live on Harbour Road now. She moved to a house near the hill last year."
"I have her suitcase by mistake," Lena said. "And I think she has mine."

At six o'clock the sun began to go down. Lena stood in front of a small green door. She took the silver key out of her pocket. Her hand was shaking a little.
"I can do this," she said. She put the key in the lock and turned it. Click! The door opened slowly.

Inside, the lighthouse was dark and smelled of old stone. Lena used the light on her phone and began to climb. One, two, three... After fifty steps she was tired, and after eighty she wanted to stop. But she did not stop.
At the top there was a round room with big windows. The sea looked orange and gold in the evening light. In the middle of the room there was a small table, and on the table there was a wooden box.
Lena was going to open the box when she heard a noise behind her. Somebody was coming up the stairs!
She turned around quickly. A tall man was standing in the door. He was wearing a brown coat, but it was newer than the coat in the suitcase.
"Please don't be afraid," he said. "My name is Daniel. I think you have my grandmother's suitcase."

parts.title: Part 1: The empty shop
parts.intro: Mia finds an old shop in a small town and makes a big decision.
paragraphs: Mia lived in a big, noisy city. Every day she took a crowded bus to an office and worked at a computer for eight hours. She was tired and a little sad. Her real dream was different: she wanted to make bread.

Last spring, Mia visited a small town called Greenfield for the weekend. The streets were quiet, the air was fresh, and everybody said hello to her. "This town is much friendlier than my city," she thought.

On Sunday morning, she walked down Mill Street and saw an empty shop. In the window there was a sign: "For rent." The shop was small, but it had a big window and an old brick oven at the back. Before, it was a shoe shop, but now it was dusty and empty.

Mia put her hand on the oven. "It is older than me," she said, "but it looks strong." She called the number on the sign. A kind woman named Mrs. Lee answered the phone. She was the owner of the building.
"The rent is not expensive," said Mrs. Lee. "It is cheaper than the rent in the city. You can see the shop tomorrow."

That night, Mia could not sleep. She thought about the shop, the oven and the smell of fresh bread. On Monday, she looked at the shop again, and then she made a decision. She was going to leave her office job and open a bakery. She was very afraid, but she was also very excited.

paragraphs: Two months later, Mia was in Greenfield with her boxes. She said goodbye to her old job and moved into a small flat above the shop. The first week, she cleaned everything. She washed the floor, painted the walls white and cleaned the big window.

At the back of the shop, she found a box from her grandmother. Inside, there was a notebook with old recipes. Her grandmother was a famous baker in her village. Mia opened the notebook and smiled. The first page said: "Good bread needs time, love and a little salt."

On Saturday, Mia tried the first recipe. She mixed the flour, water and yeast, and she waited for two hours. Then she put the dough in the old oven. But she did not check the temperature, and the oven was too hot. After twenty minutes, the bread was black and hard like a stone.

"Oh no!" said Mia. She threw the bread in the bin. She tried again on Sunday, and this time the bread was too pale and too soft. On Monday, she made a third loaf. It was better, but it was not perfect.
Mia was tired and her hands hurt. She looked at her grandmother's notebook again. On the last page, there was another sentence: "Bread is like life. Do not stop after your first mistake."

Mia laughed. She cleaned the kitchen, bought some more flour and started again. On Tuesday morning, the shop smelled wonderful. She took out a golden loaf with a crunchy top. She broke a piece and ate it. It was warm, soft and delicious.
"Now I am ready," she said quietly.

parts.title: Part 3: A new helper
parts.intro: A young man called Tom offers to help in the bakery.
paragraphs: Mia decided to open the shop on Saturday. She had a lot of work to do, and she was alone. On Thursday, she put a sign on the door: "Mia's Bread. Opening Saturday at seven."

On Friday morning, a tall young man came into the shop. He had a big backpack and a friendly smile. "Hello, I am Tom," he said. "I study at the university in the next town, but I live here. I saw your sign. Do you need some help?"
"Can you work early in the morning?" asked Mia.
"Of course," said Tom. "I am a very early riser. I usually wake up at five." Mia looked at him for a moment. He seemed honest, and she really needed help. "OK," she said. "You can start tomorrow."

That afternoon, Tom showed Mia how to use the cash register, and Mia taught him the recipes. Tom was a fast learner. He was also funnier than Mia, and he made her laugh a lot. "This is going to be a good team," Mia thought.
At night, they baked fifty loaves. Tom made the shapes, and Mia watched the oven. This time she checked the temperature three times. Then they put the bread on the shelves and cleaned the tables.
At ten o'clock, Mia was exhausted, but Tom was still full of energy. "I think everybody in town is going to love this bread," he said.
"I hope so," said Mia. "Tomorrow is the big day."

parts.title: Part 4: The big day
parts.intro: The bakery opens, but not many people come at first.
paragraphs: On Saturday, Mia woke up at four o'clock. She was so nervous that she could not eat breakfast. When Tom arrived, the shop was already warm and the smell of bread was everywhere.
At seven o'clock exactly, Mia turned the sign on the door to "Open." She waited. Nobody came. At seven thirty, an old man walked past the window and looked at the bread, but he did not come in.
"Maybe people are still sleeping," said Tom. "It is Saturday."

At eight o'clock, a woman with a small dog entered. "Good morning," she said. "I am Mrs. Green. I live next door. What is the best bread today?" Mia gave her a piece of the golden loaf to try. Mrs. Green closed her eyes. "This is wonderful," she said. "It reminds me of the bread from my childhood."

She bought three loaves and told her friends. Slowly, more people came. A boy bought a roll with cheese. A man bought a big loaf for his family. A teacher asked about cakes. By noon, the shop was full of voices and laughing.
But at the end of the day, Mia counted the money. It was not very much. They sold thirty loaves, and twenty loaves were still on the shelves. "We made too much bread," she said.
"It is only the first day," said Tom. "Tomorrow is going to be better."
That night, Mia gave the extra bread to a small family shelter in town. She was tired, but she felt proud. She did not earn a lot of money, but she made many people happy.

parts.title: Part 5: Rain
parts.intro: Rainy days are bad for business, and Tom has an idea.
paragraphs: On Monday, it started to rain. It rained all day, and it rained all night. On Tuesday, the streets were empty, and the grey sky was heavier than before. In the shop, Mia and Tom waited, but only two people came in.
"Nobody wants to walk in this weather," said Mia sadly. She looked at the shelves, full of bread. "What are we going to do with all this?"
Tom thought for a minute. "People do not want to come to us," he said slowly, "so we can go to them."
"What do you mean?" asked Mia.
"We can deliver bread to people's homes," said Tom. "Old people, busy mothers, students. They would love fresh bread at the door."
Mia was not sure. "But we do not have a car," she said. "And a van is too expensive."
"I have a bike with a big basket," said Tom. "I can take twenty loaves in one trip. It is faster than a car in this small town, and it does not cost anything."
Mia looked out of the window. The rain was getting lighter. She smiled. "OK, let us try it. But first, we need a list of people."

They made a small paper sign that said: "Fresh bread at your door. Call Mia's Bread." They wrote the shop's phone number in big letters. Then Tom put on his raincoat and went to hang the sign on every street lamp in the town.

parts.title: Part 6: Bread on a bike
parts.intro: The delivery idea works and the bakery gets busier.
paragraphs: The next morning, the rain stopped and Tom started the first deliveries. He put twenty loaves in the basket of his bike and rode through the wet streets. Mia stayed in the shop and watched the clock.

At nine o'clock, the phone rang. It was Mr. Hall, an old man who lived on Hill Road. "My legs are not strong, and the hill is steeper than it looks," he said. "Can the boy bring me two loaves, please?" Mia smiled. "Of course. He is on his way."

By noon, the phone rang six more times. A mother with three small children wanted rolls for lunch. A nurse wanted bread before her night shift. Even Mrs. Green called, because her dog was sick and she did not want to leave him.
Tom came back to the shop at one o'clock, red in the face and very happy. "It is a great idea," he said. "People are so kind. Mr. Hall gave me a cup of tea and told me three stories!"

That week, Mia and Tom delivered bread every morning before they opened the shop. Their customers told their neighbours, and the neighbours told their friends. The list of names on the wall got longer every day.
After two weeks, the small bakery was busier than ever. Some people came to the shop and said, "We saw your sign on the street lamp!" Others only wanted their bread at home.
On Friday night, Mia counted the money again. This time, there was a lot more. She showed the paper to Tom. "Look," she said. "We are making a profit."
"Do not forget the rain," laughed Tom. "It was our best friend."

parts.title: Part 7: A new bakery in town
parts.intro: A bigger and cheaper bakery opens on Mill Street.
paragraphs: One Monday, Mia saw a new sign on the corner of Mill Street. It said: "Brown's Bakery. Opening soon." The shop was much bigger than hers, with three large windows and a shiny red door.

Two weeks later, Mr. Brown opened his bakery. He was a tall man in an expensive suit. He sold bread, cakes and coffee, and everything was cheaper than in Mia's shop. A big banner said: "Special price today: two loaves for the price of one!"

On the first day, Mia had only five customers. On the second day, she had three. Tom came back from a delivery with a worried face. "Two old customers want to buy at Brown's now," he said. "It is cheaper."
Mia felt a pain in her stomach. "I cannot make my bread cheaper," she said. "Good flour is expensive, and my loaves take a long time."

That evening, Mia walked past Brown's Bakery. Through the window, she saw the bread. It was very white and very perfect, but all the loaves were the same. She went in and bought a small roll. It looked beautiful, but it tasted like paper.
Back in her shop, Mia sat down and opened her grandmother's notebook. On one page, she read: "A baker does not sell bread. A baker sells care." She read it three times.

"Tom," she said the next morning, "we are not going to be cheaper than Brown's. But we are going to be better. We will learn the names of our customers and ask about their day. And we are going to make our bread with the best flour."
Tom grinned. "Now that sounds like a plan."

parts.title: Part 8: The oven stops
parts.intro: A big job comes to Mia, but the old oven breaks the night before.
paragraphs: Mia's new plan worked slowly. She asked every customer, "How is your day?" She remembered that Mr. Hall liked seeds in his bread, that the nurse wanted small loaves, and that the boy with the cheese roll was called Sam.

One afternoon, Mrs. Lee, the owner of the building, came into the shop. "Mia, I have good news," she said. "The town festival is next month. The mayor wants a big cake for one hundred people, and he asked me for the best baker. I told him about you."
Mia's heart jumped. "A cake for one hundred people? I have never made one before."
"You are going to be fine," said Mrs. Lee. "Mr. Brown also wants the job, but the mayor tasted your bread last week. He said it was the best bread of his life."
For the next two weeks, Mia practised in the evenings. She made a lemon cake, a chocolate cake and a carrot cake. Tom tried them all and said, "They are all good, but the lemon cake is the best."

The day before the festival, Mia started the big cake. She worked until midnight. She was putting the last cake in the oven when, suddenly, there was a loud noise. Then the oven became quiet. The light went out. The old oven was dead.
Mia stared at it. "No," she whispered. "Not now. Not tonight."
She tried again and again, but nothing happened. It was one o'clock in the morning, and the cake was half cold and half raw. Mia sat on the floor and started to cry.

parts.title: Part 9: Help in the night
parts.intro: Neighbours save the festival cake.
paragraphs: At one thirty, somebody knocked on the shop door. Mia opened it with red eyes. It was Tom, with his coat on over his pyjamas. "I saw the light from my window," he said. "What happened?"
"The oven is dead," said Mia. "The cake is not ready. I am going to call the mayor and say sorry."
"Wait," said Tom. "Mrs. Green has a big oven. She used to bake with her mother. I am going to call her."

Mia did not think a neighbour could help at that hour. But ten minutes later, Mrs. Green arrived with her little dog and a big bag of eggs. "Come to my house," she said. "My oven is old, but it is bigger than yours."

They carried the cake carefully down the street. At Mrs. Green's house, they baked until five o'clock in the morning. Then Mr. Hall woke up and came to help. Then the nurse came home from her shift and joined them. Nobody asked any questions.

At eight o'clock, the cake was ready. It was tall and golden, and it smelled of lemon. Mrs. Green made a thick cream, and Sam, the boy from the shop, brought flowers from his garden to put on the top.
At noon, the festival began. The square was full of music, colours and people. Mia and her friends put the cake on a long table. When the mayor cut the first piece, everybody was quiet.
"This is the best cake in town," he said. All the people clapped their hands. Mia looked at her friends, and she felt happier than ever. The money was not important. She had a family now.

parts.title: Part 10: A new sign
parts.intro: The bakery grows and Mia plans for the future.
paragraphs: After the festival, everything changed for Mia's little bakery. People from the next towns came to Greenfield just to buy her bread. On Saturdays, there was a line outside the door, and Mia and Tom needed to start work at three o'clock in the morning.

One day, Mr. Brown came into the shop. He was not wearing his expensive suit. "Mia," he said, "I want to say sorry. I was only thinking about money. My bakery is closing next week, but your bread is the best in the region. Can I learn from you?"
With the money from the festival, Mia bought a new oven. It was shinier and faster than the old one. But she kept the old oven in the corner, with a small sign: "This oven gave me my first loaf."
She also changed the sign over the door. It was not paper now. It was a beautiful wooden sign, painted by Sam's mother. It said: "Mia's Bread. Time, love and a little salt."
Mrs. Lee came to see the new sign. She hugged Mia and said, "You were afraid in the beginning, but now you are the heart of this street."
On Sunday evening, Mia and Tom sat on the bench outside the shop with two cups of tea. "What are you going to do next?" asked Tom.
Mia thought for a moment. "Next year, I am going to teach a bread class for the children of the town," she said. "And you are going to help me."
"With pleasure," said Tom. Mia looked at the old oven through the window and smiled. She was exactly where she wanted to be.

parts.title: Everyday Inventions
parts.intro: Three small objects we use every day have surprising stories.
paragraphs: We use many small things every day, and we never think about them. But every object has a story. Somebody invented it, often a long time ago. Let us look at three simple inventions.

The first one is the umbrella. People in ancient China and Egypt used umbrellas more than 3,000 years ago. At first, they did not use them for rain. They used them to make shade and to stay cool in the sun. Later, people covered umbrellas with oil, so the water could not come in.

The second is the toothbrush. In China, people made toothbrushes with animal hair in the 1400s. Today, most toothbrushes are made of plastic and nylon, and some are electric. Dentists say we should brush our teeth twice a day.

The third is the sticky note. It was invented by accident in the 1970s. A scientist wanted to make a very strong glue, but he made a weak one. Some years later, a colleague used it to keep a piece of paper in his book. Now millions of people use sticky notes at home and at work.
Small ideas can change daily life. Next time you pick up an umbrella, remember: it is very old!

parts.title: Famous Places
parts.intro: Four famous places and what makes each one special.
paragraphs: Every year, millions of people travel to see famous places. Here are four of them.

Machu Picchu is in the mountains of Peru, about 2,400 metres above the sea. The Incas built this city in the 1400s. It has stone houses, long stairs and green fields. The city was hidden in the clouds for hundreds of years, and it became famous around the world in 1911.

The Eiffel Tower is in Paris, in France. It was finished in 1889 for a big world fair. The tower is made of iron and it is about 330 metres tall. At first, some people did not like it, but today it is a symbol of Paris. Every night, thousands of small lights shine on it.

The Taj Mahal is in Agra, in India. An emperor built it in the 1600s for his wife. More than 20,000 workers needed about twenty years to finish it. The building is made of white stone, and it changes colour during the day. In the morning it looks pink, and at night it looks silver.

The Great Wall of China is not one wall. It is many walls that people built over hundreds of years. All together, they are more than 20,000 kilometres long. Today, visitors can walk on some parts of the wall and enjoy the view of the hills.
Which of these places would you like to visit first?

parts.title: Simple Healthy Habits
parts.intro: Small daily habits can make you feel better.
paragraphs: You do not need a gym or a lot of money to be healthy. Small habits every day can help your body and your mind. Here are four easy ideas.

First, drink water. Our bodies need a lot of water, and many people forget to drink it. A good idea is to keep a bottle on your desk. Water gives you energy, and it is better for you than sweet drinks.

Second, walk every day. Doctors say that thirty minutes of walking is good for your heart. You can walk to work, take the stairs, or go to the park after dinner. It is free, and you can do it with a friend.

Third, eat fruit and vegetables. Try to have something colourful on your plate at every meal. Red tomatoes, green beans and orange carrots all give your body different vitamins. If you do not like a vegetable, try it in a different way. Maybe you will like it in soup!
Fourth, talk to people. Spending time with family and friends makes us happier. A short phone call can make a bad day better.
You do not have to change everything at once. Choose one habit this week and do it every day. After a few weeks, it will feel normal.

parts.title: The Story of Chocolate
parts.intro: Chocolate has a long history, and it began in the Americas.
paragraphs: Most people love chocolate, but not many people know its story. It is a very old one, and it begins in Mexico and Central America.

Chocolate comes from the seeds of the cacao tree. The Maya and the Aztecs used these seeds more than 1,000 years ago. They made a hot drink from them. It was not sweet. It was bitter, and sometimes people added chilli to it. For the Aztecs, cacao seeds were so important that they used them as money.

In the 1500s, Spanish travellers took cacao to Europe. People there liked the drink, but they thought it was too bitter. So they added sugar and milk, and chocolate became popular in rich homes. It was an expensive treat.

For a long time, people only drank chocolate. The first chocolate bar to eat was made in England in the 1800s. A few years later, a Swiss man made the first milk chocolate, and it was softer and sweeter. After that, chocolate became cheaper, and soon everybody could buy it.

Today, people eat millions of tonnes of chocolate every year. Some of the best cacao still grows in Latin America and in West Africa. Next time you eat a piece of chocolate, remember its long journey.

parts.title: Sports Around the World
parts.intro: Where do some famous sports come from?
paragraphs: Millions of people play or watch sports. Many sports have a long and interesting history.

Football is the most popular sport in the world. People played similar games in many countries a very long time ago, but the modern rules come from England in the 1800s. Today, billions of people watch the World Cup, which takes place every four years.

Basketball is much younger. In 1891, a teacher in the United States, James Naismith, wanted a new indoor game for his students because the winters were cold. He put two baskets on the wall and used a football. Those first baskets were for fruit, so the players needed a ladder to get the ball out after each point!

The Olympic Games are very old. The first ones took place in ancient Greece almost 3,000 years ago. After many centuries, the Games came back in 1896 in Athens. Now the summer Olympics happen every four years in a different city.
Table tennis started in England as a game for after dinner. Players used books as a net and a small ball. Today, it is a fast sport, and the best players hit the ball very quickly.
Which sport do you like most? Maybe you can learn about its history too.

parts.title: Surprising Animals
parts.intro: Some animals have very unusual bodies and habits.
paragraphs: Nature is full of surprises. Some animals have bodies or habits that seem strange to us. Here are three of them.

The octopus lives in the sea, and it is one of the cleverest animals without bones. It has three hearts and its blood is blue. Two hearts send blood to the gills, and the third sends blood to the rest of the body. An octopus can also change colour in a second to hide from other animals. Some octopuses can open a jar to get food!

The giraffe is the tallest animal on Earth. An adult giraffe can be more than five metres tall. Its neck is very long, but it has only seven bones in it, the same number as a human neck. Each bone is just much longer. Giraffes also sleep very little. Often they sleep for only thirty minutes or so in a day, and they usually do it standing up.

The hummingbird is a very small bird, and some kinds are not bigger than a coin. It moves its wings about fifty times in a second, so you can hear a soft sound like a hum. This is how the bird got its name. It is the only bird that can fly backwards. It also needs to eat very often, because it uses a lot of energy. A hummingbird drinks sweet juice from flowers many times an hour.
Which of these animals is the most surprising for you?

parts.title: Technology at Home
parts.intro: New machines in our homes make daily life easier.
paragraphs: Many homes today have technology that did not exist when our grandparents were young. Here are some useful machines and their stories.

The microwave oven was invented by accident. In the 1940s, an engineer called Percy Spencer worked with a machine that made radio waves. One day, he put his hand in his pocket and found that a chocolate bar was soft and warm. He tried again with popcorn, and it jumped and popped! A few years later, the first microwave ovens appeared. They were big and expensive, but today almost every kitchen has one.

The robot vacuum is a small, round machine that cleans the floor by itself. It moves around the room and uses sensors to find tables and chairs. When the battery is low, it goes back to its station. Many people like it because they can do other things while the floor gets clean.

A smart speaker listens to your voice. You can ask it about the weather, play your favourite song or set an alarm. It needs the internet to work. Some people also use smart lights. With your phone, you can turn on the lights in your house, even when you are not there.
Technology can save time, but we should use it with care. Sometimes the best thing is to turn everything off and talk with the people at home.

parts.title: Traditions Around the World
parts.intro: Four traditions that people enjoy every year.
paragraphs: Every country has special traditions. They bring families and friends together. Here are four from different parts of the world.

In Japan, people love the spring flowers. Every year in March and April, the cherry trees have pink and white flowers. Families and friends sit under the trees, eat food and talk. This tradition is called hanami, and it is more than a thousand years old.

In Mexico, people celebrate the Day of the Dead on the first two days of November. It is not a sad day. Families remember the people they love and put photos, food and orange flowers on a special table at home. Streets are full of colour and music.

In India, people celebrate Holi in spring. It is called the festival of colours. People go outside and throw coloured powder at each other. Everyone laughs, dances and eats sweet food. The festival says goodbye to winter and welcomes a new season.

In the Spanish town of Buñol, there is a very funny party called La Tomatina. It takes place on the last Wednesday of August. For one hour, thousands of people throw ripe tomatoes at each other. After the party, the streets are red, but firefighters clean them with water.
Traditions are a way to enjoy life and remember our history.

parts.intro: Some jobs are very different from the usual ones.
paragraphs: When you think about jobs, you may think of doctors, teachers or drivers. But there are also some jobs that are very unusual. Here are three of them.

A tea taster works in the tea industry. Every day, this person tastes many cups of tea, sometimes hundreds. The taster looks at the colour, smells the leaves and drinks a little. Then he or she decides if the tea is good and how much it should cost. This job needs a very good sense of taste and smell.

A sound effects artist makes the sounds that you hear in films. In a film, the real sounds are often not loud enough, so artists make new ones in a studio. They walk on a box of gravel to make the sound of steps in the snow. They hit two coconut shells together to make the sound of a horse. Sometimes the answer for a sound is very simple!

A colour namer works for a paint company. There are thousands of paint colours, and each one needs a name. A colour can be called Ocean Mist, Warm Sand or Morning Sky. Good names help people to imagine the colour on their walls. This person needs to be creative and to love words.
These jobs show that you can turn a special interest into work. What unusual job would you like to try?

parts.title: Why We Sleep
parts.intro: Sleep is very important for our body and our mind.
paragraphs: We spend about one third of our life asleep. Sleep may look like a waste of time, but our body works hard when we are in bed. Here are some interesting facts.

Adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep every night. Teenagers need a little more, and babies sleep for fourteen hours or more in a day. If we do not sleep enough, we feel tired, we cannot think well and we forget things easily.

When we sleep, the brain is busy. It puts the new things from the day into our memory. That is why a good night of sleep is important before an exam. The body also rests and repairs itself while we sleep.
Everybody dreams, but we forget most of our dreams. Most dreams happen in a special part of the night when our eyes move fast under our eyelids.
Animals sleep too. Dolphins have a very special way: they sleep with only half of the brain at a time, so they can keep swimming and breathing.

Do you want to sleep better? Try to go to bed at the same time every night. Keep your room dark and cool. Do not use your phone in the last hour before bed. A short nap of twenty minutes in the afternoon can also give you energy, but do not sleep too long, or you may not sleep at night.
Sweet dreams!

parts.title: A Review of The Green Table
parts.intro: A customer writes about a dinner at a small restaurant.
paragraphs: I visited The Green Table last Saturday with my sister. It is a small restaurant near the river, and it opens at six in the evening. We did not have a reservation, so we waited twenty minutes outside. The waiter was very polite and gave us a free glass of water while we waited.

The restaurant is not big, but it is warm and clean. There are plants on every table and soft music in the background. Our table was next to a large window, so we could see the river and the lights of the bridge.

For the main course, I ordered the mushroom pasta. It came with fresh bread and a small salad. My sister chose the chicken soup, and she said it was the best soup she ever tried. For dessert, we shared an apple cake. It was a little too sweet for me, but my sister loved it.

The prices are fair. Our dinner cost forty-two dollars for two people, and that included two drinks. The only problem was the noise. A big family at the next table was laughing and talking loudly for an hour.

I give The Green Table four stars out of five. I will go back soon, but next time I will book a table in advance. I recommend it for a quiet dinner with a friend, but it is not a good place for a big party.

parts.title: Two Days in Lisbon
parts.intro: A traveller shares her trip on a blog.
paragraphs: Hello again, everyone! I am writing this post from a small cafe in Lisbon. I arrived on Thursday morning, and I already love this city. It is full of hills, colourful houses and old yellow trams.

On my first day, I walked around the old part of the city. The streets are narrow and steep, so I wore comfortable shoes. This was a very good idea! I stopped at a tiny bakery and tried a famous custard tart. It was warm, sweet and only one euro.

In the afternoon, I took tram number 28. It was crowded, but the ride was fun. From a high point, I saw red roofs and the river. I took more than a hundred photos. In the evening, I had grilled fish with potatoes near the river, and I listened to a man playing the guitar.

On my second day, I visited a big park and a beautiful old tower. The tower is not far from the center, so I went there by bus. Be careful if you go there: the tickets are cheaper online than at the door.
Tomorrow I am going to take a short train to a small beach town. I will tell you all about it soon. If you have any tips for Lisbon, please write them in the comments below. See you next time!

parts.intro: A building sends its rules to all new neighbours.
paragraphs: Welcome to Maple Court! We want every neighbour to feel happy and safe in our building. Please read these simple rules and keep this paper in a safe place.

Quiet hours are from ten o'clock at night to seven o'clock in the morning. During these hours, please do not play loud music or use the washing machine. You may talk to your friends, but please keep your voice low in the hall.

Please put your rubbish in the bins behind the building. The yellow bin is for paper, and the green bin is for glass. Do not leave bags near the front door. The rubbish truck comes every Tuesday and Friday.

Bicycles must not stay in the hall or on the stairs. You can keep them in the bicycle room in the basement. To open the door, you need your key card. If you lose your key card, call the office and ask for a new one. It costs five dollars.
Pets are welcome, but dogs must stay on a lead in the garden and in the hall. If your pet makes a lot of noise, please speak to the manager.
If you have a problem, you can visit the office from nine to five, Monday to Friday. In an emergency, call the number on the front door. Thank you for helping us keep Maple Court clean and quiet!

To book a place, visit our website or come to the front desk. You can pay by card or in cash. Please book before 1 October because the course is popular and the places go quickly. We hope to see you there!

parts.title: How to Make Vegetable Soup
parts.intro: A simple recipe with steps for a family dinner.
paragraphs: This soup is easy, cheap and healthy. It takes about forty minutes, and it is enough for four people. You can eat it with bread or rice.
You need two carrots, two potatoes, one onion, one tomato, a little oil, salt and pepper. You also need one liter of water and a large pot.

First, wash all the vegetables with cold water. Then peel the carrots, the potatoes and the onion. Cut the onion into small pieces. Cut the carrots and potatoes into larger pieces, about two centimeters wide.

Next, put the pot on the stove and add two spoons of oil. When the oil is hot, add the onion. Cook it for three minutes, but do not let it turn brown. Then add the tomato, the carrots and the potatoes. Stir everything for a minute.

After that, pour the water into the pot. Add a little salt and wait until the water boils. Then turn the heat down and cover the pot. Cook the soup for twenty-five minutes. Be careful: the steam is very hot.

Finally, check the vegetables with a fork. They must be soft. Add salt and pepper if you want, and serve the soup in warm bowls. If you like a smooth soup, you can mix it with a blender. Enjoy your meal!

parts.title: Visit the City Museum
parts.intro: A leaflet gives visitors the information they need.
paragraphs: Welcome to the City Museum! Discover two thousand years of life in our town. We are in the old market building in the center, next to the main square.

The museum has three floors. On the ground floor, you can see old coins, tools and clothes from Roman times. On the first floor, there is a room about the history of our river and the boats that sailed on it. The second floor has paintings and photographs of the city from the last hundred years. Children love the top floor, where they can touch some objects and try on old hats.

We are open every day except Monday. The hours are from ten in the morning to six in the evening, and until nine o'clock on the first Friday of every month. The last visitors can enter one hour before closing time.

Tickets cost twelve dollars for adults and six dollars for students. Children under seven can enter for free. On Sundays, the entrance is free for everyone after four o'clock. You can buy your tickets at the door or on our website.

Please remember a few rules. You can take photographs, but please do not use the flash. Do not touch the paintings. Large bags must stay in the lockers near the entrance. Food and drinks are not allowed in the rooms, but our cafe on the ground floor is open all day.
Free guided tours in English start at eleven and three o'clock. Ask at the information desk. We hope you enjoy your visit!

parts.title: Part 1: A New Start
parts.intro: Elena leaves her old job and arrives in a small town to open a shop that is not quite empty.
paragraphs: Elena Ruiz had worked in a bank in Mexico City for eleven years when she finally decided to change her life. She was tired of numbers, meetings and the long journey to the office every morning. "If I stay here, I will never do anything different," she told her sister.

Three months later, she was standing in front of a small shop in a quiet town on the English coast. Her uncle Tomas, who had repaired clocks there for forty years, had moved to live with his daughter in Canada. Before he left, he had offered Elena the shop. "It isn't much," he had said on the phone, "but it's yours if you want it."

Elena had never repaired a clock in her life. However, she had always enjoyed fixing small things, and she had been learning from videos for weeks. If the shop failed, she thought, she could always go home. But she was determined to try.

Inside, the shop smelled of dust and oil. There were clocks everywhere: on the walls, on the shelves and even on the floor. While she was looking around, a man with a white apron knocked on the window. He was holding a paper bag.
"You must be Tomas's niece," he said with a smile. "I'm Mr Hale. I run the bakery next door. I've brought you some bread, because nobody should start a new job hungry."

Elena thanked him and asked how long he had known her uncle. "Thirty years," he answered. "He was a good neighbour. He told me you were coming, but he didn't say why he was in such a hurry to leave." He stopped for a moment. "Be careful, my dear. Last week, a man was asking questions about this shop."
"What kind of questions?" Elena asked.
"He wanted to know when you would arrive, and whether the shop was for sale," said Mr Hale. "I told him I didn't know anything."

That night, Elena slept in the small room above the shop. At about midnight, she woke up because she heard a noise downstairs. She took a torch and went down slowly. Nobody was there, but the door of the old oak cabinet was open, and one clock lay on the floor.

parts.title: Part 2: The Town Clock
parts.intro: Elena meets the mayor and finds an unusual object in a clock.
paragraphs: The next morning, Elena called the police, but the officer who came was not very interested. "Nothing is missing, is it?" he asked. "Perhaps it was only the wind." Elena did not believe him, but she said nothing.

Later, she phoned her uncle. "Did anyone want something from the shop?" she asked. There was a long silence. Then Tomas said, "If you ever find a small brass key, don't give it to anybody. I'll explain everything when I can." He hung up before she could ask any more questions.

At ten o'clock, a tall woman in a green coat walked in. She said she was Mrs Carter, the mayor. "The clock on the town hall has been broken for years," she explained. "Your uncle always said he would fix it, but he never did. If you repair it, the town will be very grateful."
Elena felt nervous, but she agreed. "I'll go and have a look this afternoon," she said.

The tower was cold and dark. Elena climbed up the narrow stairs with her tools and found the old machine behind a wooden door. It was covered in dust. She cleaned it carefully, and after two hours she found something strange. Behind one of the big wheels there was a small metal box, tied to the frame with wire.
She opened it. Inside was a brass key with a number on it: 14. Her heart was beating fast. She remembered her uncle's words and put the key in her pocket.
When she went down, she saw a man in a long coat near the door. He was looking at her hands. "Did you find anything up there?" he asked in a friendly voice.
"Only a lot of dust," said Elena. "Who are you?"
"My name's Grant. I buy and sell old things. I'd like to make you an offer for the shop." He took out a card. "Think about it. I'll come back tomorrow." Then he turned and walked away quickly.
Elena looked at the card. Under his name there was a telephone number, and she knew the voice: it was the same man who had been asking Mr Hale about the shop.

parts.title: Part 3: Locker Fourteen
parts.intro: Elena follows the clue and learns a secret from the past.
paragraphs: That evening, Elena sat in the shop and looked at the key. Where could number 14 be? She called Mr Hale and asked him if he had any idea.
"A key with a number? Hmm," he said, scratching his head. "The old railway station has a left-luggage room with lockers. It closed years ago, but nobody has ever taken the lockers away."

The next morning, she went to the station. The building was empty and the paint was coming off the walls. In the back room she found a row of old metal lockers. Number 14 was at the bottom. The key turned easily, and the door opened with a loud noise.
Inside there was a thick brown envelope. Elena sat on the floor and read the papers. There were old letters, bank records and a notebook written in her uncle's handwriting.

Slowly, she understood. Twenty years earlier, the town had collected money to build a new school. Mr Grant's father, who worked for the council, had said that the money was safe. But the records showed that he had taken most of it. Her uncle had found the proof by accident when he had been repairing the town clock. The council had hidden the papers inside it.
At the end of the notebook, Tomas had written: "I was afraid to tell the truth, because Grant's family was powerful. I hope someone braver than me will do it one day."
Elena's hands were shaking. As a bank worker, she knew very well what the numbers meant. She took photographs of every page with her phone. Then she heard footsteps behind her.
"I knew you would come here," said Mr Grant from the door. He was no longer smiling. "Give me the envelope, and I'll pay you a lot of money."
"I'm sorry, but I can't do that," Elena said calmly. "If I gave it to you, I would feel terrible for the rest of my life."
Grant took a step towards her. Suddenly, a loud voice shouted from the corridor: "Stay where you are!" It was the police officer from the day before, and Mr Hale was standing next to him.

parts.title: Part 4: Time to Change
parts.intro: The truth comes out, and Elena decides what to do with her new life.
paragraphs: The police took Mr Grant away, and Elena gave the envelope and her photographs to the officer. That afternoon, she went to the town hall and told Mrs Carter everything. The mayor listened without saying a word. When Elena finished, she took off her glasses and sighed.
"My grandfather lost his savings in that school project," she said quietly. "For years, we thought it was just bad luck."

The news travelled fast. In a few days, everybody in town was talking about it. The council promised to check all the old records, and a judge said that the Grant family would have to give back the money. Mr Grant told the police that he had been looking for the papers for months. His father had always warned him that someone might find them.
Elena called her uncle in Canada and told him the story. He was silent for a long time. "I should have been braver," he finally said. "You did what I couldn't do. Thank you."
"You gave me the chance," said Elena. "Without the shop, I would still be sitting in that grey office."

A few weeks later, Elena finished the repair of the town hall clock. On a sunny Saturday, hundreds of people gathered in the square to hear it ring for the first time in years. Mrs Carter made a short speech, and then the big bell began to sound. Some people cried, and Mr Hale gave out free bread to everyone.

Back in the shop, Elena felt tired but happy. People kept coming in with broken watches and old family clocks, asking if she could help. She had already fixed seven that week. Her bank in Mexico had sent her an email offering her old job back with a higher salary. She read it twice and smiled.
"No, thank you," she wrote. "I've found something I like better."

She put a new sign in the window. It said, "Ruiz & Son Clocks: Repairs While You Wait." Then she laughed, because she had no son, and decided to change it later. For now, she liked it exactly as it was, and the old clocks ticked around her like friendly voices.

parts.title: Part 1: A New City
parts.intro: Lucía arrives in Liverpool to start a new job at a small radio station with a big problem.
paragraphs: Lucía Torres had been in Liverpool for exactly two hours when it started to rain. She was standing outside a tall brick building near the river, holding a suitcase in one hand and a wet map in the other. For six years she had worked as a radio assistant in Monterrey, and last month she had finally received an email with the words she had been waiting for: "We would like to offer you the job of producer at Harbour FM."

A young woman with bright green hair was running down the stairs. "You must be Lucía! I'm Priya. I present the breakfast show, and I'm also the person who makes the tea. Come on, everyone is waiting for you." On the first floor, a tall man with a grey beard stood up from behind a messy desk. This was Mr Grant, the owner of the station. Next to him, a quiet man in a woolly hat was repairing a microphone. "That's Ben, our engineer," said Priya.

Mr Grant shook her hand warmly. "We have been on air for fifty years, and we have never missed a single day," he said. Lucía smiled, but she noticed that his smile disappeared quickly. He looked tired, and there were piles of letters on his desk.

Later, while Priya was showing her the studio, Lucía asked about the letters. Priya looked at the floor. "I shouldn't tell you on your first day," she said, "but you will find out anyway. The company that owns the land wants to sell it. If we don't find twenty thousand pounds before December, they will close the station and build flats here."

Lucía sat down slowly. She had left her family and her comfortable job for a station that might not exist in three months. For a moment she wanted to take the next train home. Then she looked at the old microphone and decided to stay for at least one week.

That evening, when everyone had gone home, she went back to the office to collect her coat. There was a white envelope on the floor, just inside the door. Her name was written on it in black ink. Inside was a single sheet of paper with only one sentence: "Be careful of the man with the blue folder."

parts.title: Part 2: The Man with the Blue Folder
parts.intro: A stranger visits the station, and Lucía has an idea to save it.
paragraphs: In the morning Lucía showed the note to Priya, who read it twice and laughed nervously. "A joke, probably," she said. But at ten o'clock, a man in an expensive grey suit walked into the office carrying a blue folder, and nobody laughed any more.

"Good morning, Mr Grant," said the man. "My name is Victor Lane, from Dockside Developments." His smile was perfect, which Lucía did not like. He opened the folder and put some papers on the desk. "This is a generous offer. We will pay you for your equipment, and you can leave quietly before Christmas. It is better than losing everything."

Mr Grant did not look at the papers. "I will think about it," he said, which was his polite way of saying no. When Victor Lane left, he took the folder with him, and Lucía noticed that he looked at the ceiling twice, as if he was interested in the top floor.

"What is up there?" she asked Ben afterwards. He shrugged. "The old archive. Tapes, records, boxes. Nobody has opened it for years because the key has been lost since before I arrived." Then he added, almost to himself, "Strange that he asked about it."

By Wednesday, Lucía had stopped feeling sorry for herself. If the station needed twenty thousand pounds, she thought, then the people who loved it should help. That afternoon she walked into the studio with a notebook full of ideas.
"We should ask our listeners to tell us their memories," she said. "Every Friday we will broadcast one of them, and at the end of each show we will ask for donations."

Priya jumped up. "I love it! We can call it Voices of the Harbour!" Mr Grant said nothing for a moment. Then he took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes. "Fifty years ago," he said quietly, "we started the same way. A few people, one microphone and a lot of hope."

The first show was scheduled for Friday at six. Lucía spent two days writing scripts and calling local shops. On Thursday night she went to bed exhausted but happy. She did not know that someone had been watching the building from the street all evening.

parts.title: Part 3: Voices of the Harbour
parts.intro: The first show is a success, but a surprising phone call changes everything.
paragraphs: At five minutes to six on Friday, Lucía's hands were shaking. Through the glass she could see Priya calmly drinking tea in front of the microphone, and Mr Grant standing at the back of the studio with his arms crossed. The red light came on. "Good evening, Liverpool," said Priya. "This is Voices of the Harbour."

For the first twenty minutes, nobody called. Lucía was thinking about how to explain the failure to Mr Grant when suddenly the first telephone light began to flash. "We have a caller," Priya said happily. "Hello, you're on the air!"

It was a retired bus driver called Frank, who told a funny story about the day a seagull stole his sandwich at the docks. After that, the lights flashed constantly. People laughed, cried and promised to send money. By seven o'clock, the total had reached nine hundred pounds. "It's not twenty thousand," said Lucía, "but it's a beginning."

The last caller was an old woman with a soft, shaky voice. "My name is Mrs Doyle," she said. "I was working in the harbour office when Harbour FM started. Do you know why the station has always had that building? Because old Captain Whitlock gave it to Mr Grant and his friend Arthur. I remember it clearly. He made them sign a paper. He said that as long as there was a radio station inside, nobody could ever take the building away."

The studio went silent. When the programme finished, he sat down heavily on a chair. "I had forgotten about that paper," he said. "Arthur and I signed it in nineteen seventy-four. But after we argued, he left the station, and I never saw the document again."
"Who was Arthur?" asked Lucía.
"Arthur Lane," said Mr Grant. "He was my best friend for twenty years. Then he took a job in London and we stopped speaking." He rubbed his forehead. "I don't know if he has any family left."

Lucía and Ben looked at each other. Lane. It could be a coincidence, but she did not believe in coincidences. "Ben," she said slowly, "how difficult is it to open a locked door?" Ben took a small tool from his pocket and smiled for the first time that week.

parts.title: Part 4: The Archive
parts.intro: The team opens a locked room and discovers a message from the past.
paragraphs: The archive was at the top of a narrow staircase behind a door that nobody had noticed for years. Ben worked on the lock for ten minutes, and then it opened with a loud click. Lucía switched on her phone torch. The room was full of dust, cardboard boxes and shelves with hundreds of tapes.

"Where do we start?" asked Priya, who had followed them upstairs with a cup of tea. "The paper must be here somewhere," said Lucía. "If I had hidden something important, I would have put it in the oldest box." They worked until midnight, opening boxes and sneezing. They found interviews with football players, a recording of a storm from 1987, and a tape marked "Christmas party – do not play!", which Priya immediately put in her bag.

At one o'clock, Ben called them over. He had found a metal box under the lowest shelf. It was locked, but the key was taped to the bottom, as if somebody had wanted it to be found by a patient person. Inside there was no contract. There were only letters, tied with a green ribbon, and one cassette tape with a handwritten label: "For whoever saves the station."
"That's a bit dramatic," said Priya, but her voice was not steady. They sat on the dusty floor and Ben pressed the button.

First there was silence, then a man's voice, young and warm. "Hello, Tom," it said. "If you are listening to this, it means the station is in trouble again. I'm sorry I left. I was proud and stupid. I'm recording this in case I never have the courage to say it to your face."
Lucía looked at Mr Grant's name on the box. "Tom," she whispered. "His first name is Thomas." She stopped the tape. "This is Arthur's voice. And it isn't for us. It's for him."

Priya wiped her eyes. "We have to give it to him," she said. "But if it contains information about the paper, and Victor Lane finds out..." She did not finish the sentence. Somewhere downstairs, a door closed.
They all froze. Ben turned off the light. Then they heard slow footsteps climbing the stairs, and a thin line of yellow light appeared under the archive door.

parts.title: Part 5: Letters Never Sent
parts.intro: Mr Grant hears a voice from the past, and Lucía prepares a trip to find the missing paper.
paragraphs: The door opened slowly, and Mr Grant's grey beard appeared in the light of his torch. "I couldn't sleep, so I came to check the building," he said. "What are you doing here at this time of night?" Lucía held out the cassette. "We found this. I think you should listen to it alone." He read the label, and his hand began to shake. "I'd rather not be alone," he said quietly.

They played the tape again. Arthur's voice explained that he had regretted leaving for thirty years, but pride had always stopped him from picking up the telephone. "I kept a copy of the paper with Captain Whitlock's solicitor, Ms Okoro, in the city centre," the voice said. "If the station is ever in danger, she can help. I should have told you before. Tell the young ones to look after the old microphone. It was always lucky."

When the tape ended, nobody spoke for a long time. Mr Grant took the letters from the box and opened the first one. "These are all for me," he said. "He wrote one every Christmas and never sent a single one." He read the last date. "This one is from last year. He must have known he was ill." Then he put his face in his hands, and Priya sat next to him.
The next morning, Lucía had hardly slept, but she felt strangely hopeful. "If Ms Okoro still has the paper," she said, "they won't be able to close us."

At nine o'clock, Victor Lane arrived again, even smoother than before. "I need an answer by Monday," he said, tapping his blue folder. "My company has been very patient." Lucía watched his face carefully. There was one detail she could not forget: he had a small scar above his left eyebrow.
"Thank you, Mr Lane," said Mr Grant firmly. "You will have my answer on Monday." When the door closed, Lucía turned to him. "Do you want me to go to the city centre this afternoon?"

Mr Grant looked at her for a long moment. "You've been here for one week," he said, "and you are already more loyal than some people who worked here for years." He wrote an address on a piece of paper. "Take Ben with you."

parts.title: Part 6: Ms Okoro's Office
parts.intro: Lucía and Ben meet a lawyer, but they are one step behind.
paragraphs: Ms Okoro's office was above a shoe shop in the city centre, at the top of a narrow staircase. A secretary led Lucía and Ben into a small room full of files. Behind the desk sat a woman of about seventy, with silver hair and very sharp eyes. "Harbour FM," she said before they could introduce themselves. "I wondered when somebody would come."

Lucía explained everything quickly. Ms Okoro listened without interrupting, and then she sighed deeply. "I'm afraid you are late by eight days," she said. "Last Tuesday, a man came here with a letter of authority signed by Arthur Lane. He said he was Arthur's grandson and needed the copy of an old agreement. The signature looked correct, so I gave it to him."
"A man with a scar above his eyebrow?" asked Lucía. Ms Okoro raised her own eyebrow. "You know him." "Victor Lane," said Ben angrily. "He has been stealing our paper!"

"Please be careful with accusations," said Ms Okoro. "Arthur died last winter. If the letter was genuine, the family is allowed to take the document. If it was false, that is a serious crime." She opened a drawer and took out a thin folder. "However, I am an old-fashioned woman, and I never give away the only copy of anything. I made a photocopy before he left."

"A photocopy isn't a legal document," Ms Okoro continued. "The company will say that it is false. What you need is the original registered with the council. If I send a request today, we may receive it in ten days." "It will be tight, but it is possible."

"Then we have to stop Mr Grant from selling anything on Monday," said Lucía. "We only have three days." "Four, if you count today," said Ms Okoro dryly. She gave them the photocopy. "And, Miss Torres, if I were you, I wouldn't walk home alone."

They left through the shoe shop and stopped on the pavement. Ben pretended to read a phone message, but his eyes were moving. "Don't turn around," he whispered. "There's a grey car on the other side of the street. It was outside Harbour FM yesterday, and it has been following our bus since the river."

parts.title: Part 7: Across the River
parts.intro: A chase ends with an honest conversation.
paragraphs: "Walk normally," whispered Ben, "and when I say run, run." They joined a crowd of tourists walking towards the river. When they reached the ferry terminal, a boat was about to leave. "Now!" said Ben. They ran along the dock, jumped over a rope and landed on the deck just as the engines started.

Lucía was laughing and breathing heavily when she saw the grey car stop at the water's edge. A man got out, and even from far away she recognised the grey suit. Victor Lane stood there watching the boat leave. He did not look angry. He looked almost sad.
"When we return, he will still be there," said Lucía. "Maybe it's better to talk to him." Ben stared at her. "Are you crazy?" "Probably," she answered.

Forty minutes later, they walked down the ramp and found Victor sitting on a bench, as if he had been waiting for a bus. "I wasn't following you to hurt you," he said before they could speak. "I wanted to ask you something. Did you open the archive?"

"You took the paper from Ms Okoro," said Lucía. "You lied to her." Victor rubbed the scar above his eyebrow. "I told her the truth. Arthur Lane was my grandfather. Did he sign that letter? No. I did, using his old signature. It was wrong." He took a deep breath. "But all my life my grandfather told me that Thomas Grant had cheated him and kept the station for himself. When my company bought the land, I thought I could finally correct an injustice. I only wanted to see if his name was on that paper."
Lucía took the photocopy from her bag and gave it to Victor. "Read the names," she said. He read slowly. His face changed. "Two names," he whispered. "Arthur's and Thomas's. Equal partners."

"There is something else you should hear," said Lucía. "A tape. Your grandfather recorded it for Mr Grant. I think it will tell you what really happened." Victor looked at the river for a long time. "I'll listen to it," he said at last. "But my director, Mrs Dalton, does not care about old friendships. If she knew about this conversation, she would be furious."

parts.title: Part 8: Two Old Friends
parts.intro: Victor listens to the tape, and the team prepares a surprising plan.
paragraphs: On Sunday evening the studio was quiet. Victor Lane was sitting in the corner of the room with his coat still on. Mr Grant came in last. He stopped when he saw the young man, and for a moment the two of them looked at each other without speaking.

"You have Arthur's eyes," said Mr Grant at last. Victor stood up awkwardly. "I owe you an apology, sir. I have said terrible things about you, and I have done something I'm not proud of." He told the whole story, and Mr Grant listened without interrupting.

Then Lucía pressed the button. Arthur's voice filled the room. "I was proud and stupid," it said. Victor covered his mouth. When the tape finished, he whispered, "He never told me that. He always said that you had betrayed him."

"We both said things that we didn't mean," said Mr Grant slowly. "He wanted to move to London. I told him that he would be a traitor if he left. If I had known that thirty years of silence would follow, I would have swallowed those words." He put his hand on Victor's shoulder. "You aren't responsible for our mistakes, young man."

"Then let me help," said Victor. "Mrs Dalton is coming here tomorrow at noon with two lawyers. She knows that you are going to refuse, so she wants to bring the contract herself. If you don't sign, she says she will start the process to close the station immediately."
"But Ms Okoro's request won't arrive for another week," said Lucía, "so we have nothing to show her." Suddenly she stopped. "Unless we show everybody else."

She explained her idea quickly. At noon, Harbour FM would broadcast a special programme, live from the street outside the building. They would tell the story of the station and invite everybody to come and listen. "If a hundred people are standing there when Mrs Dalton arrives," she said, "it will be much harder for her to close us quietly."

Mr Grant stared at the old microphone for a long time. Then he smiled, really smiled. "Fifty years ago, we started with nothing," he said. "I suppose we can finish the way we began, with a voice and a lot of people who care."

parts.title: Part 9: Noon on the Pavement
parts.intro: A crowd, a broadcast and a surprise delivery change the day.
paragraphs: By eleven forty-five on Monday, Lucía had given up counting the people in the street. There were at least two hundred, and more were arriving every minute. Frank the bus driver was there, and Mrs Doyle was sitting on a folding chair next to the speakers.

At twelve o'clock exactly, Priya's voice came out of every speaker. "Good afternoon, Liverpool. This is Harbour FM, and today we are broadcasting from the pavement. Today, we want to tell you why it matters." The crowd went quiet.

At twelve-ten, a black car stopped at the end of the street. A tall woman stepped out, followed by two men with briefcases. She stopped when she saw the crowd. Victor, standing beside Mr Grant, whispered, "That's Mrs Dalton."

She walked slowly through the people, who moved aside without saying a word. "Mr Grant," she said coldly, "I see that you have organised a small party. It's very touching. However, feelings don't change a contract. If you don't sign, we will begin the legal process this afternoon."

Mr Grant held the microphone in both hands. "Mrs Dalton," he said, and his voice came out of the speakers, "this station belongs to everyone who has ever listened to it. I'm not selling it." A loud cheer rose from the street. Mrs Dalton did not smile. "Then you leave me no choice," she said to her lawyers. "Prepare the documents."

"Wait," said Victor. Everybody turned to look at him. He walked forward, pale but steady. "I work for your company, Mrs Dalton, and I made a serious mistake. I used a false signature to take a paper from a lawyer's office. I'm going to tell the whole truth."
"You are finished at Dockside," she said quietly. "I know," said Victor, "but I would rather be honest than rich."

At that moment, a motorbike appeared at the end of the street and stopped beside the crowd. The rider pushed through the people, holding a large brown envelope above his head. "Delivery for Harbour FM," he shouted. "From the council registry. The lady in the office said it was urgent."
