parts.title: Part 10: A Voice for the Harbour
parts.intro: The story reaches its end, and Lucía makes an important decision.
paragraphs: Mr Grant opened the envelope with shaking fingers. Inside there was a thick document with a red stamp and two signatures at the bottom: Thomas Grant and Arthur Lane. One of Mrs Dalton's lawyers took it, read it quietly for two minutes and whispered something in Mrs Dalton's ear. "The land can only be used for a radio station," he said finally. "If it stops being one, it returns to the community. We have been wrong from the start."

Mrs Dalton looked at the crowd. "My company will not be wasting any more time here," she said at last. She turned and walked back to her black car without looking at anyone. The street exploded in cheering, and Priya shouted, "We did it, Liverpool!"

The rest of the autumn passed like a happy dream. Listeners continued to send donations, and by the end of November, the station had collected almost twenty-seven thousand pounds. They used it to repair the roof and buy new equipment. Victor Lane lost his job, but he did not seem to mind. Every Saturday he came to Harbour FM as a volunteer, bringing sandwiches and bad jokes.

In December, Mr Grant called everyone into the studio. "I am seventy-four years old," he said, "and I would like to read Arthur's letters. Harbour FM needs a new manager." He took the old microphone from its stand and placed it in Lucía's hands. "Arthur said it was lucky. I think it was waiting for you."

Lucía could not speak. Priya cried, Victor clapped, and Ben stared at the floor. "Ben," she asked suddenly, "was it you who wrote that note on my first night? The one about the blue folder?" He blushed. "I saw Victor looking at the building, and I got nervous. I didn't know how to tell you in person."

That evening, Lucía telephoned her mother in Monterrey. "Mamá," she said, "I think I'm going to stay here for a while." Her mother was quiet for a moment. "Are you happy, mija?" "Yes," answered Lucía, looking out of the office window at the river and the new sign above the door. Somebody had finally repaired the missing letter. It said, in bright gold paint: HARBOUR FM. "I'm very happy."

parts.title: Working from Home: Good and Bad
parts.intro: This article looks at the advantages and problems of working from home.
paragraphs: More and more people work from home today. Before 2020, only a small number of employees did this, but now millions of people around the world have a desk in their bedroom or kitchen. For many workers, this change has brought clear advantages.

The biggest benefit is time. When you work from home, you don't have to travel to an office every day. A person who used to spend two hours on the train can now use that time to sleep a little longer, exercise or have breakfast with the family. Workers also save money, because they spend less on transport, lunches and work clothes. Many say they are more productive at home, since there are fewer interruptions from colleagues.

However, working from home is not perfect. Some people feel lonely because they rarely see other human beings during the day. Others find it hard to separate work from private life. If your laptop is always on the kitchen table, it is tempting to answer one more email at ten o'clock at night. In addition, not everybody has a quiet room, and it is difficult to concentrate when children are playing or neighbours are making noise.

Experts give several tips to make it easier. First, create a special place for work, even if it is only a corner of a room. Second, keep a regular schedule: start and finish at the same time every day. Third, take short breaks to walk or stretch, and try to talk to your colleagues by video call instead of only writing messages. Finally, leave the house at least once a day, for example to buy bread or go for a walk. This simple habit helps you feel that the day has a beginning and an end.

Many companies now offer a mix of both systems. Employees go to the office two or three days a week and stay at home the rest of the time. This "hybrid" model seems to give people the best of both worlds: contact with colleagues and the freedom of home.

parts.title: Learning a Language as an Adult
parts.intro: This article gives advice and facts about learning a new language when you are not a child.
paragraphs: Many adults believe that learning a new language is impossible after a certain age. They think that only children can do it well. In fact, this is a myth. Researchers have found that adults can learn languages very successfully, and in some ways they even learn faster than children.

Adults have several advantages. They already know how to learn, and they can understand grammar rules when someone explains them. They also have clear reasons for studying, such as a better job, a trip abroad or a partner who speaks another language. This motivation is very powerful. Children, on the other hand, usually learn a language simply because they live in a place where everybody speaks it.

It is true, however, that adults often have problems with pronunciation. Children who start very young can sometimes sound like native speakers, while adults usually keep a slight accent. This is not a big problem. Most people can understand an accent without difficulty, and nobody needs a perfect accent to communicate well.

What is the best way to learn? Experts say that regular practice is more important than long lessons. Studying for twenty minutes every day is better than studying for three hours once a week. It also helps to use the language in real situations. You can listen to songs, watch films with subtitles, read short news articles or chat with someone online. Don't be afraid of making mistakes. Mistakes are a natural part of the process, and every time you correct one, you learn something new.

Another useful tip is to learn words in groups, not alone. For example, instead of memorising the single word "decision", learn the phrase "make a decision". In this way, you remember how the word is normally used. Writing a small diary in the new language is also a good habit, because it forces you to think about vocabulary and grammar.

Finally, be patient. Progress is sometimes slow, and there are days when you feel that you are not improving at all. But if you keep going, you will look back after a few months and be surprised by how much you can already understand and say.

parts.title: Social Media in Our Lives
parts.intro: This article explains how social media has changed the way we communicate.
paragraphs: Twenty years ago, social media did not exist in the form we know today. Now billions of people use it every day to share photos, send messages and read the news. For many of us, checking our phone is the first thing we do in the morning and the last thing we do at night.

Social media has some clear benefits. It helps friends and families stay in touch, even when they live in different countries. It allows small businesses to find customers without spending a lot of money on advertising. It also gives a voice to ordinary people, who can now share their ideas and organise events or charity campaigns very quickly. During difficult times, such as storms or other emergencies, these platforms can spread important information in minutes.

On the other hand, there are some real concerns. One of them is time. Many people say they spend much longer online than they planned, moving from one video to another without noticing the hours pass. Another problem is that people usually show only the best moments of their lives. When you see friends on holiday, at parties or wearing new clothes, you can start to feel that your own life is boring. Studies suggest that this comparison can make some people, especially teenagers, feel unhappy or less confident.

There is also the question of privacy. Every photo, comment and "like" gives companies information about you, and they use it to show advertisements that match your interests. In addition, false news can travel very fast, because people often share a post before checking if it is true.

So how can we use social media in a healthy way? Experts recommend a few simple rules. Decide how much time you want to spend online and use the settings on your phone to control it. Turn off notifications, so your phone doesn't interrupt you all the time. Follow accounts that teach you something or make you smile, and stop following those that make you feel bad. Before you share a surprising story, check where it comes from. And remember that meeting a friend face to face is still one of the best ways to enjoy life.
Social media is only a tool. Like any tool, it can be useful or harmful, depending on how we use it.

parts.title: Cities and Bicycles
parts.intro: This article explains why many cities want more people to ride bicycles.
paragraphs: In many big cities, traffic is a daily problem. Cars move slowly, the air is dirty, and finding a parking space can take half an hour. For this reason, more and more city governments are asking people to use bicycles for short journeys.

Cycling has many advantages. First, it is cheap. A bicycle costs much less than a car, and you don't need to pay for petrol or parking. Second, it is good for your health. Riding for thirty minutes a day helps your heart, strengthens your legs and can reduce stress. Third, it is good for the environment, because a bicycle produces no pollution. If a few thousand people leave their cars at home, the air in a city becomes cleaner and the streets become quieter.

Some cities are already famous for cycling. In Amsterdam and Copenhagen, about half of all journeys to work or school are made by bike. These cities didn't become bicycle-friendly by accident. They built thousands of kilometres of separate bike lanes, so cyclists don't have to share the road with fast cars. They also put traffic lights for bicycles and created safe parking areas near train stations.

In other places, however, cycling can be dangerous. Where there are no bike lanes, riders have to move between buses and trucks, and many people feel frightened. Bad weather is another problem. Few people want to cycle in heavy rain or in very hot summers. In addition, some jobs are too far from home to reach by bike, or workers need to arrive in clean clothes.

Cities are trying different solutions. Some of them offer bicycles to rent for a small price, so visitors and residents can pick one up in one place and leave it in another. Others give money to people who buy electric bikes, which are easier to use on hills and over long distances. Many companies now provide showers and secure parking for employees who cycle to work.

Of course, bicycles will not solve every problem. People will still need buses, trains and sometimes cars. But with good planning, a city can give its inhabitants a real choice, and the results are usually positive for everybody, including drivers, who find the roads less crowded.

parts.title: Fast Food or Home Cooking?
parts.intro: This article compares fast food with meals cooked at home.
paragraphs: After a long day at work, many people don't feel like cooking. It is much easier to stop at a restaurant, order a burger and be home in twenty minutes. Fast food is cheap, quick and tasty, which explains why millions of people eat it every week. But is it really the best choice?

The main advantage of fast food is convenience. You don't need to plan, shop, cook or wash dishes. For people who work long hours or live alone, this can be a big help. Fast food restaurants are also everywhere, and the prices are often lower than those of other places.

The problem is what is inside the food. A typical fast food meal contains a lot of salt, sugar and fat. If you eat it very often, you can gain weight and increase your risk of heart problems. Many dishes also have few vegetables, so your body doesn't get all the vitamins it needs. In addition, the portions are often so big that people eat more than they intended.

Cooking at home has several benefits. You decide exactly what goes into your meal, so it is easy to use fresh ingredients and less salt. Home cooking is usually cheaper too, especially if you plan your week and buy only what you need. A pot of soup or rice and beans can feed a family for two days. And cooking can be a pleasant activity: you can listen to music, talk to your children or enjoy the smell of the kitchen.

Of course, home cooking takes time and energy, and not everybody enjoys it. The good news is that you don't have to choose one or the other. Experts say that a balanced diet allows some fast food from time to time. The important thing is that it should be the exception, not the rule.

If you are very busy, there are some simple tricks. Cook a large amount on Sunday and keep portions in the fridge for the week. Prepare easy recipes with only five or six ingredients. Keep healthy snacks, such as fruit or nuts, so you don't buy chips or sweets when you are hungry. Even small changes, like cooking dinner three times a week instead of one, can make a real difference to your health and your wallet.

parts.title: The Power of Volunteering
parts.intro: This article explains what volunteers do and why volunteering is good for everyone.
paragraphs: A volunteer is a person who gives their time to help others without receiving money. Around the world, millions of people volunteer every year. They serve food in shelters, clean parks and beaches, teach children to read, visit elderly people or help animals that have no home. Without volunteers, many charities simply could not exist.

The most obvious benefit of volunteering is the help it gives to other people. A few hours of your time can make a real difference. For example, a retired teacher who helps students with their homework once a week can improve their marks and their confidence. A group of neighbours who clean a river can protect fish and birds for many years.

However, volunteers also receive a lot in return. Studies show that people who help others often feel happier and less stressed. Meeting new people is another advantage, because volunteers usually work in teams and make friends who share their interests. Volunteering is also a good way to learn new skills. A young person who helps to organise an event can practise planning, speaking in public and solving problems, and these abilities can be very useful when looking for a job. Many employers say they like candidates who have done volunteer work.

If you want to start, the first step is to think about what you enjoy. Do you like working with children, with animals or outdoors? Do you prefer to help for one afternoon or every week? Many organisations have websites where you can search for opportunities near your home. You can also ask at your local library, school or community centre.

Some people worry that they don't have enough time. The good news is that even small amounts of time are useful. Some volunteers help only a couple of hours a month. Others volunteer from home, for example by translating documents, answering questions online or making phone calls to people who live alone.

It is important to choose carefully and to be honest about how much time you can give. A charity needs people it can depend on, so don't promise more than you can do. But once you find the right activity, you will probably discover that you receive more than you give. Many volunteers say it is one of the most satisfying experiences of their lives.

parts.title: How to Save Money
parts.intro: This article gives practical advice for people who want to save money each month.
paragraphs: Many people finish the month with an empty bank account and wonder where all their money went. Saving money is not only for rich people. With a little planning, almost anybody can put some money aside. The key is to change small habits, not to live a sad and boring life.

The first step is to understand your spending. For one month, write down everything you buy, from rent and bills to a cup of coffee on the way to work. Many people are surprised to see how much they spend on small things. A daily coffee that costs three dollars adds up to almost ninety dollars in a month. Once you know where your money goes, it is easier to decide what is really necessary.

The second step is to make a budget. A popular rule is to divide your income into three parts: about half for essential things such as food and housing, about thirty per cent for things you want, and about twenty per cent for savings. These numbers are not exact, and you can change them according to your situation. What matters is that you decide in advance, instead of spending first and hoping something is left.

Another useful idea is to pay yourself first. As soon as you receive your salary, move a fixed amount to a separate savings account. If you don't see the money in your daily account, you are less likely to spend it. Many banks offer automatic transfers, so you don't even have to think about it.

There are also many ways to reduce everyday costs. Cook at home more often, take your lunch to work and compare prices before buying something expensive. Turning off lights, using less water and cancelling subscriptions you never use can reduce your monthly bills. Buying second-hand clothes or furniture is another way to save, and it is often good for the environment.

Finally, set a goal. It is much easier to save when you know what you are saving for, such as an emergency fund, a trip or a new computer. Put a picture of your goal where you can see it every day. Be patient: saving is like exercise, and the results appear slowly. But after a year, you may find that you have a comfortable amount of money and, even better, a healthy habit for life.

parts.title: Travelling on a Budget
parts.intro: This article shares simple ideas for travelling without spending too much money.
paragraphs: Many people think that travelling is only for those who have a lot of money. In reality, it is possible to visit interesting places on a small budget if you plan carefully and are ready to be flexible. Here are some ideas that thousands of travellers use.

The biggest cost is usually the transport, so start there. Flight prices change every day, and they are often lower on Tuesdays and Wednesdays than at weekends. If you can choose your dates, compare several days and use websites that show the cheapest options. Travelling in the low season, when fewer tourists visit a place, can save you a lot of money, and the destination is usually less crowded as well. For short distances, buses and trains are often cheaper than planes, and the journey lets you see the countryside.

Accommodation is the second big cost. A hotel is not the only choice. You can stay in a hostel, where you share a room with other travellers, or rent a private room in someone's home. Many hostels have a kitchen, which allows you to cook your own meals. Some people also exchange houses with families in other countries, so nobody pays for a place to sleep.

Food can also take a large part of your money. Restaurants near famous monuments are usually expensive. Instead, walk a few streets away and look for places where local people eat. Markets are another excellent option: you can try fresh fruit and typical dishes for a very low price. Carry a bottle of water and fill it when you can, instead of buying drinks all day.

Finally, remember that many of the best experiences cost little or nothing. Many cities offer free walking tours, and museums often have a free day each month. Parks, beaches and old neighbourhoods are interesting places to explore, and walking is a great way to discover a city.

Travelling cheaply does require some compromises. You may have to carry your own bag, wake up early for a cheap bus or sleep in a small room. But many people discover that these small difficulties make the trip more memorable. You meet more local people, you learn how to solve problems, and you come home with good stories and money still in your pocket.

parts.title: Understanding Stress
parts.intro: This article explains what stress is and gives simple ways to control it.
paragraphs: Almost everybody feels stress at some point. You may feel it before an exam, when you have too much work or when you are worried about money. A little stress can actually be useful. It makes your heart beat faster and gives you energy to react quickly. This system helped our ancestors to escape from danger. The problem begins when stress continues for weeks or months.

Long-term stress affects both the body and the mind. Common physical signs include headaches, tiredness, stomach problems and difficulty sleeping. People can also feel nervous, angry or sad, and find it hard to concentrate. Some people eat too much or too little, or stop doing activities they used to enjoy. If these symptoms last a long time, it is wise to talk to a doctor.

What causes stress? The reasons are different for each person, but common ones include work pressure, money problems, family conflicts and big changes such as moving house. Modern life adds more causes: we receive messages all day and often feel that we must always be available.

Fortunately, there are many simple ways to control stress. Exercise is one of the best. A thirty-minute walk can improve your mood and help you relax, because physical activity produces chemicals that make you feel better. Sleep is also essential. Most adults need seven or eight hours a night, and tired people find problems harder to solve.

Some techniques take only a few minutes. Deep breathing, for instance, slows the heart and calms the mind: breathe in slowly for four seconds, hold for a moment and breathe out for six seconds. Writing down your worries can also help, because it moves them from your head to the paper and makes them easier to organise. Planning your day and saying no to extra tasks can reduce pressure, too.

Talking is just as important. Spending time with friends or family, or telling someone how you feel, often makes a problem seem smaller. Hobbies such as music, gardening or cooking give your mind a break from daily worries.
Remember that stress is a normal part of life, and nobody can remove it completely. The aim is not to have no stress at all, but to know how to manage it so that it doesn't control you.

parts.title: Pets in the City
parts.intro: This article discusses the joys and challenges of having a pet in a city.
paragraphs: More people than ever live in cities, and a large number of them share their homes with a pet. Dogs, cats, rabbits, birds and fish all live in flats and small houses. For many owners, an animal is a member of the family. But life in a city can be difficult for animals, and it is important to think carefully before getting one.

The benefits of having a pet are clear. Animals offer company, especially for people who live alone. Studies suggest that stroking a cat or a dog can lower stress, and dog owners often exercise more because they take their pets out every day. Pets can also help children to learn about responsibility, since they have to feed the animal and keep it clean.

However, a city flat is not the same as a house with a garden. Dogs need regular walks, space to run and time to play. A big dog left alone for ten hours in a small flat can become bored and unhappy, and may bark or damage furniture. Cats are more independent, but they still need attention, and indoor cats need toys and places to climb. Noise is another point: if a pet barks or cries all day, neighbours may complain.
Money matters too. Owning an animal means paying for food, vaccinations, medicine and visits to the vet, and these costs can be high, especially if the animal gets ill.

Before you choose a pet, ask yourself some honest questions. How many hours will I be at home? Do I have the time and energy to give daily attention? Can I afford the costs for ten or fifteen years? Is my home big enough for this type of animal? If you decide that a dog is not right for you, there are smaller options, such as a cat, a rabbit or fish.
If you do want a dog or a cat, consider adopting one from a shelter. Thousands of healthy animals wait there for a family, and adoption usually costs less than buying a puppy from a shop.
A pet can bring great happiness to a city home, but it is a long-term responsibility. When owners are ready for it, both the person and the animal can live very happy lives together.

parts.title: Part 1: An Email to My Supervisor
parts.intro: Marco writes to his supervisor to ask for a different work schedule while he studies.
paragraphs: Subject: Request to change my work schedule next month
Dear Ms Alvarez,

I hope you are well. I am writing to ask if I can change my work hours for the month of March. I know that the team is very busy at the moment because of the new customer system, so I want to explain my situation clearly and offer some solutions.

From the first of March, I will start an evening course in project management. The classes are on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 6:00 to 8:30 p.m., and the school is across the city. If I leave the office at 5:30 p.m. as usual, I will probably arrive late. For this reason, I would like to start work at 7:30 a.m. on those two days and finish at 4:00 p.m. instead. On the other three days, my schedule would stay exactly the same.

I have thought about how this change could affect the team. The customer calls are busiest between 10:00 a.m. and 2:00 p.m., so I would be at my desk during that time. I would also finish my daily report before I leave, so Daniel would have all the information he needs in the afternoon. If there is an urgent problem after 4:00 p.m., I will answer my phone as long as I am not in class.

I believe this course will help me in my job. I would learn how to plan projects better, and I could use these skills when we start the new website next summer. Of course, I would be happy to share what I learn with the rest of the team.
Could we talk about this on Monday? I am free all morning, and I can bring a written plan with the exact hours. If you think another arrangement would work better, I am open to suggestions.
Thank you very much for your time and for considering my request.
Kind regards,
Marco Silva, Customer Support

parts.title: Part 2: Job Advert: Café Assistant
parts.intro: A local café is looking for a new team member, and the advert lists what the job needs.
paragraphs: Join Our Team at The Green Cup Café

The Green Cup is a friendly neighbourhood café in the centre of Riverton. We serve fresh coffee, homemade cakes and light lunches to about two hundred customers every day. Because we are growing, we are looking for a full-time café assistant to join our small team.
About the job

You will welcome customers, take orders and prepare hot and cold drinks. You will also help to keep the café clean and tidy, and sometimes you will serve food at the tables. After a few months, you may learn to use our cash register and help with ordering supplies. You will work five days a week, including one weekend day. Your hours will be from 7:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m., with a thirty-minute break.
What we need

You do not need a lot of experience, but you must be reliable and arrive on time every day. It is important that you enjoy talking to people and can stay calm when the café is crowded. You should speak good English, and a second language is an advantage because many tourists visit us in the summer. You must be at least eighteen years old. If you have a food hygiene certificate, that is great, but we can train you if you do not.
What we offer

We pay 12 dollars an hour, and you will receive extra pay for working on public holidays. You will get twenty days of paid holiday each year and a free lunch on every shift. We also give all staff a discount on coffee and cakes to take home. Our manager, Helen, has worked here for ten years and loves to teach new people.
How to apply

Please send your CV and a short message about yourself to jobs@greencup.example by 30 April. Tell us why you would like to work with us and which days you are available for an interview. We will contact the best candidates within one week. Unfortunately, we cannot reply to everyone, so if you do not hear from us by 10 May, please try again next time.

parts.title: Part 3: Our Company Policy on Working from Home
parts.intro: A company explains its rules for staff who work from home.
paragraphs: Working from Home Policy
Last updated: 1 September

At Brightline Software, we believe that people do their best work when they have some freedom. For this reason, most employees can work from home for part of the week. This policy explains who can work remotely, what we expect from you, and what support the company provides.
Who can work from home?

All full-time employees who have finished their first three months can ask to work from home. New employees must be in the office during their first three months so that they can meet the team and learn how we work. Some jobs, such as reception and building maintenance, cannot be done from home, so these staff are not included in this policy.
How many days?

You may work from home for up to three days a week. Every team must decide together which two days everyone will be in the office, so that meetings and group work are easy to plan. Your manager must approve your plan, and it can be changed if the team's needs change.
What we expect

When you work from home, you should be available during normal office hours, from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. You must answer messages quickly and join all video meetings with your camera on, unless your manager says it is not necessary. Please choose a quiet place with a good internet connection. If you have a technical problem, tell your manager and the support team as soon as possible.
What we provide

The company will give you a laptop and a headset. We will also pay 30 dollars a month towards your internet costs. If you need a better chair or desk, you can ask for help, but you must get approval before you buy anything. Remember that company equipment must not be used by other people, including family members.
Security

Never save company documents on your personal computer, and do not work in public places such as cafés unless you use the company's secure connection. Always lock your screen when you leave your desk.
Questions about this policy should be sent to the Human Resources team.

parts.title: Part 4: A Product Review: The Quiet Blender
parts.intro: A customer shares an honest opinion about a kitchen blender after using it for two months.
paragraphs: Review: Good Machine, but Not Perfect
Rating: 4 out of 5 stars

I bought the QuietMix blender two months ago, and I have used it almost every morning since then. My old blender was so loud that it woke up my neighbours, so the name of this one caught my attention. I wanted to write this review because I think other buyers should know both the good and the bad points.

First, the good news. The blender really is quieter than most machines I have tried. It still makes some noise, of course, but I can make a smoothie at six in the morning and my family keeps sleeping. It is also very easy to clean. You just add warm water and a little soap, press one button, and thirty seconds later the jar is ready to rinse. The jar is made of strong glass, not plastic, so it does not keep the smell of garlic or onions.

The machine is powerful enough for most things. It crushes ice without any trouble, and it makes soft soups and sauces in about one minute. However, I found that it has problems with very hard foods. When I tried to blend frozen mango and nuts together, it stopped, and I had to take half of the food out. This does not happen often, but it is annoying when you are in a hurry.

Another small problem is the size. The blender is quite tall, so it does not fit under my kitchen cupboard. I keep it on the counter, which takes up space. Also, the cable is rather short, so you need a socket close to where you work.

The price was 79 dollars, which I think is fair. There are cheaper blenders, but they are usually much louder and break after a year. The company also gives a three-year guarantee, and when I called with a question, the customer service was polite and helpful.

Overall, I would recommend this blender to anyone who wants a quiet and simple machine for daily smoothies and soups. If you often blend hard or frozen food in large amounts, you may need something stronger. I gave it four stars instead of five because of the size and the problem with hard foods.

parts.title: Part 5: A Cover Letter
parts.intro: Nadia applies for a job at a bookshop and explains why she is a good choice.
paragraphs: Dear Mr Thompson,

I am writing to apply for the position of sales assistant at Page One Books, which I saw advertised on your website last week. I have loved reading since I was a child, and I would be very happy to work in a place where I can share that passion with customers.

At the moment, I work part-time at a stationery shop in the city centre, where I have been for almost two years. My daily tasks include serving customers, organising the shelves and checking new deliveries. I also manage the shop's social media page. Last year, I started posting short videos about our products, and the number of followers grew from 300 to more than 2,000. My manager was so pleased that she asked me to train two new colleagues.

I believe that I have the skills you are looking for. I am friendly and patient, and I enjoy helping people find exactly what they need. Customers often tell me that I give good advice, and several of them now ask for me when they visit. I am also organised, and I can work under pressure. For example, during the busy weeks before the school year, I often served more than a hundred customers a day without making mistakes.

In addition, I speak English and Spanish, and I am learning French. I know that many visitors to your area do not speak the local language, so this could be useful. I have also studied literature at college for two years, which means that I know a lot about different kinds of books.

The reason I am interested in Page One Books is that you organise events for readers, such as author talks and book clubs. I would love to help with these activities, and I have some ideas for a reading night for teenagers.

I have attached my CV, and I would be happy to come in for an interview at any time that suits you. I am available to start from the first of June, and I only need to give two weeks' notice to my present employer.
Thank you for reading my application. I look forward to hearing from you.
Yours sincerely,
Nadia Ortiz

parts.title: Part 6: Minutes of a Team Meeting
parts.intro: A short record of what a team discussed and decided in a meeting.
paragraphs: Minutes of the Weekly Team Meeting
Date: Wednesday, 12 June. Time: 10:00 to 10:45 a.m. Place: Meeting Room 2.
Present: Laura (chair), Tom, Priya, Carlos, Sunita. Absent: Greg (on holiday).
1. Minutes of the last meeting

Laura asked if everyone had read the minutes of the previous meeting. Tom said that one date was wrong: the training day is on 20 June, not 21 June. Laura agreed to correct it. After that, the minutes were accepted.
2. Customer survey

Priya reported that 180 customers had answered the survey so far. Most of them are happy with the service, but about a third said that they waited too long on the phone. The team agreed that this is the biggest problem at the moment. Carlos suggested adding a new phone line during the busiest hours, from 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. Laura said that this would cost money and that she would ask the director if it was possible. Priya will send the full results to everyone by Friday.
3. New office equipment

Sunita explained that the printers on the second floor are very old and often break. She showed two prices for new ones. The cheaper machine costs 400 dollars, but it is slower and uses more paper. The team voted, and four people chose the more expensive one, which costs 650 dollars. Sunita will place the order next week.
4. Summer holidays

Laura reminded everyone to put their holiday dates in the shared calendar before the end of the month. No more than two people can be away at the same time. Tom asked if he could take his holiday in two parts, and Laura said that this was not a problem.
5. Any other business
Carlos said that the kitchen needs a new coffee machine. Everyone laughed, and it was agreed to discuss this next time.
The meeting ended at 10:45 a.m. The next meeting will be on Wednesday, 19 June, at the same time.
Written by Priya.

parts.title: Part 7: A Guide for New Students
parts.intro: A student advisor gives practical advice to people who are starting at a new college.
paragraphs: Welcome to Hillside College! A Short Guide for New Students
Starting at a new college is exciting, but it can also feel a little stressful. This guide will help you to feel comfortable during your first few weeks.
Getting around

The campus is bigger than it looks, so it is easy to get lost on the first day. Pick up a free map at the main entrance, and download the college app, which shows the way to every classroom. If you cannot find your room, ask any student in a green jacket. They are volunteers, and they will be glad to help you.
Your timetable

You will receive your timetable by email one week before classes begin. Check it carefully, because some classes are in different buildings and you may need ten minutes to walk between them. If two classes are at the same time, contact the student office immediately. Do not wait until the end of the month.
Making friends

Many students are nervous about meeting new people. The best way to start is to join a club. We have more than forty, from football and chess to photography and cooking. On Friday of the first week, there is a Clubs Fair in the main hall, where you can try different activities. You do not have to be an expert, and nobody will mind if you are a beginner.
Managing your time

At college, you will have fewer hours in the classroom than at school, but you will need to study much more on your own. Many students make the mistake of leaving their work until the last minute. We suggest that you write down every deadline in a calendar and divide big tasks into small steps. The library is open until midnight, and it has quiet rooms where you can work alone or in a group.
Getting help

Everyone needs help sometimes, and there is no reason to feel embarrassed. Teachers have office hours every week when you can ask questions. The writing centre can check your essays, and the counselling service offers free, private conversations if you feel worried or lonely. All of these services are in the Student Centre, next to the cafeteria.
We hope you enjoy your time here. Good luck, and remember that every student was new once!

paragraphs: Important Notice: Changes to Bus Services from 3 March

Riverton Transport would like to inform all passengers that some bus routes will change for three months, from Monday 3 March until Friday 30 May. The changes are necessary because the city is repairing the main bridge over the river. We are sorry for any problems this may cause, and we thank you for your patience.
Route 12 (Central Station to Hospital)

Buses will not cross the main bridge. Instead, they will use the North Road Bridge, which is about two kilometres further away. The journey will take approximately ten minutes longer than usual. The stop at Market Square will be closed, and passengers should use the temporary stop in Park Street, only a two-minute walk away.
Route 25 (University to Airport)

This route will not run on weekends during the repairs. On weekdays, buses will leave every thirty minutes instead of every twenty. If you need to travel to the airport on a Saturday or Sunday, please take Route 40 from the Central Station. This service will continue as normal.
Route 7 (Old Town Circle)

There are no changes to this route. However, because many people will choose it as an alternative, it may be very busy at 8:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. We suggest that you leave a little earlier if you can.
Tickets and refunds

All tickets and monthly passes can still be used on every route. Passengers who usually travel across the main bridge may ask for a refund of one week's fare if they decide not to use the bus during this period. Please bring your pass to the ticket office in Central Station before the end of March.
More information

Maps showing the new routes will be displayed at every bus stop from Monday 24 February. You can also find them on our website or by calling our information line, which is open from 7:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. every day. Drivers have been told about the changes and will be happy to answer your questions.
We apologise again for the inconvenience.

parts.title: Part 9: Interview with a Young Entrepreneur
parts.intro: A magazine talks to a woman who started a small business selling handmade bags.
paragraphs: From Kitchen Table to Shop: Lucia Ramos Tells Her Story
Three years ago, Lucia Ramos was working in an office and sewing bags in her free time. Today she owns a company with six employees. We met her in her workshop to ask how it all started.
Interviewer: When did you decide to start a business?

Lucia: It was not a big decision. I made a bag for my sister's birthday, and her friends kept asking where they could buy one. After I sold ten bags in a month, I realised that people really liked them. A year later, I left my job.
Interviewer: Was that frightening?

Lucia: Very! I had some savings, but I did not have a plan. In the first six months, I made almost no money, and I nearly gave up. My mother told me to be patient and to try selling online. That was good advice, because on the internet I could reach people from other cities.
Interviewer: What was the most difficult part?

Lucia: Learning to manage money. I loved making bags, but I did not know how to calculate prices. For months I charged too little, so I worked a lot and earned nothing. A friend who is an accountant taught me to include the cost of my time. It changed everything.
Interviewer: What have you learned?

Lucia: First, listen to your customers. They often have better ideas than you do. For example, many people asked for smaller bags, and these are now our best sellers. Second, start small. You do not need an expensive shop or a lot of equipment. I began with one old sewing machine. And third, do not be afraid of mistakes. I have made many, and each one taught me something.
Interviewer: What are your plans for the future?

Lucia: We are going to open a small shop next spring, and I would like to start using recycled materials for all our products. I also want to teach a sewing class for young people, because I think it is important to share what you know.
Interviewer: Any final advice?
Lucia: If you have an idea, test it. Sell one product to one person. If they like it, you have a start.

parts.title: Part 10: Home Safety Tips
parts.intro: A short list of advice that helps families avoid common accidents at home.
paragraphs: Ten Minutes to a Safer Home
Most accidents happen at home, not on the road or at work. The good news is that many of them are easy to prevent. Here are some simple tips that you can follow this weekend.
In the kitchen

Never leave a pan on the stove when you are not watching it. Oil can catch fire very quickly. If this happens, do not use water. Turn off the heat and cover the pan with a lid. Keep sharp knives in a drawer or a block, and turn the handles of pans away from the edge of the stove so that children cannot pull them down.
Electricity

Check your cables regularly. If you see one that is old, hot or broken, replace it. Do not connect too many machines to the same socket, because this can cause a fire. Also, keep electrical things away from water, and never touch a switch with wet hands.
Smoke alarms

Every home should have at least one smoke alarm on each floor. Test them once a month by pressing the button, and change the batteries every year. A good way to remember is to do it on your birthday. If the alarm sounds, leave the house immediately and call the emergency number from outside.
Stairs and floors

Falls are very common, especially for older people and young children. Make sure that there is good light on the stairs, and do not leave shoes or toys on the steps. Use a non-slip mat in the bathroom, and clean up spilled water as soon as you see it. If you have a small child, put a gate at the top and bottom of the stairs.
Medicines and cleaning products

Keep all medicines and cleaning products in a high cupboard, out of reach of children. Always read the label before you use something, and never mix different cleaning products, because this can produce dangerous gases. Keep chemicals in their original bottles, so you always know what is inside.
Be prepared

Write the numbers of the police, fire service and ambulance on a card and put it near the telephone. Keep a small first-aid box in a place that everyone knows. Finally, talk to your family about what to do in an emergency. A plan that everyone understands can save lives.

parts.title: Part 1: The Locked Room
parts.intro: A young engineer starts her first week at a small company that seems almost too successful.
paragraphs: Nina Torres had been told that Veridan was the most exciting start-up in the city, and on her first morning she could see why. The office was bright and noisy, and every screen showed the same graph: a line climbing steadily upwards. Veridan sold software that predicted what customers would buy next, and its predictions were so accurate that larger companies were queuing up to sign contracts.

"Don't be nervous," said Daniel Reyes, the senior engineer who had been assigned to show her around. He was tall, relaxed and always smiling. "By Friday you'll feel as if you've worked here for years."

Nina wasn't so sure. She had left a secure job at a bank to join Veridan, and her parents had thought she was making a terrible mistake. If the company failed, she would have no safety net. Even so, she couldn't help feeling that something extraordinary was happening here.
The tour went smoothly until they reached the third floor. At the end of a quiet corridor stood a heavy grey door with a keypad. A low, steady hum was coming from behind it.
"What's in there?" Nina asked.

Daniel's smile didn't change, but he answered a little too quickly. "Just the main servers. Only Elena has access. She's the founder, and she's very protective of the code. You know what founders are like."
"Surely the servers would be in the basement," Nina said. "Or in a data centre somewhere."
"Most people would say so." He shrugged and moved on. "Come on, I'll show you the kitchen. The coffee is the best thing about this place."

That afternoon, Nina met Elena Vargas herself. The founder was a small woman in her fifties with sharp eyes and a very quiet voice. She shook Nina's hand and held it for a moment longer than necessary.
"I read your application three times," Elena said. "You must be extremely careful with data. That's rare, and I need it."
"I try to be," Nina replied. "At my last job, one wrong number could cost a customer a lot of money."
"Good. Because here, nothing is as simple as it looks." Elena looked at her for a long second. "Whatever you do, never ask me about the third floor. Not yet."

Nina nodded, but the warning only made her curious. All week she found herself walking past the grey door. Each time, the hum seemed to be slightly louder, almost as if the machine behind it were alive and waiting.

On Thursday night she stayed late to finish a report. The office was empty except for the cleaners. When she walked to the lift, she noticed something odd: a thin line of light was shining under the grey door. Someone must have been inside, yet nobody had entered the corridor all evening.

parts.title: Part 2: The Midnight Login
parts.intro: Nina notices a strange record in the system and begins to doubt the people around her.
paragraphs: On Monday morning, Nina could not stop thinking about the light under the door. She told herself that there was probably a simple explanation: the cleaners might have used a different entrance, or Elena might have arrived before sunrise. Nevertheless, a small voice in her head kept asking questions.

At ten o'clock she began a routine check of the company's access logs. It was a boring task, and she had expected nothing unusual. Then she saw it. At 3:12 a.m. on Saturday, someone had logged in with her username and copied an enormous file to an outside address.
Nina stared at the screen. She hadn't been near the building on Saturday. She had been at her cousin's wedding, dancing and eating cake until after midnight. The login couldn't have been hers.

Her hands began to shake. If she had reported the strange login immediately, the company might have stopped the copy in time, but she had only found it two days later. Now the file was gone, and her name was attached to the crime.

She considered going straight to Elena. Then she hesitated. Who could have known her password? She had only written it down once, on a note that she'd given to Daniel on her first day so that he could set up her laptop. He had promised to throw it away.
"You look terrible," Daniel said at lunch, putting a tray down beside her. "Did you sleep badly?"
"I'm fine," Nina lied. She didn't want to accuse anyone without proof. "It's just a lot of new information."

"You're doing great, you know." He lowered his voice. "Between you and me, Elena has been very strange lately. She spends whole nights on that third floor. If I were you, I wouldn't trust her too much."

The comment surprised Nina. Only an hour earlier, Daniel had spoken about Elena with great respect. Either he had changed his opinion very suddenly, or he was trying to push her in a particular direction.

That evening she changed her password and added a second security step to her account. Then she did something far more risky. She copied the suspicious log entry onto a small memory stick and put it in her pocket.

By Wednesday, she had made up her mind. The only way to learn the truth was to see inside the locked room. She knew that the keypad accepted a code, and she had noticed that Elena always typed it with her left hand, very fast, on the left side of the pad. Nina could not read the numbers, but she could see which keys had become worn and shiny.
Only four keys showed any wear. The code was a combination of those four numbers, repeated or reordered. It would take time, but it was possible.
At nine that night, when the building was silent again, she walked quietly towards the grey door.

parts.title: Part 3: What the Servers Were Hiding
parts.intro: Nina finally enters the forbidden room and finds an answer that raises even bigger questions.
paragraphs: It took Nina forty minutes to find the right code. When the lock finally clicked, she held her breath and pushed the heavy door open.

She had expected rows of machines and blinking lights. Instead, the room was small and surprisingly cold. A single computer glowed on a desk in the corner. The humming noise was coming from a large cooling unit fixed to the wall. Everything else was almost empty.
"This can't be the main server," she whispered. "It's far too small."

She sat down and woke the screen. The computer wasn't protected by a password, which struck her as bizarre in such a secretive company. A folder was open, and its name made her heart sink: Brightwell Archive.

Brightwell was a rival firm that had gone out of business two years earlier. Its customer data had never been made public, and everyone had assumed it had been destroyed. Yet here were thousands of records, with dates, names and purchase histories. The huge file that had been copied on Saturday was sitting in the folder as well.

Nina felt sick. So Veridan's famous accuracy was based on stolen information. No wonder the predictions had been so remarkable. The company must have used the Brightwell data to train its software from the very beginning.
"I told you not to ask about this room."
Nina spun round. Elena Vargas was standing in the doorway, wearing a coat over her pyjamas, with a mug in her hand. She looked exhausted rather than angry.
"It was you," Nina said, standing up. "You stole their data. And you used my account to copy it so that I would take the blame."
"That's what you think happened?" Elena asked calmly.
"What else could have happened? Nobody else has the key code."

"A great deal could have happened." Elena closed the door behind her. "If I had wanted to hide this, I would have changed the code months ago. Did you never wonder why I kept the same one for so long?"
Nina hesitated. It was true that the worn keys had made the code easy to guess. Almost as if it had been left like that on purpose.
"Sit down," Elena said. "You have two choices. You can call the police now, and Veridan will be finished by tomorrow. Or you can listen to me for ten minutes. Then you can decide."
Nina looked at the screen, then at the tired woman in front of her. Her instincts told her to run. But her curiosity, as usual, was stronger.
"Ten minutes," she said. "Start talking."

parts.title: Part 4: The Trap
parts.intro: Elena finally explains the truth, and Nina learns who she can really trust.
paragraphs: Elena sat on the edge of the desk and rubbed her eyes. "The data is real," she said. "But I didn't steal it. Brightwell's owner sold me its archive legally, years ago, when the company closed. I should have told our clients, and I didn't. That was my mistake, and I will answer for it."
"Then why is it hidden?" Nina asked.

"Because someone has been trying to blackmail me. Six months ago, a message arrived demanding money. If I hadn't paid, they said, they would tell everyone that I had used Brightwell's records. I paid once. Then I started to look for the person responsible."
Nina frowned. "You think it's someone inside Veridan."

"I know it is. Only a few people could have found this room. So I set a trap. I kept the same code, I left the computer unlocked, and I waited for someone to copy the file. I also made sure the thief would believe your account was the easiest to use."
"You used me as bait?" Nina said, furious.

"I did. And I'm sorry. But I needed somebody new, somebody who hadn't been involved in anything yet." Elena took a small tablet from her pocket. "The thief didn't know that this room records every visitor with a camera. Look."

On the screen, a grainy video showed a figure entering the room at 3:10 a.m. on Saturday. The man sat at the computer, copied the file and left. When he turned his face towards the camera, Nina's stomach turned over.
It was Daniel.
"He told me not to trust you," Nina said slowly. "He wanted me to believe you were the villain. He must have planned to leave my name on the logs and disappear."
"He was selling the data to a competitor," Elena said. "The blackmail was his idea too. He could easily have taken the money and left, but greed made him careless."

The next morning, the police were waiting in the lobby when Daniel arrived. He didn't even try to run. He simply looked at Nina and said, "I'd never have used your password if I'd thought you were clever enough to catch me." Nina almost laughed. It was the nicest compliment he had ever given her, and also the last.

Veridan survived, although not without difficulty. Elena informed every client about the archive, paid a large fine and accepted strict new rules about her data. As for Nina, she was promoted within the year. Her parents finally stopped worrying, and she still has a habit that colleagues find strange: she never writes down a password, and she always notices which keys on a keypad are wearing out.

parts.title: Part 1: The Envelope
parts.intro: A village reporter receives an anonymous envelope that raises a worrying question.
paragraphs: Ruth Calder had worked for the Marrow Bay Courier for eleven years, and in that time the biggest story she had covered was a dispute about a seagull that kept stealing chips from the harbour café. She did not complain. A local newspaper, she liked to say, was a village's memory, and somebody had to keep it.

On a grey Monday in October, an envelope was waiting on her desk. It had been pushed through the letterbox during the night, and there was no stamp and no name. Inside was a single sheet of paper: a bank statement belonging to the Marrow Bay Sea Wall Fund.

Ruth knew the fund well. Two years earlier, the whole village had raised money to repair the old sea wall, which protected the harbour from winter storms. There had been bake sales, a sponsored swim and a concert in the church. By the spring, the fund had reached two hundred and forty thousand pounds, and the mayor, Helen Frost, had announced that work would begin "very soon".
The statement showed a balance of eleven pounds.

Ruth read it three times. Then she checked the dates: the money had been withdrawn in four large payments over the previous summer. Across the bottom, someone had written one sentence in blue pen: Ask where it went.

She was still staring at the page when her editor, Sam Whitlock, put his head round the door. Sam was a nervous man with an untidy beard, and he looked more worried than usual. "Have you heard about Gordon Pike?" he asked. "He resigned as treasurer this morning. He told the council that he was leaving for personal reasons, and then he went home and apparently locked the door."

Ruth slowly turned the statement face down on the desk. She had known Gordon for most of her life. He had taught her mathematics at school, and he was the most honest person she could think of: the kind of man who would return a pound if a shop gave him too much change.
"It could be a coincidence," Sam said, when she showed him the paper. "Or someone might be trying to cause trouble. Statements can be forged, you know."

"Perhaps," Ruth said. But she had already noticed something that a forger would probably have missed. The small reference number in the corner was identical to the one on the fund's official letters, which she had kept in her files since the original announcement.

That evening, as she walked home along the harbour, she stopped to look at the old wall. Waves were already crashing against it, throwing white spray into the dark, and she suddenly realised that she couldn't remember seeing any scaffolding, any workers or any repairs at all.

parts.title: Part 2: The Treasurer
parts.intro: Ruth visits the man who resigned and finds him frightened and silent.
paragraphs: Gordon Pike lived in a narrow cottage at the top of Lantern Lane, and for three days nobody had seen him. Ruth knocked at eight o'clock on Tuesday morning. When there was no answer, she called through the letterbox that she hadn't come to cause him any trouble.

After a long silence, the door opened a few centimetres. Gordon looked ten years older than he had the previous month. His shirt was creased, and his usually tidy white hair was standing up in tufts. Behind him the house was completely silent, and Ruth noticed that the clock in the hall had stopped.
"I have nothing to say to the newspaper," he said.
"I'm not here as the newspaper," Ruth replied. "I'm here because you taught me that numbers always tell the truth." She held up the statement. "These numbers don't add up."

He stared at the paper for a long time. Then, without a word, he let her in. The kitchen smelled of burnt toast. Gordon sat down heavily and told her that he hadn't slept properly for weeks. He said that he had been asked to keep a secret, and that the secret had become heavier every day.
"Whose secret?" Ruth asked.

He shook his head. He explained that he had given his word, and that a man who broke his word had nothing left. Ruth pointed out that the villagers had also given their money, and that they deserved the truth. For a moment she thought he might break. His hands were trembling around his mug of tea.

"Everything was done for the right reasons," he said at last. "That's all I can tell you. Please, Ruth, don't print anything until you've spoken to Helen." He added that the fund had never been touched by a thief, and that he would swear it on his mother's grave.
"Then who did touch it?" she asked. But Gordon had closed his mouth again, and she knew the conversation was over.

As she was leaving, she noticed a pile of letters on the doormat that nobody had opened. One of them carried a bright red warning: FINAL NOTICE. Another had been sent by a firm called Strand Developments, and its envelope was thick and expensive. Ruth hesitated, and then she wrote the name in her notebook. A man doesn't hide from the world for three days because of a guilty conscience alone, she thought, and certainly not over one unpaid bill. Somebody is putting pressure on him.

parts.title: Part 3: The Mayor
parts.intro: Ruth interviews the mayor and receives answers that sound too perfect.
paragraphs: Helen Frost had been mayor of Marrow Bay for fourteen years, and she looked the part. She was tall, silver-haired and always perfectly dressed, and she had a gift for making every villager feel like her personal friend. Ruth had always admired her, and that made the interview on Wednesday afternoon much harder.

The mayor's office overlooked the harbour. Helen poured tea from a china pot and asked about Ruth's mother before Ruth could say a word. Only then did she smile and say, "I suppose you've come about Gordon."
"I've come about the Sea Wall Fund," Ruth said. She placed the statement on the table.
Helen did not touch it. She looked at it as if it were a small, unfriendly animal. "Where did you get that?"
"It was delivered anonymously. Is it genuine?"
"The balance is accurate," Helen said calmly. "I won't pretend otherwise. But the money has not been stolen, and it has not been wasted. It was invested."
"Invested in what?"

"In the future of this village." She folded her hands. "I'm afraid I can't say more at present. There are legal reasons. When the time is right, the council will make an announcement, and I promise you will be the first to hear it."

Ruth had interviewed enough politicians to recognise a prepared answer. She asked again, in three different ways, and received the same smooth reply each time. In the end she closed her notebook and thanked the mayor for her time.

It was while she was putting on her coat that she noticed two things. The first was the mayor's boots, which were standing by the door. They were green rubber boots, and they were covered in wet grey mud, the kind that is found only at the bottom of the harbour. The second was a business card lying on the desk, half hidden under a folder. It read: Dr Anil Rao, Coastal Engineer.
"Are those your boots, Helen?" Ruth asked lightly.
"I like to walk by the sea," the mayor answered, and for the first time that afternoon her voice was not entirely steady.

Outside, the wind had risen. Ruth stood on the steps and watched fishing boats being pulled in early. Somebody had told her once that you could judge a person by what they hid when they were relaxed, not by what they said when they were nervous. Helen Frost had been relaxed, she realised, until the moment the statement appeared.

parts.title: Part 4: The Warning
parts.intro: Ruth's editor receives a threat, and an old neighbour describes strange nights at the harbour.
paragraphs: On Thursday morning, Sam Whitlock closed his office door, which he never did, and asked Ruth to sit down. He was twisting a paperclip into a tiny silver knot.

"I've had a phone call," he said. "From Mr Strand himself. He owns Strand Developments and, as you may know, half of the buildings that advertise in this newspaper. He said he had heard that we were asking questions about the Sea Wall Fund. He wanted to remind me that rumours can ruin reputations."
"Whose reputation?" Ruth asked. "Strand's? What does he have to do with the fund?"

"That's what I asked him. He didn't answer. He just laughed and said I would be a fool to lose our advertisers over a story with no evidence." Sam let the paperclip fall. "I've worked here for twenty years, Ruth. This paper has never been bullied. But we have eleven staff and one very thin bank account."

Ruth realised that he wasn't telling her to stop. He was telling her to be careful, and to be right. "Give me one more week," she said. "If I can't prove anything, I'll drop it." Sam nodded slowly. "One week. And, Ruth, whatever you find, I want it checked twice."

That afternoon she went to see Mrs Penhallow, who lived in the last cottage before the sea wall and who, at ninety-one, noticed everything that happened on the shore. The old woman was knitting by her window and did not stop when Ruth came in.

"I wondered when someone would come," she said. "Nobody ever asks the old ones anything until it's too late." She explained that she didn't sleep well, and that for almost three months she had been watching the wall at night. Heavy lorries had arrived after midnight with their lights switched off. Men in orange jackets had worked until dawn, and by morning every trace of them had been cleared away.
"Do you know who they were?" Ruth asked.

"Strangers, mostly. But one night I saw Helen Frost standing on the slipway with a torch. She was talking to a young man, and she looked as if she hadn't slept for a week." Mrs Penhallow finally put down her knitting. "I asked myself why a mayor would hide a repair. Then I remembered what my husband used to say: the people who whisper are not always the people who are guilty. Sometimes they are simply the people who are frightened."
Ruth wrote down every word. As she was leaving, the old woman called after her, "Go early, dear, when the tide is out. A wall always tells its own story if you look at the bottom of it."

parts.title: Part 5: Low Tide
parts.intro: At dawn, Ruth discovers what is hidden at the bottom of the sea wall.
paragraphs: The tide was at its lowest at ten past six on Friday morning, and Ruth was standing on the shingle with a torch in one hand and a flask of coffee in the other. She had borrowed her brother's waders, which were two sizes too big, and she walked like a duck.

The sea had drawn back, and for the first time in weeks she could see the foot of the wall. She had expected old, green, crumbling stone. Instead, along a stretch of almost sixty metres, a thick band of fresh concrete had been poured against the base, smooth and pale and obviously new. Steel rods stuck out of it like the bones of a giant fish.
"So the work was done," she said aloud. "It just wasn't announced."
"Please don't shout," said a voice behind her.

Ruth turned so quickly that she nearly fell. A young man in a hooded jacket was sitting on an upturned boat, eating a sandwich. He was perhaps nineteen, thin and freckled, with the cautious look of someone who had been told not to talk.

"I'm Arlo," he said. "I work at the boatyard, and I've worked on this wall every night since July. We heard you'd come eventually." Ruth asked who had said so. Arlo shrugged. "Everyone knows a reporter is asking questions. The village is small, you know."

He told her, very quickly, that the men had been paid in cash and had signed an agreement to say nothing. The lorries had been hired from a firm two towns away, so that nobody in Marrow Bay would recognise them. Nobody had explained why, and Arlo had stopped asking. "It was good money," he said. "But it was also the most careful job I've ever done. Everything was checked twice, as if somebody was afraid the wall would fall on us."
"Or afraid that somebody would find out," Ruth said.

Arlo hesitated. Then he pulled a crumpled piece of paper from his pocket. It was a delivery note from a company called Harcourt Marine Contractors, and at the bottom, beside a date in July, was a signature that Ruth knew immediately. It was Gordon Pike's.

"I shouldn't give you this," Arlo said. "But I keep thinking about the village, and what happens to a place when nobody tells the truth." He pushed the note into her hand and walked quickly away across the shingle. By the time Ruth had folded it into her notebook, he had disappeared around the harbour, and she was alone with the sound of the waves and one very large question: if the wall had really been repaired, why had two hundred thousand pounds been spent in secret?

parts.title: Part 6: Dinner at the Anchor
parts.intro: A powerful businessman offers Ruth a folder of evidence, but she notices a strange detail.
paragraphs: Ruth was not surprised when her phone rang that evening, but she was surprised by who was calling. "Miss Calder? This is Victor Strand. I wonder whether you would join me for dinner at the Anchor Hotel. I think we may be able to help each other."

The Anchor was the most expensive restaurant in the district, and Victor Strand was exactly the kind of man who kept a permanent table there. He was about fifty, with a smooth, tanned face and a voice that seemed to be speaking from a long way above you. He ordered for both of them without looking at the menu.

"Let me be honest," he began, which in Ruth's experience was how dishonest people usually started. "I was rude to your editor, and I apologise. I don't dislike newspapers. I dislike stories that are only half true."
"And what is the whole truth?" Ruth asked.

Strand smiled and slid a thick folder across the tablecloth. "Two hundred and forty thousand pounds were taken from the fund. Helen Frost authorised the withdrawals, and Gordon Pike signed them. They have been spending public money in secret for months. I have copies of everything. All I ask is that you print it quickly, before they have time to destroy the evidence."
"Why do you care so much about the Sea Wall Fund, Mr Strand?"
"I'm a citizen," he replied. "And I'm the biggest taxpayer in Marrow Bay. If that doesn't give me the right to care, I don't know what does."

Ruth thanked him, and she even managed to eat some of her fish. But all through dinner she watched his hands and listened to his voice, and by the time the coffee arrived she had made two decisions. The first was that she would not print a single word that night. The second was that she would take the folder home.

At her kitchen table, under the lamp, she spread out the pages. There were bank statements, withdrawal slips and even an email between Helen and Gordon. Everything seemed perfect, and that was exactly what bothered her. Real evidence is usually untidy. Then she placed the first page of the folder beside the statement she had received on Monday.

A faint grey line ran diagonally across the left side of both pages, in exactly the same place. It was the kind of mark that is left by a scratched photocopier. Whoever had sent her the anonymous envelope had used the same machine as Victor Strand. Ruth sat very still. The man who had threatened her editor was also the man who had started her investigation, and she had no idea why.

parts.title: Part 7: The Engineer's Report
parts.intro: An engineer reveals why the wall mattered and who wanted the repair delayed.
paragraphs: Dr Anil Rao worked from a converted lighthouse keeper's cottage on the headland, and when Ruth arrived on Saturday morning he was already making tea, as if he had been expecting her.

"Mayor Frost told me you might call," he said. "She also asked me not to talk to you. I've been thinking about that all night, and I've decided that I'm an engineer, not a politician. I don't take orders from anyone about what is true."

He opened a laptop and showed her a report dated last February. It was forty pages long, but the summary was only three sentences: The sea wall has failed structurally. It is expected to collapse during a winter storm. Immediate repair is essential.
Ruth read the words twice. "Collapse," she said. "You mean the harbour would have flooded?" Dr Rao nodded. "The harbour, the lower village and eighty houses. Not in ten years. This winter."
"Then why did the council ignore the report?"

"They didn't ignore it," he said. "They voted on it. In March, by five votes to four, the council decided that the repair could wait until next year, when the budget would be larger. Councillor Dunmore led the argument. I later discovered that Councillor Dunmore is Victor Strand's brother-in-law."
A cold feeling moved slowly down Ruth's back. "And the villagers' fund?"

"That is where Helen made her choice," Dr Rao said quietly. "The fund belonged to the village, not to the council, and it was managed by two trustees: Helen and Gordon. She said that she would not stand by and watch a disaster. She asked me how quickly the work could be done, and I told her that if it were started in secret, it could be finished by October. It was finished two weeks ago."
"But it was against the rules, wasn't it? To spend the money without permission."

Dr Rao took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes. "I'm not a lawyer. I only know that the wall is standing, and that without it there would be no story to write." He paused. "But I also know that somebody wants a very different story, Miss Calder. Somebody who would be happy to see this village flood."

Ruth looked out of the window at the sea wall, grey and ordinary in the morning light, and thought of Victor Strand's smooth voice. A flooded village would sell very cheaply. A scandal about its leaders would make it cheaper still.

parts.title: Part 8: A Confession
parts.intro: Ruth confronts the mayor and the treasurer, and a hidden plan becomes clear.
paragraphs: Ruth did not go to the mayor's office this time. She went to Helen Frost's house, a tall, narrow building near the church, and she took with her the engineer's report, Arlo's delivery note and her own notes from the week.

Helen opened the door herself. She looked at Ruth's face, then at the bag in her hand, and stepped aside without a word. In the front room Gordon Pike was already sitting by the fire, as if he had been waiting there as well. Nobody offered tea.
"I know about the report," Ruth began. "I know about the vote, and the night work, and the signatures. What I don't know is why you didn't simply tell the village."

Helen sat down slowly. "Because the council would have stopped us," she said. "Dunmore had already announced that any spending would need a full vote. We would have been tied up for months, and the first storm was expected in November. I asked myself what would happen if I did the right thing the slow way." She shook her head. "People would have been standing on their roofs."
"You broke the rules," Ruth said, as gently as she could.

"Yes," said Gordon. It was the first word he had spoken. "We did. We spent money without proper authority, and we hid it. I have never lied in my whole life, Ruth, and I lied to everyone for four months. I'm not proud of it. But I would do it again."
Helen turned towards him with an expression of pain. "Gordon signed because I asked him to. If anyone is to be punished, it should be me."

"Somebody knows," Ruth said. "Somebody sent me a bank statement with a message written on it." She described the grey line on the paper, the folder and the dinner at the Anchor Hotel. As she spoke, Helen's face became very still.

"Strand," she said. "Of course. He asked me to sell him Mill Meadow two years ago, and I refused. It is the last open land beside the harbour. If I were forced out of office tomorrow, the council would elect Dunmore, and Dunmore would approve every building that Strand wanted." She laughed, but there was no happiness in it. "He didn't need the wall to fall. He only needed me to fall."

Nobody spoke. The fire cracked quietly, and from somewhere outside came the slow, steady sound of the sea. Then Ruth said the sentence she had been dreading all week. "I have to decide what to publish, and I don't know what the right thing to do is."

parts.title: Part 9: The Third Option
parts.intro: Ruth must decide how much of the truth to print and what it will cost.
paragraphs: Ruth did not sleep that night. She sat at her kitchen table until three in the morning with two piles of paper in front of her: one that said Helen Frost was a thief, and one that said she was a hero. Neither pile was completely true.
At seven she knocked on Gordon Pike's door again. This time he opened it at once. "The letter from Strand Developments," Ruth said. "The one that was on your doormat last Tuesday. Did you open it?"
Gordon was silent for a moment. Then he walked to a kitchen drawer and took out a single sheet. It had been photocopied, and across its left edge ran a faint grey diagonal line.

"It arrived a week before I resigned," he said. "It said that Mr Strand knew about the withdrawals. If I resigned quietly and told nobody, he would not go to the police. If I refused, he would ruin Helen. I thought that if I disappeared, the matter might end. I was wrong. He simply used my silence to send you his own version of the story."

Ruth held the letter in both hands. It was a perfect match, and it was also the proof she needed. Strand had known everything, had used the secret to threaten an honest man, and had then tried to turn a repaired wall into a crime.

Back at the office, she told Sam everything. He listened without interrupting, and when she had finished, he took off his glasses and cleaned them very slowly. "Strand's lawyer rang this morning," he said. "If we mention his name, he says he will sue us. We could lose the paper." He looked up. "Or we publish nothing, and Strand wins."
"There's a third option," Ruth said. "We publish all of it."

She explained. The story would say that the mayor and the treasurer had broken the rules and must answer for it. It would say that the wall had been saved, and by whom. It would say that a businessman had known about the secret for months and had tried to use it to take control of the council. Every statement would be supported by a document, and every document would be checked twice.
"It will end Helen's career," Sam said quietly. "And Gordon's good name."

"I know," said Ruth. "But the villagers gave their money, and they deserve to decide what they think of it. Not Strand. Not me." She looked at the clock on the wall. It was nearly noon. "The paper goes to the printer at six."
