parts.title: A Welcome Speech at a Professional Conference
parts.intro: The opening speech of an international conference, delivered by its chairperson.
paragraphs: Good morning, everyone, and welcome. It is a genuine pleasure to see so many of you here, and I would like to begin by thanking the organisers, who have spent the better part of a year making this conference possible.

When the first of these gatherings took place, there were barely forty of us in a borrowed lecture hall, and the main topic of discussion was whether our field would ever be taken seriously. Today we number more than eleven hundred, representing thirty-four countries, and the question has changed entirely. We no longer ask whether our work matters; we ask how we can ensure that it matters in the right ways.

That shift in emphasis is what I would like to reflect on this morning. For most of our history, success in our profession has been measured by speed and novelty. We have rewarded those who publish first, build fastest and launch earliest. These habits have served us well, and I would be the last person to dismiss them. Yet I suspect that many of you, like me, have begun to feel that something is missing from that equation. Speed without reflection can leave us with remarkable tools and no clear idea of what they are for.

This year's programme is designed, quite deliberately, to encourage a slower kind of thinking. You will notice that the sessions are longer than usual, that the breaks are generous, and that several panels have been arranged so that people who disagree with one another must share a stage. This is not an accident. In my experience, the most valuable ideas rarely emerge from conversations in which everyone already agrees. They arise at the uncomfortable edges, where assumptions are challenged and where we are obliged to explain ourselves to someone who does not share our vocabulary.

I would therefore invite you to do three things over the next three days. First, attend at least one session outside your own specialism. You may well find it bewildering at first, but bewilderment is often the beginning of insight. Second, speak to someone you have never met, preferably someone considerably younger or older than yourself. Third, and perhaps most difficult, resist the temptation to check your phone during the talks. I confess that I am not entirely confident of managing the last one myself.

I should also acknowledge the people who are not in this room. Many colleagues were unable to join us because of visa restrictions, financial constraints or caring responsibilities. We have tried to make the proceedings accessible to them through recordings and online discussion, but I am under no illusion that this is a perfect substitute. It is a reminder that a community is only as strong as its willingness to include those who cannot easily attend.

Finally, let me say something about generosity. Every one of us is here because somebody once took the time to answer our naive questions, to read our clumsy first drafts, or to give us an opportunity before we had earned it. The best way to repay that debt is not to thank those people, though that is no bad thing, but to do the same for someone else.
With that, I declare the conference open. Please enjoy the next three days, challenge one another generously, and above all, listen.

parts.title: Opinion: The Four-Day Week and the Limits of Enthusiasm
parts.intro: An economics columnist argues for a more cautious view of a popular workplace idea.
paragraphs: Every few years, a fashionable idea sweeps through the business world and leaves a trail of confident predictions. The latest is that the four-day working week will inevitably raise productivity, and that any company resisting it is clinging to an outdated model. The evidence, however, is more nuanced than the enthusiasts admit, and the debate deserves a calmer tone than it usually receives.

Let us begin with what the advocates get right. Several trials, mostly involving small and mid-sized firms, have reported that employees given an extra day off produced about as much as before while reporting lower stress and better health. Absenteeism fell, resignations declined and some managers noted that meetings became shorter, since people had less time to waste. Such results are not trivial, and they should prompt any serious employer to ask whether its own working hours are really optimal.

Yet these trials share a weakness that rarely appears in the headlines. The companies that volunteered were, almost by definition, the ones most likely to succeed: they were enthusiastic, relatively flexible and often engaged in knowledge work that can be organised around results rather than presence. A hospital ward, a factory production line or a customer helpline cannot easily be compressed in the same way. If a nurse works four longer days instead of five normal ones, patient care may be affected in ways that productivity statistics will not capture.

There is also a question of time horizons. A new arrangement tends to energise people in its first months, much as a new diet inspires strict discipline in its first weeks. Whether the gains persist after the novelty fades is a matter on which we have remarkably little data. Researchers sometimes call this a novelty effect, and a responsible analysis would treat the early results with caution rather than treating them as settled fact.

Nor should we overlook the distribution of benefits. A shorter week is most easily granted in sectors where profit margins are healthy and employees have bargaining power. For lower-paid workers on hourly contracts, a reduced schedule may simply mean reduced income. If the policy is celebrated as a triumph for workers generally, while in practice it benefits those already well placed, it will widen existing inequalities rather than narrow them.

None of this amounts to an argument against experiment. On the contrary, the case for careful pilots has never been stronger, and governments could usefully fund them across a wider range of industries, including the awkward ones. What I would resist is the temptation to treat a promising trial as a universal prescription. Good policy, like good medicine, depends on knowing for whom a treatment works, in what dose, and at what cost.

The question facing employers is therefore not whether to follow a trend, but whether they can design a schedule suited to their own circumstances and honest enough to measure its effects. Those who answer yes may well discover a competitive advantage. Those who adopt the slogan without the scrutiny may find that they have exchanged one set of problems for another.

parts.title: Best Practice: Running Effective Remote Meetings
parts.intro: A practical guide that gives leaders seven principles for better online meetings.
paragraphs: Running effective remote meetings: a guide to good practice for team leaders

Remote meetings have become a permanent feature of working life, yet many remain tiring, unfocused and poorly attended in spirit if not in body. The recommendations below are drawn from the experience of managers who have run distributed teams for several years. They are not rules but principles, and you should adapt them to your own circumstances. Where a suggestion does not suit your team, discard it without guilt and try another.

1. Decide whether a meeting is necessary. Before sending an invitation, ask what the meeting will achieve that a written update could not. Meetings are justified when a decision requires discussion, when people need to build trust, or when a topic is sensitive enough that tone matters. If the purpose is merely to share information, a concise message will usually save everyone's time.

2. Circulate an agenda in advance. An agenda should state the purpose of the meeting, the decisions required and the time allotted to each item. Send it at least a day beforehand, together with any documents participants need to read. Insist that people read them. Nothing wastes time so reliably as summarising material that attendees could have absorbed on their own.

3. Keep the group small and the time short. Every additional participant increases the likelihood of side conversations and silent disengagement. Invite only those who must contribute or decide, and offer everyone else the minutes. Aim for thirty minutes rather than an hour; work tends to expand to fill the time available, and meetings are no exception.

4. Create space for quieter voices. In online settings, confident speakers can easily dominate while others hesitate to interrupt. Invite contributions by name, use a round of brief comments at the start, and encourage written input through the chat window. Be aware that people in different time zones may be joining early in the morning or late at night, and avoid scheduling that places the same colleagues at a disadvantage every week.

5. Manage the technology without making it the focus. Test your equipment beforehand, but do not allow technical hitches to consume the first ten minutes. Have a fallback, such as a dial-in number, and agree in advance what will happen if the leader loses connection. Cameras should be encouraged rather than demanded; some participants have good reasons, including poor bandwidth or a lack of private space, for keeping them off.

6. Close with clarity. In the final five minutes, summarise the decisions reached, name the person responsible for each action and state the deadline. Send written notes within twenty-four hours. A meeting that ends without clear commitments is, in practice, only a conversation, and conversations are rarely remembered accurately.

7. Review and adjust. Every few months, ask your team for candid feedback. Which meetings are valuable? Which feel like obligations? Be prepared to cancel regular meetings that have outlived their purpose. The aim is not to hold more meetings or fewer, but to ensure that each one earns its place in the calendar.

parts.title: A Diplomatic Email to Resolve a Conflict
parts.intro: A training director writes to a partner after a scheduling change caused offence.
paragraphs: Subject: Our recent exchange regarding the joint training programme
Dear Ms Ferreira,

Thank you for your message of Tuesday, and for the candour with which you set out your concerns. I write in the hope that we can resolve the present difficulty before it affects the participants, who have, after all, done nothing to deserve it.

I should begin by saying that I regret the way in which the revised schedule was communicated. You were informed of the change by a brief notice rather than by a conversation, and I understand why this was received as discourteous. That was an oversight on our side, and I offer my apology without qualification. It was certainly not our intention to treat your organisation as a junior partner, and I would be sorry if it appeared so.

At the same time, I would like to explain, not to excuse, why the change was made. Our facilities will be closed for structural repairs from the second week of October, and we learned of the closure only two weeks ago. Moving the first module forward seemed the least disruptive option, but I accept that we should have consulted you before reaching that conclusion, particularly since your own staff must now reorganise their commitments at short notice.

I have read with care your suggestion that the programme be postponed until January. I can see its attractions, yet I am concerned that a delay of this length would cause us to lose several participants, whose funding is tied to the current academic year. Might I propose a compromise? The first module could be held at your premises, if you are willing, with our trainers travelling to you for the first four sessions. We would cover the costs of transport and of any additional room hire, and we would revert to our own facilities once the repairs are complete.

I recognise that this proposal places a further burden on your team, and I do not make it lightly. Should you consider it unworkable, I would be glad to explore other alternatives, including a shorter introductory module or a delayed start of two weeks. What matters most to me is that the programme proceeds on terms that both parties find acceptable.

More broadly, I believe this episode has shown that our channels of communication need strengthening. I would welcome a short call each fortnight between our coordinators, together with a shared document in which any planned change is recorded before it is announced. Such arrangements are not elaborate, but they might have prevented the misunderstanding that now confronts us.

Over the past three years, our collaboration has produced results of which both institutions can be proud, and I would not wish a single lapse to undermine that record, or the goodwill that has taken so long to build. I would be grateful if we could speak by telephone at your earliest convenience, and I am available at any time on Thursday or Friday.
With kind regards and renewed apologies,

parts.title: Organisation Profile: The Meridian Seed Trust
parts.intro: A profile of a fictional charity that protects traditional food crops.
paragraphs: Organisation profile: The Meridian Seed Trust

In a modest brick building on the edge of a market town, a small team of botanists, volunteers and retired farmers is quietly preserving something that most of us rarely think about: the diversity of the food crops our grandparents once grew. The Meridian Seed Trust, a fictional charity founded twenty-two years ago, maintains a collection of more than 4,000 traditional varieties of vegetables, grains and fruit, many of which have disappeared from commercial farming.

The Trust's origins were unglamorous. Its founder, a schoolteacher named Ilse Baumgartner, noticed that the pumpkins of her childhood, with their pale green skin and unusually sweet flesh, had vanished from every shop. After several months of searching, she found a handful of seeds in the garden shed of an elderly neighbour. She planted them, saved the seeds of the best fruits, and within a few years had begun exchanging packets with other enthusiasts. What began as a hobby gradually acquired a structure, a board of trustees and a modest grant from a regional foundation.

Today the organisation operates on three fronts. The first is conservation. Seeds are dried, catalogued and stored at low temperature in a purpose-built vault, while living collections are maintained in trial gardens so that varieties continue to adapt to local conditions. The second front is education: every year, some six thousand schoolchildren visit the gardens, where they sow, harvest and, perhaps most memorably, taste vegetables that look nothing like those in supermarkets. The third is a seed-lending library, through which members may borrow packets, grow them, and return a portion of the harvested seed to the collection.

The Trust's argument for its work is both practical and cultural. Modern agriculture, it points out, relies on a strikingly narrow range of crop varieties, selected for uniformity, transport and shelf life. This efficiency has a price. A single disease or a shift in climate can devastate fields planted with genetically similar plants, whereas a more varied stock offers resilience. Older varieties, the Trust contends, may contain traits, such as drought tolerance or resistance to particular pests, that breeders will need in the decades ahead.

Not everyone is convinced. Some agricultural economists regard the project as admirable but marginal, arguing that large-scale food production will always depend on a handful of high-yielding varieties, and that the real work of preserving genetic diversity is done in major national seed banks. The Trust accepts the first point but not the second. Its director, Tomas Reyes, observes that institutions are only as good as the funding they receive, and that distributing seeds among thousands of ordinary gardeners provides a kind of insurance that no single vault can offer.

Financially, the Trust remains fragile. About half of its income comes from membership fees and the sale of seed packets, while the remainder depends on grants that must be renewed annually. A recent appeal for funds to expand the vault was oversubscribed, which suggests that public interest is growing, yet the staff are wary of expansion that could dilute their character. They speak, with evident pride, of knowing every volunteer by name.

For visitors, the experience is unexpectedly moving. Walking between rows of knotted beans and speckled lettuces, one begins to understand that these plants are not merely food but a form of inherited memory, carried forward by thousands of unrecorded hands. That is perhaps the Trust's most persuasive achievement: it makes an abstract idea like biodiversity feel personal, tangible and urgent.

parts.title: Exhibition Review: Quiet Rooms
parts.intro: A critic reviews a retrospective of a fictional painter of empty interiors.
paragraphs: Exhibition review: "Quiet Rooms", paintings by the fictional artist Lucía Armand

It is a rare exhibition that asks visitors to slow down, and rarer still one that rewards them for doing so. "Quiet Rooms", the first major retrospective of the painter Lucía Armand, occupies six galleries of the city's museum and presents some forty canvases made over three decades. Its subject, almost without exception, is the interior of a house in which nobody seems to be at home.

Armand's early work, hung in the first room, is the least assured. Her studies of kitchens and corridors are competent, even charming, but they betray the influence of her teachers, and the tight brushwork suggests an artist anxious to be taken seriously. The transformation begins in the second room, where a modest painting of an unmade bed in morning light announces her mature manner. The brushstrokes loosen; the colours, previously cautious, warm and deepen; and the empty room acquires a presence of its own, as though absence were not a lack but a substance.

The heart of the show is the central gallery, devoted to the series she painted after moving to a coastal village in her forties. Here windows dominate. A pale curtain stirs in a draught, a chair stands in a rectangle of sunlight, a teacup remains on a table beside a book left open. These are not scenes of loneliness, as some critics have claimed. They are, rather, studies of waiting, and the difference matters. Loneliness is a condition; waiting is an activity, charged with expectation, and Armand's genius lies in suspending that expectation just before it resolves.

Technically, the paintings are remarkable for their restraint. Armand works with a narrow range of tones, yet she achieves an astonishing variety of light: the cool grey of early morning, the amber glow of late afternoon, the bluish half-darkness that comes before a lamp is lit. In one canvas, a single stroke of pale yellow along the edge of a door conveys an entire summer evening. Such economy is deceptive, for it conceals hours of patient revision, as the curators' helpful notes on her working methods reveal.

The exhibition is not without flaws. The final room, which contains her late experiments with larger and more abstract forms, feels hurried and slightly unconvincing, as if the artist had grown impatient with her own subject. The wall texts, moreover, lean too heavily on biography, repeatedly inviting us to read the paintings as confessions rather than as the carefully constructed objects they plainly are. One would prefer to be left alone with the pictures, a courtesy which, appropriately, the paintings themselves seem to request.

Still, these are small complaints. The hanging is intelligent, the lighting sympathetic, and the pacing of the rooms allows the work to accumulate quietly rather than overwhelm. I left the museum with the odd conviction that the street outside had become noisier and less attentive than before. That, surely, is the highest compliment one can pay a painter of silence. Visitors should allow at least two hours and, if possible, avoid the crowded weekend afternoons, when the very quality the pictures celebrate becomes difficult to find.

parts.title: Part 1: The Pane of Glass
parts.intro: A veteran translator receives a posthumous manuscript and boasts that she will remain invisible inside it.
paragraphs: I have always held that a good translator is a pane of glass: clean, unremarked, and, if the work is done properly, forgotten the moment anyone looks through it. It is a creed I recommend to the young, partly because it is true and partly because it keeps them quiet.

The manuscript arrived on a Tuesday in November, in a box that had clearly been sealed by someone who distrusted tape. Inside lay four hundred and twelve typed pages, a note from the publisher in the clipped dialect of people who pay late, and nothing else. No photograph of the author, no biography, not even a pencilled apology for the state of the footnotes. The title page read The Salt Ledger, by one Anselm Voss, deceased, which I took to be a professional courtesy: the dead make the least troublesome clients.

I should say at the outset that I am not a woman given to fancy. My flat is on the fourth floor of a building whose lift has been out of order since the previous administration, and I climb the stairs each evening with the grim satisfaction of someone who has never once asked for help. My sister says this is a character flaw. I say it is a pension plan.

For the first sixty pages the book behaved itself. It concerned a harbour town, a family of ropemakers, and a quarrel over an inheritance, all rendered in the long, rolling sentences that Voss's language permits and mine merely tolerates. I worked from nine until one, then from three until seven, with the discipline of a monk who has been told the monastery is being sold. I ate standing up. I translated 'the sea declined to forgive them' three different ways before settling on the plainest, which is, I have found, usually the one that wounds.

It was on page sixty-one that the heroine, a woman named Ilka, sat down at her kitchen table and stirred three sugars into a cup of tea she did not intend to drink. 'It was a habit,' wrote Voss, 'that she had inherited from her mother along with the chipped blue cup, and she would have denied it under oath.'

I put down my pencil. This was not, I wish to be clear, the response of a woman given to fancy. It was the response of a woman who had, that very morning, stirred three sugars into a cup of tea she did not intend to drink, using a chipped blue cup that had belonged to her mother, and who would have denied it under oath.

Naturally, I laughed. Three sugars is hardly a fingerprint. Half the continent sweetens its grief. As for the cup, chipped blue crockery is the common currency of dead mothers; one could furnish a small museum with it. I made a fresh pot, drank it black and in protest, and returned to the page with the faintly theatrical briskness of someone resolved to notice nothing.

But a translator is, by trade, a person who notices everything and then says it in another language. That is the whole difficulty of the profession. By evening I had found Ilka's habit of counting the stairs aloud when she was frightened, which I do, and her distaste for the colour yellow, which I share, and a limp, the legacy of an old fall from a bicycle, that Voss placed in the left ankle, which is precisely where mine lives.

I closed the manuscript at seven exactly, as a matter of principle. Then I stood at the window for some time, watching the streetlamps come on in their orderly sequence, like an argument being made by someone who has already won it.
'Coincidence,' I said aloud to the empty room, and the room, being a good listener, did not contradict me.

parts.title: Part 2: A Hardy Plant
parts.intro: The coincidences refuse to stay coincidences, and a phone call with her sister unsettles the narrator's memory.
paragraphs: Coincidence, I discovered, is a hardy plant: it will grow in almost any soil, provided one waters it daily with denial. I watered mine assiduously for a week.

By the second week, however, the book had stopped pretending. In chapter nine, Ilka received a letter from a man she had once refused to marry, and she read it standing in the hallway with her coat still on, then filed it, unanswered, between the pages of a cookery book. I have such a letter. I have such a cookery book. I did not, I assured myself, need to check the shelf, and so I checked the shelf, and there it was, the spine cracked at exactly the chapter on preserves, the envelope still furred with a decade's dust.
I rang my sister that evening. Perpetua and I speak on Sundays by custom and on other days by catastrophe, and she answered on the second ring, which told me she had already assumed the latter.
'Nothing is wrong,' I said. 'I am merely conducting a small survey. Do you remember whether I ever told you about Tomas's letter?'
'Which Tomas?'
'Precisely.' I was pleased with this; it was the answer of a witness who has not been coached. 'And the cup. The blue one. Do you remember who had it last?'
'You did,' said Perpetua. 'You took it from the house the week we cleared it. You said it would be wasteful to throw away a perfectly good cup, and then you cried in the car for forty minutes.'
'I did nothing of the kind.'
'Helena, I was driving.'

I let that pass, as one lets pass a bus that is going in the wrong direction. It was, after all, my sister's version of events, and my sister has always had a weakness for the dramatic; as a child she insisted that the wardrobe contained a bishop. I thanked her, promised to call on Sunday, and hung up with the cool dignity of a woman who has not been contradicted by anyone of consequence.
Then I sat for a long while with the receiver in my lap, listening to the flat, patient hum of the dial tone as if it were a verdict.

The difficulty, you understand, was not that Voss knew things. A novelist is a kind of burglar; he enters the house of the human heart through the window and takes whatever he finds. The difficulty was that Voss knew them in my order. Ilka's secrets emerged in the same sequence in which I had arranged my own, the small shames first, set out like the good china, the large ones kept in the cellar for as long as the furniture would allow. No stranger shuffles another person's guilt so exactly. It was the work of someone who had sat in the next room for forty years with a glass pressed to the wall.

I made enquiries, naturally, with the thoroughness of a woman who prefers facts to feelings, mostly because facts do not ask how you are. The publisher's assistant, a pleasant young man who pronounced my name as though it were a diagnosis, told me that Anselm Voss had died in a hospice by the coast, that he had left no family, and that the manuscript had been found in a drawer 'with a note addressed to the translator.'
'Which translator?' I asked.
'Well,' he said, and I heard him turn a page, 'it says "to whoever is sensible enough to be afraid of it". We assumed that was a joke.'
'Naturally,' I said. 'A joke.'

I did not sleep that night, which I put down to the tea. I had, of course, resumed drinking it with sugar. There seemed little point in resisting any longer, and it is a curious comfort, when one is being written, to be at least a consistent character.

parts.title: Part 3: Eleven Visits
parts.intro: A chapter threatens to expose a fact the narrator has hidden for years, and she tests the limits of her professional rule.
paragraphs: There is a rule in my profession, rarely spoken aloud because it flatters no one: the translator may smooth, may soften, may even, in extremity, omit; but she may not lie. I had lived by it for thirty years, and it had never once been tested, for the simple reason that nobody had ever written down anything I wished to keep hidden.
Chapter fourteen tested it in the first paragraph.

Ilka's mother, in the book, grew old in a house by the water and was moved, in the autumn of her eighty-first year, to a care home forty miles inland. Ilka signed the papers on a Thursday. She chose the home, Voss tells us, for its gravel drive, its fresh paint, and its distance, and she told everyone that the distance was a matter of the garden. She visited eleven times in two years. Voss does not comment on the number; he merely lists the dates, with the unblinking courtesy of a clerk reading out a will.

I know the number. I have never told it to anyone, not to Perpetua, not to the priest whom I stopped visiting, and not, for most of the last decade, to myself. It lives in the cellar with the good wine and the bad news.

I did what any person of principle would do: I made tea, and I made a plan. The plan was elegant, and it had the great advantage of being entirely professional. Voss's syntax at this point grows tangled; a certain looseness in the tenses leaves it unclear whether Ilka visited eleven times or merely intended to. A translator is permitted, indeed obliged, to resolve ambiguity, and I resolved it in the kindest direction. Ilka visited often. Ilka visited, in my English, so frequently that the nurses knew her by name.

I read the sentence back and found it excellent. It had a warmth I should have been proud of in any other circumstances. Then I read the original again, and the original, which was not warm in the least, looked back at me with an expression I can only describe as patience.

It is a remarkable thing to be corrected by a dead man. I had always imagined that the dead, if they spoke, would raise their voices. Voss did nothing of the kind. He had simply set down the truth in a clean, rather beautiful sentence, and left it lying on the page like a coin on a counter, certain that I would eventually pick it up.

I should record, in fairness to myself, that I resisted for three days. I took long walks. I cleaned the oven, a task I had not undertaken since the Berlin Wall came down. I wrote to the publisher proposing that the chapter be cut on grounds of pace, and received a reply so courteous that it could only have been written by someone who had not read it. On the fourth morning I climbed the four flights with a bag of shopping, felt the old ankle protest as it always does, and counted the steps aloud in the stairwell, quietly, as I have done since childhood, and understood that I had been counting them for the whole of this book.

That afternoon I translated the chapter as it stood. Eleven visits. Eleven, in plain English, with no adverbs to cushion the fall. My hands, I noticed, were perfectly steady, and that frightened me more than a tremor would have done, because a steady hand is only a sign that the heart has stopped arguing.

When I had finished, I did something I have not done since I was a girl. I went to the window, opened it, and said the number into the evening air, once, aloud, to see whether the street would object. The street did not. A man walked a dog. A bus sighed at the corner. The world, as ever, was too busy to forgive me, and for that small mercy I was almost grateful.

parts.title: Part 4: The Missing Verb
parts.intro: The final pages arrive, and the narrator must choose how a sentence, and perhaps a life, will end.
paragraphs: The last chapter reached me on the twenty-third of December, which is to say that I reached it, having approached it for weeks in the manner of a swimmer testing cold water with one toe. It was only four pages long. Voss, who had never hurried anything, seemed to have lost patience with himself in the closing stretch, and the sentences came shorter, plainer, stripped of their ropes and rigging, like a ship that has decided to stop pretending it is going anywhere but home.

I have withheld one fact until now, and you will forgive me; a translator, like a good host, saves the cheese for the end. In the final chapter we learn that Ilka, the ropemaker's daughter, has spent her life translating other people's books. She sits at her kitchen table with a stranger's manuscript, a cup of sweet tea going cold at her elbow, and discovers that the pages describe her. She laughs. She tells herself it is coincidence. She is, Voss writes, 'a woman not given to fancy.'
I read that line eleven times, which seemed fitting.

There was a second discovery, smaller and in some ways worse. I had spent a month admiring Voss's typescript for its clean, old-fashioned look, and only now, in the clear light of a winter morning, did I notice that the lowercase e sinks slightly below the line, a defect that no one would choose and that I would know anywhere. I owned a typewriter with that flaw. I sold it in 1994 to a man who did not give his name and paid, I recall, in coins.
I do not draw conclusions from this. I am a translator, not a detective, and the profession teaches one to distrust anyone who is too sure of what a sentence means.

The book ends in mid-air. Ilka types the final full stop, rises from the table, takes her coat from its hook, and the last line of the manuscript reads, in the original, 'Then Ilka put on her coat and' and there it stops, without a verb, without a full stop, hanging over the white margin like a foot over a stair. Beneath it, in pencil, in a hand that trembles but is not unkind, are three words: 'Yours to finish.'

For a day I did nothing. I let the line sit in the flat like a guest who has not been asked to leave. I thought of the tea, and the cup, and the eleven dates, and the long gravel drive that I have, in the privacy of my own cellar, driven up in my head a great many times without ever once reaching the door. I considered the verbs available to me. A weaker woman would have chosen 'wept', a vainer one 'wrote', and a woman wishing to be admired by the critics would have chosen something with a great deal of weather in it.

On Christmas Eve, at about four in the afternoon, I typed one word, on a modern machine with a perfectly behaved e, and closed the file. I will not tell you which word it was. A translator, like a confessor, is trusted precisely because she is not heard. The publisher may print the book as it stands; the critics may admire or ignore it; the verb, I suspect, will matter only to two people, one of whom is dead.

But I will tell you what happened afterwards, since it is a matter of record. I took the cup down from the shelf, washed it, and placed it, with a certain ceremony, in the cardboard box I had set aside for the post. I looked up the timetable for the inland train. It leaves at ten. I have bought a ticket, as a matter of research, and my coat is on the chair.
Then I went out to the stairs, and, from habit, began to count them aloud. There are sixty-one. I had never known.

parts.title: Part 1: A Note on Veracity
parts.intro: A retired pianist swears to tell the whole truth in his memoirs, and he sounds suspiciously confident about it.
paragraphs: Let me begin, as every honest memoirist does, by swearing on whatever is nearest that I shall tell the truth. At present the nearest object is a biscuit tin, which is not a holy text, but I have found it more reliable than most. It has never once changed its story, and it contains, at last count, three biscuits and a button.

My name is Leopold Fenwick, though the posters of my youth preferred 'Leo Fenwick, Piano', as if there might be some doubt about the instrument. I am seventy-six, I live in a bungalow at the unfashionable end of a seaside town, and I have been, in my time, a concert pianist of what the newspapers once called 'unusual temperament'. Newspapers are generous with that phrase. It covers a multitude of cancelled engagements.

My publisher, a woman named Phyllida Crane, has asked for a memoir. She sent a letter in which the word 'legacy' appeared four times and the word 'deadline' only twice, which I took as a mark of respect. Phyllida is perhaps forty and carries a red pencil the way other people carry a small, well-trained dog: affectionately, but with the clear understanding that it can bite. I imagine she will want to correct me. I intend to make that difficult by being right.

Here, then, are the principles of this book. First, nothing will be exaggerated. Second, nothing will be flattered, least of all the author. Third, where my memory and the documents disagree, I shall side with the documents, although I should add that most of the documents were lost in a flood in 1994, so the principle is largely theoretical, like honesty in politics. Memory, I have always maintained, is a poor accountant but a magnificent novelist, and I prefer, whenever possible, to employ the novelist.

I shall begin with the facts that are beyond dispute. In 1971 I played the Beethoven fourth concerto at Carnegie Hall, to a full house, under a conductor who wept openly in the second movement. I remember the dark velvet of the seats, the particular cough of a man in the third row, and the cold marble smell of the stage door afterwards, where a young woman asked me to sign a programme and I wrote, with a flourish I am still proud of, 'To Margaret, who listened.'

I mention the programme because it survives. It is in a drawer, in this room, beneath a stapler and a clutch of expired guarantees. I have looked at it only briefly. I have no need to look at it again, for the simple reason that nothing in it could possibly surprise me.

The conductor, I should say, was Sir Aldous Penrose, a man of such ferocious dignity that he once reprimanded an oboe for sneezing out of tune. He told me afterwards that I had played like a man who had never been told that music was difficult. It was the finest compliment of my career, and it was, I now realise, as ambiguous as most compliments from conductors.

Phyllida has written 'Source?' in the margin of the first draft, beside that remark. I have crossed it out. A source is merely a memory with a better lawyer. Besides, Sir Aldous is dead, as are the man with the cough and, I suspect, the velvet, and the dead are notoriously poor at filing objections.

So we begin. Let the record show that the author is of sound mind, reasonable health, and only moderately bitter. Whatever follows, I ask you to remember that I warned you in the first chapter that I would be perfectly honest, and that a man who announces his honesty so early is either a saint or a very careful liar. I leave you to decide which, and, I confess, to do so in the dark.

parts.title: Part 2: The Prodigy of Cobbler's Row
parts.intro: Leo recalls his childhood genius, and his sister-in-law remembers it rather differently.
paragraphs: I was born in 1949, in the front bedroom of a terraced house on Cobbler's Row, during a thunderstorm so dramatic that the midwife later claimed it had been arranged. My father, Walter Fenwick, was a piano tuner, which is to say a man who spent his life correcting other people's instruments and, by extension, their characters. My mother, Ada, ran the household with the severity of a small, underfunded navy.

It is a matter of record that I played Bach at the age of five. I remember it with perfect clarity: the Prelude in C major, performed for the neighbours on a Sunday afternoon, while my father stood in the doorway with his tuning fork held aloft like a man about to bless the congregation. Mrs Pettigrew from number nine wept. Her husband, who disliked music and most other things, asked for a second helping of trifle, which in that house was the equivalent of a standing ovation.

I should deal at once with the rumour, circulated by my late brother Francis, that I could not play a note before the age of nine. Francis was jealous. He was also, to be fair, present, which is the sort of inconvenience that every memoirist learns to rise above.

The instrument itself was an upright of great age and uncertain morals, which my father had accepted in lieu of payment from a widow in Hexham. Its middle C stuck unless struck with a sort of persuasive tenderness, and the lowest octave sounded like furniture being moved in a distant flat. Critics later praised my 'distinctive touch', my 'unhurried attack', my 'extraordinary sensitivity to the weight of a single note'. I have never corrected them. It is not for a man to explain that the weight in question was a sticking hammer.

My father taught me nothing, as a matter of principle. He believed that a child should discover music the way a person discovers a draught: by suddenly noticing it and then being unable to stop. Every evening he tuned the piano a little wrong, deliberately, so that I would have to listen. I would like to say that this was pedagogical genius. It is more likely that he was tired.

There was, of course, the matter of the Bach. In the interest of completeness, and because Phyllida has begun to hover, I asked my sister-in-law Dorothy about that Sunday afternoon. She is ninety-one, sharp as a drawing pin, and lives in a care home where the tea is a disgrace. She told me that the piece I played was not the Prelude in C major but 'a sort of march, with a great many mistakes', that I was not five but nearer eight, and that the only person who wept was my mother, who had hoped for something shorter.

I note these corrections with the calm of a man who has never needed them. A prodigy is not defined by arithmetic. If I was eight, I was a very young eight, and if it was a march, it was a march with Bach in its heart, and I will thank Francis's widow to keep her recollections for the crossword.

One detail, however, I can vouch for absolutely. When the guests had gone, my father closed the lid of the piano and sat beside me in the dark front room, and neither of us said anything for a very long time. Later I would spend a career in halls where silence was something the audience paid for. None of it ever equalled that room, which smelled of polish and gravy and was, as far as I can reconstruct, the only place where I have ever been completely believed.

parts.title: Part 3: The Silver Cup
parts.intro: Leo recounts how he beat his great rival at the conservatoire, and then examines the archive.
paragraphs: At seventeen I was admitted to the Royal Northern Conservatoire, a building of such confident ugliness that one assumed it had been designed by someone who disliked music. I arrived with one suitcase, one borrowed overcoat, and a settled conviction that I was the most gifted person in the north of England. The conviction lasted until lunchtime, when I heard Tobias Rennick practising in Room 14.

I shall be brief about Tobias, since he does not deserve length. He was tall, pale, and in possession of a left hand that could have been used to settle international disputes. He played Chopin as if he were dictating it to the composer. He was also unfailingly polite, which I found unforgivable. I have often compared our rivalry to that of Mozart and Salieri, and have always been careful to explain that I was Mozart.

In the spring of 1967 we both entered the Harcourt Prize, the most coveted competition in the college and, in its modest way, the Olympic Games of the sitting-down professions. There were nine finalists, a panel of five judges, and a silver cup of such grotesque size that it was rumoured to have been used as a font. I played the Schumann Fantasie. I played it with a fury that I attribute to an unhappy breakfast. When the final chord faded, there was a silence of the kind that is later described as 'profound' by the people who caused it.

The cup went to me. I recall the weight of it, the cold of the metal, and Tobias's smile as he shook my hand, a smile with something dignified and wounded in it, as if he were being gracious about an amputation. I carried that cup through three lodgings and one regrettable flat, and it stood on every mantelpiece I owned until I discovered that polishing it was beneath me.

A word about my teacher, Madame Orlova, who had once played for a tsar, or possibly for a man who resembled one. She was eighty if she was a day and taught entirely by sighing. One sigh meant 'faster', two meant 'slower', and three, which I heard rather often, meant that I should consider a career in the civil service. She told me once that talent was a loan from the future and that the future always collected. I assumed she was talking about Tobias.

I should, in fairness, set down the other version, because Phyllida has been circling my desk with the expression of a woman who has already opened the file. According to the college archive, which a pleasant young librarian was kind enough to photograph and send me, the Harcourt Prize of 1967 was awarded to T. Rennick. I was listed seventh of nine finalists, and was 'Highly Commended', a distinction that took the form of a certificate the size and shape of a bookmark.

I have examined this evidence carefully, and I find it misleading. Archives are compiled by clerks, and clerks have always favoured the neat over the true. It is entirely possible that the clerk simply transposed our names, as clerks do, and that Tobias has been living off my cup for half a century. I could, naturally, ask him. I have no intention of doing so. Some questions are best left in the care of the unanswered.

As for the cup itself, I will say only that I know exactly where it is. It is in a place of honour, in this very house, beside the biscuit tin. Or it was. There was a period in the nineties when it was used, I am told, as an umbrella stand by a former landlord, and it may well still be doing that somewhere, protecting someone's umbrellas with a dignity the original prize was never required to show.

parts.title: Part 4: The Programme in the Drawer
parts.intro: Under pressure from his editor, Leo finally reads the programme he keeps beneath the stapler.
paragraphs: Phyllida telephoned on Monday, which is a day I have always regarded as a clerical error. She wished to know whether I had, as promised in my first chapter, looked at the Carnegie programme. I said that I had looked at it briefly. She said that 'briefly' was not a word she associated with honest research. I told her I would consult it at once, and I put the telephone down with the dignity of a man hanging up on a minor deity.

The drawer, when I opened it, released a smell of old paper and mild reproach. There lay the stapler, the guarantees, and, beneath them, a single folded sheet of cream-coloured card that had once, no doubt, been crisp. I unfolded it with the care usually reserved for defusing things. Across the top, in a typeface that might be called ambitious, were the words: 'Spring Benefit for the Friends of the Municipal Band'.

I read this twice. I then read the next line, which gave the venue as 'Rehearsal Room B, Third Floor, Carnegie Hall', the date as a Tuesday afternoon, and the starting time as two o'clock, an hour at which no great artist has ever been fully awake. The programme listed a raffle, a speech by the Treasurer, and, at the bottom, 'Beethoven: Piano Concerto No. 4 (first movement only), L. Fenwick, accompanied by the Riverside Amateur Strings'.

I am, as the reader will have gathered, a reasonable man, so I shall merely observe that every word of this document is technically compatible with my account. It was Carnegie Hall. It was the fourth concerto. It was a full house, if one agrees that thirty-one people can fill a room, and I would argue that, in a small room, thirty-one people are an audience of almost suffocating intimacy. The velvet seats, I concede, were folding chairs. But the velvet in my memory is not a lie; it is an upgrade.

The conductor is a graver problem. The programme names him as 'Mr A. Penny', and a handwritten note beside it, in my own unmistakable scrawl, reads 'choirmaster, Presbyterian, sneezes'. Sir Aldous Penrose, then, did not exist, or exists only in the way that great men exist in the memory of those who have spent too long among small ones. I have no explanation for the title, except that 'Mr Penny' lacks a certain gravity, and that the sneezing, at least, is accurate. The tears in the second movement were hay fever. I have since come to suspect that this is true of most tears in concert halls.

There remains the matter of Margaret. For fifty years I have cherished the image of a young woman at the stage door, her face turned up like a sunflower, and my hand moving across her programme in a gesture of mingled modesty and genius. I rang my cousin Nell, who was present at most of my youth and some of my adulthood. 'Margaret?' said Nell. 'That was your Aunt Margaret. She came for the sandwiches. She was sixty-three, and she asked you to sign it because she thought you were the man who had brought the urn.'

I allowed this to settle for a while, in the manner of tea. Then I did what any responsible author would do. I wrote to Phyllida and told her that the memoir would, after all, describe the Carnegie evening as 'a fully authenticated engagement at an internationally famous address', which I submit is the exact truth, and which has the added merit of being impossible to disprove.

She replied within the hour. Her message consisted of a single line: 'Why does the programme say "first movement only"?' I have not yet answered. I am told that dignity is the last thing to go. I suspect that mine left some time before the furniture.

parts.title: Part 5: A Letter from Lisbon
parts.intro: Leo tells the sad story of his marriage, until a letter arrives from the woman herself.
paragraphs: It is a truth universally acknowledged that a man in possession of a bad memory must be in want of a good wife, and I had one. Her name was Celeste Marchetti, she played the cello, and she was, in my considered opinion, the only person in the Western Hemisphere who could make Brahms sound like a reasonable man. We were married in 1976 in a registry office where the registrar mispronounced both our names and, I felt at the time, our prospects.

I come now to the painful part, which I shall treat with the restraint it deserves. In 1979, Celeste left me. She left for a conductor named Marcello Bruni, a man with a magnificent head of hair and, as far as I could ever detect, no opinions. I returned one afternoon from a tour of the Midlands to find the cello gone from its corner and a note on the piano that said, simply, 'Gone to rehearse.' I have always admired that note. It is the finest piece of understatement ever composed in this country.

For months I wandered the flat like a ghost who has lost the instructions. I wrote melancholy music, which was admired, and drank cold tea, which was not. People said that grief had made me a deeper artist, and I did not contradict them, since I was in no position to prove that it was merely indigestion. Phyllida has asked whether any of that music survives. I told her that it does, and that she should hope it does not.

I have not seen Celeste for forty years, and I have no wish to. Imagine my irritation, therefore, when a letter arrived last Thursday, postmarked Lisbon, in the large, impatient handwriting that I had last seen on a note about milk. I considered burning it unread. Instead, I read it eleven times, once aloud, for the benefit of the biscuit tin.

'Dear Leo,' she wrote. 'Phyllida Crane has been kind enough to send me the chapter in which I run off with Marcello. I laughed so much that my neighbour came to check on me. Marcello Bruni sold us our refrigerator, and has never conducted anything except the occasional argument with his wife. I did not leave you for a man, my dear. I left you for a quieter life, and for a farm of pomegranates in the Alentejo, which has been, on balance, a better listener.'

'The note said "Gone to rehearse",' she continued, 'because you never once asked where I was going, and I wished to give you the chance. You were, of course, in the bath, composing, and did not hear me say goodbye. You did not hear me say it four times. I stood on the landing with the cello and counted the bubbles.'

I present the letter here in full, not because I consider it accurate, but because a historian must preserve even the testimony of the hostile. Celeste has always had a gift for revision. She once told a waiter that I had written the menu, and he asked for my autograph, so the evidence is mixed.

And yet. After her signature there is a postscript, which I record merely for completeness. 'P.S. Dear Leo, I was at Carnegie. Third row. I kept the programme too. Yours was better than you remember, and shorter than you say.' I have put the letter in the drawer with the programme. I notice that the drawer is beginning to resemble a small and rather unforgiving court of law.

parts.title: Part 6: Nocturne for a Tuesday
parts.intro: The famous recording that made Leo's name turns out to have a longer history than he remembers.
paragraphs: Every artist has one work by which the world insists on remembering him, and the world, in my case, has chosen 'Nocturne for a Tuesday', a piece of eleven minutes and forty seconds that has been used to sell sofas, to console the bereaved, and, on one occasion, to calm a hospital lift. It is, I am told, my masterpiece. I tolerate this the way a man tolerates a nickname from his schooldays.

The facts of its creation are simple and, I believe, rather beautiful. On the night of the fourteenth of March, 1974, I woke at three in the morning with the whole melody in my head, entire and glowing, like a lamp somebody had left on in a house I did not know I owned. I walked to the studio in my overcoat and pyjamas, sat at the piano, and played it once, straight through, without a single revision. The engineer wept. The tape was never touched. It is, as the critics have noted, the sound of an artist taken by surprise by himself.

I have told this story at dinners for fifty years, and it has never failed to produce a respectful silence followed by a request for the salt. I have occasionally been asked how the engineer, a man named Gordon Pike, came to be at the studio at three in the morning. I reply that great art attracts witnesses, as honey attracts bears, and I leave the matter there.

It is a story, I might add, with a distinguished literary ancestry. Coleridge dreamed his Kubla Khan in a doze and wrote it down in a single burst, until a person from Porlock came knocking and ruined everything. I, too, was nearly interrupted. A milk float went by during the sixth minute. You can hear it, if you listen, as a faint rattle. The critics call it 'the heartbeat of the city'. It is, in fact, a milk float, but I have long ceased to argue with promotion.

Last month, a young man from the archive of a record company wrote to tell me that they had discovered, in a vault, the full session tapes of that night. He asked if I would care to hear them. I said I would be delighted, in the voice of a man who is not delighted. He sent them by courier, in a box with a sticker that said 'Fragile', which seemed to me tactless.

I listened on Sunday. The tapes ran to nearly nine hours. They began at ten in the morning, with Gordon Pike saying, 'Take one, Mr Fenwick, whenever you're ready.' There followed a take two, a take three, and so on, in what I can only describe as a long and increasingly weary meditation on a single melody. The version known to the world is take thirty-eight. I know it because the slate is clearly marked, and because on take thirty-seven, in a small but audible voice, I say a word I will not reproduce.

Phyllida, who has been given the tapes, says that at no point do they contain anyone weeping, and that the milk float appears in takes nineteen, twenty-six and thirty-eight, which suggests that it was either a very punctual milk float or a deeply loyal one. I say only that memory is a kind of editing, and that I have simply trimmed thirty-seven takes from the story, as Gordon Pike trimmed them from the tape.

There is one further discovery, which I mention only because I promised the reader complete candour. At the very start of take one, before I begin, a woman's voice can be heard humming the opening phrase, quite clearly, and rather better than I play it. The label identifies her as 'O. Vance, page-turner'. I have no recollection of anyone called Vance. The humming is, of course, a piece of unfortunate studio noise.

parts.title: Part 7: The Wise Silence
parts.intro: Leo explains his retirement as the dignified exit of an artist, and others offer less flattering explanations.
paragraphs: Rossini retired from opera at thirty-seven and spent the rest of his life eating, and Sibelius lived thirty years in silence after his Seventh Symphony without anyone being sure whether he had stopped composing or merely stopped finishing. I mention these gentlemen because I intend to stand beside them in the history of the well-judged exit. I retired in 1988, at the summit of my powers, in a single, dignified announcement. The newspapers called it 'a loss to the nation'. I have kept the cutting, which is more than the nation did.

The decision was entirely artistic. I felt, as I climbed the steps to the platform of a hall in Leeds, that I had said everything the piano could say to me, and that anything further would be repetition. A true artist knows when to leave the stage, as a good guest knows when to leave a party: just before the hosts start looking at the clock. I therefore gave a farewell recital, laid my hands on the lid of the piano one last time, and walked into a quiet and well-earned silence.

I should record, since the memoir demands it, that a few uncharitable souls have suggested other reasons. My cousin Nell maintains that my right hand had by then become, in her words, 'a bag of angry twigs'. It is true that I had developed a certain stiffness in two fingers. I have always regarded it as a sort of editorial comment from my own body, and, like all editors, it arrived rather late.

There was also the matter of the review. I mention it only to dispose of it. A critic on a Manchester newspaper, a young man with an unfortunate moustache, wrote of my final tour that 'Mr Fenwick played all the right notes, though not necessarily in the right order.' I wish to make clear that this line was stolen from a comedian, who had himself stolen it from a conductor. It is therefore not a review but a folk saying, and no more applicable to me than 'a stitch in time'.

No one accepts a folk saying as the reason for a career's end. I did, however, write that week to my agent, Bertram Soames, a gentle man in a waistcoat who represented me for twenty-two years and understood, I think, almost nothing about me. I enclosed my farewell statement. His reply was a single sentence: 'Splendid, Leo, I shall have the posters withdrawn from the other eleven towns.'

I have been told that the eleven towns had all sold out, and I find it hard to believe. A man of my reputation, booked into eleven towns in a single month? One does not, I think, associate such a schedule with a man at the summit of his powers. One associates it with a man who needs the money.

The truth, if one insists upon the word, is that I stopped because the audiences were no longer certain whether I would arrive. The telephone, which had once rung with offers, began to ring with enquiries, and then with condolences, and then, in the end, not at all. Silence, as I discovered, is only wise when one has chosen it. When it is chosen for one, it is merely quiet.

I do not, of course, regret it. Regret is the occupation of those who still believe the past could be improved, and I have no such illusions, having tried it repeatedly in these pages. Rossini had his cooking. Sibelius had his cigars. I have a bungalow, a biscuit tin, and a view of the sea that is regarded as magnificent by those who stand on the correct side of the kitchen.

parts.title: Part 8: Lemon Cake and Other Evidence
parts.intro: Leo invites his old rival to tea, expecting to gloat, and gets an unexpected surprise.
paragraphs: I invited Tobias Rennick to tea. I did so, I should explain, for purely scientific reasons, in the spirit of a naturalist who wishes to observe a rare bird in its habitat. I also hoped to be gracious in victory, an activity I had not had the chance to practise in some decades. Phyllida had traced him in an afternoon to a retirement flat in Harrogate, and he accepted by return of post, in handwriting so elegant that I resented it.

He arrived on Thursday at four, exactly, leaning on a stick of polished ebony and carrying a lemon cake in a tin. He was seventy-seven, thinner than I remembered, and the famous left hand trembled slightly as he set the tin on my kitchen table. I looked at it with the suspicion that any man feels towards a gift from a rival. Then he lifted the lid, and the smell of lemon and butter filled the room, and I was suddenly seventeen, in a corridor of the Conservatoire, being offered a slice by a tall, polite boy whom I intended to despise.

Proust, as everyone is obliged to remember, was undone by a small cake dipped in tea, and spent several thousand pages recovering. I was luckier. I was undone for approximately four seconds, which I used to say, 'Do sit down.'

We talked of the Conservatoire, and I was careful to be generous. I told him that I had always known the Harcourt Prize might have gone either way, and that I held no grudge about his poor showing. Tobias looked at me with the tenderness one reserves for the very old and the very small. 'Leo,' he said, 'I have wanted to say this for fifty-five years. You were magnificent that day. I came second, and I spent a decade telling anyone who would listen that the judges were deaf. I am so sorry.'

I put down my cup, a chipped one, I am afraid, though not blue. 'Second?' I said. 'Tobias, you won. I have the archive on this very table.' I fetched the photograph, and he put on a pair of glasses of extraordinary thickness and read it twice, with his lips moving. 'Rennick, T.,' he said at last. 'Well. That does look like me.'

There followed a silence in which two old men, each of whom had spent half a century nursing a defeat, discovered that the other had been nursing a victory. I will not describe it. I am a pianist, not a poet, and the silence did that kind of thing better than I could. I will say only that Tobias began to laugh, and that I, having no dignity in reserve, began to laugh as well, and that the lemon cake suffered.

We agreed, eventually, that the other man had deserved the cup, which I believe is the only unanimous verdict in the history of the Harcourt Prize. We also agreed that the archive might be mistaken, since archives are compiled by clerks. I record, however, that Tobias did not share my low view of the profession. 'The clerk,' he said, 'was Miriam. I married her in 1969. She was never wrong about anything.'

He stayed until the light went. At the door he held my hand a moment longer than manners required and said, 'You know, you really did play the Schumann like a man who had never been told that music was difficult.' I stood on the step for a long time after the taxi had gone. It was, as it happens, the very sentence I had given to Sir Aldous Penrose, who never existed, and I have not yet decided whether I borrowed it from Tobias or he from me. Phyllida will certainly ask for a source.

parts.title: Part 9: Emotional Accuracy
parts.intro: Phyllida arrives with a folder of corrections and an unexpected proposal.
paragraphs: Phyllida arrived by the ten o'clock train, wearing a raincoat the colour of an apology and carrying a folder so thick that the biscuit tin seemed, by comparison, a minor character. She declined tea, which I took as a bad sign, and sat at the kitchen table with the posture of a surgeon who has been told that the patient is talkative.

'I have checked everything,' she said. 'Nell, Dorothy, Celeste, the archive, the record company, a retired registrar in Ealing.' She opened the folder. 'You have claimed, to date, that you played Carnegie Hall, that you won the Harcourt Prize, that you played the Bach at five, that you improvised the Nocturne in one take, and that you retired at the summit of your powers. I have found something to correct in each of these. I have also found that the registrar, who is ninety, says she pronounced both your names perfectly, and that you were an hour late.'

I said nothing for a while. Then I delivered, with some feeling, a speech I had prepared in the bath. A memoir, I said, is not a deposition. It is not an inventory of what happened but an account of what it was like, and any competent reader knows that the second kind of truth is the more demanding. I called it emotional accuracy. I said the phrase twice, in case it should be needed in court.

'Emotional accuracy,' Phyllida repeated, in the tone of a woman tasting something she suspects has been left out. 'Leo, I have read the first eight chapters nine times. Do you know what I noticed? In every chapter, you tell me you are being honest, and then you tell me something that cannot be true, and then, two pages later, you tell me, quite cheerfully, that it was not. You are the only narrator I have ever met who does his own fact-checking and then publishes the results.'

I began to protest, but she held up a hand. 'It is not a flaw,' she said. 'It is the book. Sterne did it in Tristram Shandy, in which the hero takes so long to describe his own birth that he is not born until the third volume. Borges imagined a map as large as the empire it describes. Nobody has ever managed to put a whole life on a page, so the next best thing is to show the man trying, and failing, in front of everybody.'

I should like to say that I took this well. I took it as a man takes a compliment from a dentist: with gratitude and a certain wariness about where it was leading. 'You want me,' I said, 'to publish the mistakes.' 'I want you to publish both,' said Phyllida. 'The version you wanted and the version I found. With footnotes. In the end, a reader will believe the footnotes, and fall in love with the man who needed them.'

I considered the proposal for the length of a long, hostile silence, and then I said that I would think about it, which in my experience is what people say before they agree. Phyllida smiled for the first time that morning, with the faint, tired satisfaction of a gardener who has finally persuaded a tree to grow in the right direction. She accepted a cup of tea.

At the door she paused and said, as if she had only just remembered it, 'By the way, Leo, I looked for the piano. The one from Cobbler's Row, with the sticking middle C. The widow in Hexham says that her piano was a spinet, and that she never gave it to anyone. Whose piano did you learn on?' I replied that this was a profound question. She said it was a practical one. She left on the eleven-forty, and I stood in the hall for some time, listening to the house, which has never quite agreed with anyone about anything.

parts.title: Part 10: The Preface, Revised
parts.intro: Leo rewrites his preface after one last discovery inside the piano.
paragraphs: I have rewritten the preface. It was Phyllida's idea, and I resisted it for nearly four hours, which by my standards amounts to surrender. The new version is short, sober, and written in the plain style of a man with nothing to hide. It begins, as every honest preface should, by swearing on the nearest object. This time the nearest object was the piano, which seemed to me a more reliable witness than a biscuit tin, though it has, I admit, the same tendency to keep its counsel.

I should therefore deal with the piano. It stands against the wall of my front room, an upright of great age and, as Phyllida has been unkind enough to suggest, uncertain provenance. Its middle C sticks. I have always told people that it was my father's, accepted in lieu of payment from a widow in Hexham, and that I have carried it, like a wounded comrade, through every address of my life.

On Saturday, for the first time in thirty years, I opened the lid and looked inside. Behind the lowest octave, written in pencil on the wood in a small, upright hand, was a note: 'W. Fenwick. Bought for twelve pounds at the Crown and Anchor, Dec. 1953. Middle C sticks; do not fix. L. needs to listen.' I read it three times. It was the only sentence of my father's that I had ever seen in writing, and it was, I should add, the only sentence of his that nobody has ever misquoted.

So there was no widow. There was a pub, a dozen pounds, and a man who understood that a boy who has to coax one note will learn to hear all the others. I sat down on the stool and, before I could stop myself, I played. Not the Bach, and not a march. I played the opening of the Nocturne as I now know it must have sounded in take one, hesitant and plain, with the middle C sticking exactly where it had always stuck.

I am not a sentimental man. I played for about an hour, the stiff fingers complaining, the house listening. At some point I became aware of a small sound from the doorway, and I turned and found no one there; it was, I think, the radiator, which has a great sense of occasion. I mention it because Celeste wrote that I had played better than I remember. I now suspect that this is the only compliment of my life that was not ambiguous.

Phyllida has accepted the new arrangement. The book will carry two columns: what I said and what was found, side by side, like a bilingual edition of a language I have never entirely learned. Celeste will write a foreword, if I behave. Tobias has promised to review it, a decision I regard as rash in a man who still owes me a cup. We are, I am told, in the first bloom of a late friendship, which proceeds by letter.

And so, to end where honest books end, with a final declaration. I have told you everything in these pages that matters. Where I erred, Phyllida has footnoted me; where I embroidered, Nell has corrected me; where I forgot, the dead have been kind enough to say nothing. If you remember one thing, remember that I was loved by a cellist, taught by a piano tuner, and humbled, for the better, by a lemon cake. Everything else is a matter of record, and the record, as you have seen, is in excellent hands.

I will put down my pen now. The sea is doing something theatrical against the rocks, the kettle is complaining, and there is a faint, patient knocking from the front room that I have decided to treat as the radiator. Let the record show that I have written this book with a clear conscience and a steady hand. Let it also show, in the interest of the strictest accuracy, that I have never in my life owned a biscuit tin.

parts.title: The Myth of the Untranslatable
parts.intro: An essay on what is truly lost when words cross a border.
paragraphs: Every few months, a list circulates online of foreign words said to be impossible to translate: a Portuguese term for a particular longing, a German compound for a mood that has no English equivalent, a Japanese phrase for the quiet beauty of fading things. The lists are charming, and they flatter our sense that languages are windows onto radically different souls. They are also, in an important sense, misleading.

The word untranslatable usually means something more modest than it claims. What the lists really show is that no single word in the target language covers the same ground. But translators rarely work with single words. They work with sentences, paragraphs, whole books, and in that larger space almost anything can be rendered, if not in one stroke then in a phrase, a footnote, or a carefully built context. The German compound that supposedly defeats English can be explained in a sentence; the fact that it takes a sentence is a fact about English vocabulary, not about the limits of thought.

Yet it would be equally naive to conclude that nothing is ever lost. Translation does not fail at the level of meaning so much as at the level of texture. A poem depends on sound, rhythm, and the faint associations that cling to words through centuries of use. A rhyme cannot survive the journey intact, because the words that rhyme in one language rarely share a meaning with those that rhyme in another. The translator must therefore decide what to sacrifice: the sense, the music, or the tone. There is no formula for the choice, and two excellent translators will often disagree.

This is why the old Italian quip, which equates translators with traitors, has endured. It captures a genuine discomfort. Every translation is a series of small betrayals, undertaken in the hope of a larger fidelity. Literal accuracy can produce a text that is faithful to the dictionary and false to the author, stiff where the original was supple, grammatical where it was daring. A free rendering may restore the original effect while quietly rewriting its content. Neither path is innocent.

What the debate often overlooks is the translator as a writer in their own right. A good translation is not a transparent pane of glass through which the original shines unaltered; it is a second performance of the work, with its own interpretive choices. We readily accept that two pianists can play the same sonata differently and that both may be legitimate. We are slower to grant the same latitude to people who carry novels across languages, perhaps because the words on the page look so deceptively stable.

There is, finally, a paradox in the romance of the untranslatable. The very fact that we can discuss a foreign word, explain its shades, and feel its pull shows that translation is already succeeding. We could not be moved by a concept we were wholly unable to grasp. The so-called gaps between languages are crossed constantly, in conversation, in the classroom, in the quiet work of anyone who has tried to explain a joke to a friend from elsewhere.

The most honest position is perhaps a middle one. Languages do carve up experience differently, and habits of speech may nudge attention in subtle ways, but they do not imprison us. Translation is difficult, never perfect, and nonetheless possible, and it remains one of the humblest and most remarkable of human achievements. To insist on its impossibility is to flatter ourselves; to insist on its ease is to ignore the labor involved. The truth lies in the effort, and in the grace with which a good translator accepts what must be given up.

parts.title: In Praise and Suspicion of Nostalgia
parts.intro: An essay on why the past looks warmer from a distance.
paragraphs: Nostalgia has had a curious career. The word was coined in the seventeenth century to describe a kind of illness, a physical ache suffered by soldiers and servants far from home, and doctors prescribed remedies as they might for a fever. Today it is more often treated as a mild vice, the affectation of people who insist that music was better, summers were longer, and neighbors were kinder in some unspecified yesterday. Neither view quite does justice to an emotion that is at once common, complicated, and surprisingly useful.

The case against nostalgia is easy to make. It edits. Memory does not store the past as a recording; it reconstructs it each time, and the process favors a flattering version. The tedious afternoons drop away, the humiliations soften, and what remains is a glow that the original moments rarely possessed. To long for such a past is to long for something that never entirely existed. Worse, when this longing migrates from private feeling to public argument, it can become a tool of manipulation. Politicians have long understood that a golden age, however vaguely described, offers an irresistible contrast with an unsatisfactory present.

Yet the dismissal is too quick. Research on the subject, as far as it can be summarized, suggests that nostalgic reflection tends to leave people feeling more connected to others and more confident that their lives have meaning. This should not surprise us. Most nostalgic memories are social ones: a family table, a group of friends, a teacher who noticed something in us. To revisit them is to be reminded that we have been, at some point, held within a web of attachments. The feeling is bittersweet, but the sweetness is not trivial.

There is also a subtle distinction worth drawing between two ways of looking back. One is restorative, and it seeks to rebuild the lost home, to return in fact or in policy to what once was. The other is reflective, and it dwells on the longing itself, accepting that the past is gone while treasuring what it contained. The first is often naive and sometimes dangerous. The second is closer to what artists have always done: novelists, composers, and photographers who turn absence into form.

What makes nostalgia so potent in our own era is perhaps the speed of change. When the familiar disappears within a decade, whether a shop on the corner, a way of working, or a device we learned to love, the sense of loss arrives early, and we begin to mourn things that our grandparents would still have recognized in old age. Technology, paradoxically, feeds the habit by supplying endless archives of our former selves, ready to be scrolled through on a quiet evening.

None of this means that we should surrender to the pull of the past without resistance. A healthy relationship with nostalgia requires a measure of irony, a readiness to ask what has been left out of the picture. Who was excluded from the golden age? Who paid for its comforts? Such questions need not destroy the pleasure of remembering. They simply keep it honest, preventing affection from hardening into a falsehood.

The wisest nostalgic, then, is one who can hold two thoughts at once: that something precious has been lost, and that the loss is partly an invention of the mind. This double vision is not a weakness. It is a mature way of caring about time, of recognizing that every present will one day be somebody's cherished past. If we can learn to look at our own moment with the tenderness we reserve for memories, we might notice, before it is gone, that it was worth loving all along.
