parts.title: Laughing Up, Laughing Down
parts.intro: An essay on humor as an instrument of power and a threat to it.
paragraphs: Rulers have always had an uneasy relationship with laughter. Medieval courts kept professional fools who were permitted to say what no counselor dared; modern dictatorships have jailed comedians for far less. The contradiction is only apparent. A joke is a small act of freedom, and power, whether benevolent or brutal, can never be entirely sure what that freedom will do once it has been let out.

Consider first how humor works against authority. Satire punctures pretension by placing the solemn beside the absurd. A minister who speaks of sacrifice while dining lavishly becomes ridiculous the moment someone draws the two facts together. Laughter, in this sense, is a form of knowledge: it reveals the gap between what an institution claims and what it does. It is also contagious, which makes it politically dangerous. People who hesitate to protest alone may find themselves laughing together, and a crowd that laughs at an official has already begun to withdraw its respect.

But the same instrument can be turned in the opposite direction. Ridicule has been used for centuries to keep the weak in their place. Jokes about minorities, the poor, or the foreign serve to mark a boundary between those who laugh and those who are laughed at, and they do so with a convenient deniability. Anyone who objects can be accused of lacking a sense of humor, as though the problem lay in the listener rather than the joke. The question that matters, then, is not whether a joke is offensive but whom it is aimed at, and what it is quietly doing to the social order.

The old distinction between punching up and punching down is a useful, if imperfect, guide. Humor directed at the powerful tends to function as a corrective; humor directed at the powerless tends to function as a sedative, reassuring the comfortable that the existing arrangement is natural. Yet the distinction cannot settle every case. A joke told by a member of a group about that group's own experience may serve solidarity or self-contempt, depending on who is listening. Context, intention, and effect refuse to line up neatly.

Powerful people, for their part, have learned to adapt. The cleverest politicians now deploy humor themselves, laughing at their own flaws before an opponent can, and thereby disarming mockery in advance. Self-deprecation can be genuinely endearing, but it can also serve as a shield: if a leader treats every criticism as a joke, nothing said against him can be taken seriously. Authoritarian figures have been known to make jokes with a menace in them, in which the audience must laugh on cue, and the laughter becomes a ritual of obedience rather than a release.

This is the strange duality of humor. It can free or it can bind, expose or conceal, bring a community closer or draw a line around it. Its meaning lies not in the words but in the relations they enact. A society in which people can laugh at their rulers without fear is probably a healthy one; a society in which they can laugh only at one another is probably not.

We should be wary, then, of both extremes: the humorless zeal that would police every joke, and the careless assumption that laughter is always innocent. A thoughtful sense of humor includes the capacity to ask, in the middle of a laugh, who is being served by it. That question does not spoil the joke. If anything, it is the mark of an audience mature enough to deserve the best ones.

parts.title: The Lonely Genius and Other Fictions
parts.intro: An essay on why great achievements are rarely the work of one mind.
paragraphs: The image is familiar from a thousand biographies and films: a solitary figure, usually male, usually dishevelled, toiling in an attic until inspiration strikes and the world is changed. It is a flattering picture, for it suggests that greatness is a quality of rare individuals rather than something that might emerge from circumstance. It is also, on closer inspection, largely a fiction.

Begin with the simple matter of timing. Many of the discoveries credited to a single name were made almost simultaneously by several people working independently. When the necessary instruments, mathematical tools, and unanswered questions have accumulated, the discovery becomes, in a sense, ready to be made, and it is made by whoever happens to be standing nearby. Historians have documented this pattern so often that it has acquired a name of its own. The genius, in such cases, is less a lone peak than the highest point of a mountain range.

Then consider the unseen collaborators. Behind the famous novelist stand editors, early readers, and a language inherited from millions of speakers. Behind the celebrated scientist stand technicians, assistants, and rival researchers whose objections sharpened the argument. Many of these contributors are women, or members of groups that were not permitted to claim credit, and the myth of the solitary genius has made their absence seem natural. Remove them from the story and it becomes simpler, and also considerably less true.

The cult of the genius is not merely inaccurate; it carries real costs. It encourages institutions to search for the one extraordinary hire and to neglect the ordinary conditions in which good work flourishes: time, funding, open conversation, and tolerance of failure. It teaches young people that if they are not immediately brilliant, they are not meant for the field, a belief that discourages precisely those who might have become excellent through patient effort. And it excuses bad behavior, since a person who is regarded as irreplaceable can be forgiven almost anything.

None of this is to deny that individuals differ, or that some minds make exceptional leaps. Originality exists, and it deserves admiration. The point is rather that originality is rarely exercised in a vacuum. It generally takes the form of an unexpected combination of existing ideas, which means that the person who combines them needs access to those ideas, and to people who understand them. A great mind in an impoverished environment produces little, however powerful it may be.

If the genius is a fiction, why does it persist? Partly because stories need protagonists. A narrative about a network of colleagues, funding decisions, and gradual refinements does not move us as readily as one about a heroic individual. Partly, too, because the myth serves our own interests: it allows us to admire without feeling obliged to imitate, since genius, by definition, is something we do not possess and therefore cannot be blamed for lacking. Consider how often a breakthrough is retold as a flash of insight, when the surviving notebooks reveal years of false starts, abandoned drafts, and conversations that shaped each step. The tidy anecdote is a kindness to memory, not to truth.

A more accurate picture would honor both the individual and the web of relationships that made the individual possible. It would speak of achievement as something earned collectively and recognized unevenly. Such a picture is less cinematic, but it is more generous and, I suspect, more useful, for it suggests that the conditions of great work are within reach of any community willing to create them.

parts.title: What the Camera Cannot Swear To
parts.intro: An essay on how far a photograph can be trusted.
paragraphs: For much of the nineteenth century, the photograph enjoyed a privileged status among images. A painting was plainly someone's interpretation; a photograph, it was widely assumed, was simply what had been there, recorded by light itself. The phrase the camera never lies entered everyday speech, and with it a faith that has proved remarkably durable, even as evidence against it has accumulated for almost as long as the technology has existed.

The difficulty begins with the most basic act in photography: choosing where to point the device. A frame is a decision about what to include and, more importantly, what to leave out. Two pictures of the same street demonstration, one showing a few angry figures in the foreground and another showing a calm, orderly crowd beyond them, can support entirely opposite stories, and each would be literally accurate. The photograph does not lie in the sense of inventing facts; it tells the truth selectively, which is a more insidious thing.

Then there is the matter of staging. Some of the most celebrated images in history were arranged, or at least adjusted, by the people who made them. Objects were moved, subjects were asked to repeat a gesture, and a second attempt was preferred to the first because it looked more convincing. These interventions were often small and well intended, yet they remind us that a photograph is made rather than found. Its apparent spontaneity may be the product of careful labor.

Editing, of course, has always existed. Darkroom technicians learned to brighten faces, remove blemishes, and, in the worst cases, erase unwelcome people from official portraits. What has changed in the digital age is not the possibility of manipulation but its scale and invisibility. Alterations that once demanded expertise can now be performed in seconds, and entirely synthetic images can be produced by software with a realism that would have astonished earlier generations. The ordinary viewer, confronted with a persuasive picture, no longer has any reliable way to tell whether it corresponds to anything that happened.

One might expect this to produce a healthy skepticism, and in part it has. But skepticism has its own pathology. When every image can be doubted, authentic evidence of real suffering or wrongdoing can be dismissed with a shrug, and those who wish to avoid accountability gain a convenient defense: that is probably fake. The corrosion of trust therefore does damage in both directions, enabling forgeries to be believed and genuine records to be rejected.

What, then, should we ask of a photograph? Perhaps we should stop treating it as testimony and begin treating it as a claim, one that deserves to be weighed against its source, its context, and independent corroboration. A photograph says, in effect, this is how something looked from a particular position at a particular moment, according to a particular person. That statement can be true and still insufficient. The effect can be seen in how readers react to dramatic pictures today: some hurry to share them, others hurry to deny them, and few pause to ask where the image came from.

None of this diminishes the power of the medium. A single image can alter public understanding of an event more profoundly than a thousand pages of argument, precisely because it seems to bypass the intermediary of language. That power is the reason we owe photographs a more disciplined kind of attention. The camera cannot swear to anything. It can only show, and it is our task, as viewers, to ask what we are being shown, by whom, and why.

parts.title: The Uses of Idleness
parts.intro: An essay on leisure, and why it is harder than it looks.
paragraphs: It is one of the oddities of modern life that people who have more free time than any previous generation so often report having none. Machines have shortened the working day for many, yet the sense of being perpetually behind has hardly lifted. Leisure, which every era has praised in the abstract, has become something we pursue anxiously, as if it were another task on the list.

The ancient Greeks distinguished sharply between work and what they called leisure, which for them was not rest but the freedom to engage in activities worthwhile in themselves: thought, conversation, music, civic life. Labor existed for the sake of leisure rather than the other way around. The notion would strike most of us as strange. We tend to justify rest by its usefulness: we sleep to be productive, exercise to stay efficient, and take holidays to return refreshed. Even our relaxation has acquired a performance indicator.

This habit of mind has a history. The rise of industrial discipline taught societies to measure time as a resource that could be spent or wasted. Once the hour became a unit of cost, idleness began to look like a form of loss, and moral language followed economic logic: the idle were not just inefficient but faintly sinful. The attitude outlived the factories that created it and migrated into offices, homes, and, more recently, the devices in our pockets, which make every moment potentially available for work or its imitation.

The consequences are subtle but real. People who cannot be idle often cannot be bored, and boredom, however unpleasant, has a function. It is the state in which attention, no longer commanded by external demands, turns inward and wanders. Many creative insights seem to occur in just such moments, in the shower, on a train, during a walk with no destination. A culture that eliminates empty time may be eliminating the conditions in which new ideas ripen.

There is also a social dimension. Leisure used to be largely shared: festivals, evening strolls, a long meal that lasted until the light failed. Much contemporary leisure is solitary and mediated by screens, and it is often arranged to avoid friction. This is pleasant enough, but friction is part of what binds people. Time spent together without purpose is where friendships quietly deepen, and where communities learn that they are more than a collection of schedules.

It would be unwise, however, to romanticize idleness. For many people, free time is a privilege purchased at someone else's expense, or simply unavailable because of the demands of survival. A serious defense of leisure must acknowledge that its distribution is unequal, and that arguments for slowing down are easiest to make from a comfortable position. The goal should be not a pious praise of doing nothing but a society arranged so that everyone has some hours that belong to them. A holiday that is photographed, rated, and reported on is already half converted into work, and the person who wants simply to sit in the sun may feel guilty for failing to optimize the experience.

What would it mean to use leisure well? Perhaps only this: to engage in something for its own sake and to allow it to be inefficient. To read without taking notes, to walk without counting steps, to talk without an agenda. These are modest acts, but they contain a quiet resistance to the idea that a person is nothing more than what they produce. Idleness, rightly understood, is not the opposite of a meaningful life. It may be one of its preconditions.

parts.title: The City as a Text
parts.intro: An essay on reading streets, signs and ruins as language.
paragraphs: A city can be read. This is more than a metaphor, though it began as one. Anyone who has walked through an unfamiliar neighborhood has performed a kind of interpretation: noticing which shops are open, which buildings are neglected, which streets feel welcoming and which seem to warn you away. The city speaks in architecture, signage, rhythm, and silence, and a patient reader can learn a great deal about its priorities without exchanging a word with anyone who lives there.

The comparison with a book is instructive, but it needs refinement. A book is composed by an author, whereas a city is written by thousands of hands across centuries, none of them in full control. A cathedral is begun by one generation and completed by another; a medieval wall is demolished to make way for a boulevard; a factory becomes a gallery. The result resembles less a novel than a manuscript that has been repeatedly overwritten, in which earlier layers show through the later ones like faint traces of ink beneath a newer text.

Reading such a document demands attention to what has been erased as much as to what remains. Street names, for instance, are a compressed political history: they commemorate heroes, battles, and ideologies, and they are renamed when regimes change. A square named after a revolutionary may later bear the name of a saint, then of a poet, each alteration announcing a new account of who matters. Monuments perform the same task in stone, and the controversies over them reveal how contested a city's story remains.

Yet the most eloquent passages in the urban text are often the unplanned ones. A worn step tells of generations who climbed it. A shop sign repainted many times shows the stubborn persistence of a trade. The informal market that appears every weekend on an empty lot demonstrates a need that official planning did not foresee. These are the idioms of ordinary life, and they escape the grand narratives imposed from above.

Planners have not always been good readers. The twentieth century produced many schemes that treated the city as a blank page, to be cleared and rewritten according to rational principles: wide roads, separated zones, towers set in empty space. Some of these projects were well-meaning, and some produced real improvements, but many destroyed the dense tangle of relationships that had made neighborhoods livable. They paid attention to the grammar and ignored the conversation. Observe how an old quarter, left alone, often develops a character that no designer could have drawn in advance, with narrow lanes, mixed uses, and corners where people linger.

The best contemporary approaches are humbler. They start by listening to existing patterns, asking why people gather where they do, how they cross a square, what makes a street feel safe at night. Intervention then resembles careful editing rather than demolition: a bench here, a crossing there, a protected old facade that anchors the memory of a place. The aim is to add a sentence without ruining the paragraph.

To think of the city as a text is, finally, to recognize that it has readers as well as writers, and that every resident is both. Our daily routes inscribe small marks on the urban fabric, and the fabric shapes us in return. Perhaps this is why a familiar city feels, to those who love it, like an extension of memory itself. We carry it with us long after we have left, and we continue to read it, in dreams, with the confidence of those who know the language by heart.

parts.title: Progress and Its Discontents
parts.intro: An essay on what it means to say that things are getting better.
paragraphs: Few ideas are as deeply embedded in modern thinking as that of progress. We speak of advanced economies and backward customs, of moving forward and falling behind, and the metaphors assume a single road along which societies travel at different speeds. The assumption is so natural that it is rarely examined, and yet it conceals several distinct claims, some of them strongly supported by evidence and others considerably less so.

Begin with what is hard to deny. Over the past two centuries, in most parts of the world, people have come to live longer, to suffer fewer deadly infections, and to enjoy a degree of material comfort that earlier generations would have considered miraculous. Literacy has spread; many forms of cruelty once regarded as ordinary are now widely condemned. Anyone who dismisses these changes as illusions should be invited to spend a week in the dentist's chair of a bygone age.

The trouble starts when technical advance is quietly equated with moral or human advance. Better tools can serve worse purposes. The same knowledge that eases suffering can be turned to destruction, and societies that excel in engineering are not thereby more just or more wise. History offers no guarantee that the curve of capability and the curve of conscience will rise together. Indeed, it suggests that they often diverge, and that the gap between them is where catastrophe tends to occur.

A second difficulty is the question of cost. Progress is rarely free, and its expenses are seldom shared equally. The factory that raised living standards also poisoned rivers and uprooted communities; the highway that shortened journeys divided neighborhoods. Gains tend to be visible and measurable, while losses are diffuse and hard to quantify: the disappearance of a craft, a language, a way of belonging. A ledger that lists only the first kind of entry will always appear to show a profit.

There is, too, a philosophical objection. To call something progress is to assume a destination, and destinations imply values. Yet societies disagree about where they want to go, and even individuals discover that goals attained are not always goals desired. A world that is wealthier, faster, and more connected may nonetheless be one in which many people feel anxious and adrift. The experience of improvement, it seems, depends less on absolute conditions than on expectations, which rise as quickly as circumstances do. It is worth remembering how many improvements, from clean water to schooling, came not from inevitable forces but from stubborn campaigns that many contemporaries thought unrealistic.

None of this should lead to a fashionable pessimism. The belief that everything is declining is as unexamined as the belief that everything is improving, and it has a similar function: it spares us the labor of discrimination. A more useful stance treats progress not as a law of history but as an achievement, local, fragile, and reversible, which has to be defended repeatedly. Rights that were won can be lost; knowledge that was gained can be neglected; institutions that took generations to build can be dismantled within a few years.

Seen in this light, progress is less a force that carries us than a task we undertake. It requires honest measurement, attention to those left behind, and a willingness to ask not only whether something can be done but whether it should be. The word forward is easy to say. The harder question, and the one worth the effort, is always forward toward what.

parts.title: A Defense of Politeness
parts.intro: An essay on why small courtesies matter more than they seem.
paragraphs: Politeness has a poor reputation among people who consider themselves serious. It is dismissed as superficial, a veneer of pleasantries laid over real feelings, and sometimes as outright hypocrisy: why say thank you when you do not feel grateful, or ask after someone's health when you do not much care? Such objections have a certain bracing honesty. They are, I think, mistaken, and the mistake is instructive.

The first error is to suppose that manners are merely decorative. In fact, they are a technology for living among strangers. Human beings are not naturally gentle toward those they do not know, and the situations of modern life, crowded trains, queues, shared offices, put us constantly in contact with people who owe us nothing and whom we may never see again. Courtesy is what makes these encounters tolerable. A small gesture, such as holding a door, signals that the other person is recognized as a person rather than an obstacle, and it does so at almost no cost.

The second error concerns sincerity. It is true that good manners can be performed without warmth, but it does not follow that they are therefore false. When a person says please, the statement is not a report on their emotions; it is a ritual act that acknowledges the other's freedom to refuse. Like a handshake, it has meaning because it is conventional. We would not accuse a bow of lying merely because the bowing person is tired. Etiquette creates a shared language in which respect can be expressed even when affection cannot.

Notice, too, how unevenly the rules vary between cultures. In one society, directness is a sign of honesty; in another, it is an insult. Silence may signal agreement, awkwardness, or contempt. This diversity is sometimes taken as proof that manners are arbitrary, but it shows something subtler: that people everywhere feel the need for rules of regard, and everywhere work out their own. The grammar differs, but the underlying purpose, avoiding needless injury, is remarkably constant. In many places, the same words that sound warm in one setting may sound cold in another, and the sensitive speaker learns to adjust tone as well as vocabulary.

None of this makes politeness invulnerable to abuse. Elaborate courtesy has often been used to exclude, with its subtle codes distinguishing those who belong from those who do not. It can also serve as a mask for cruelty, in which an insult is delivered in flawless diction. And a demand for civility can silence legitimate anger, as when the oppressed are told that their complaint would be heard if only it were phrased more nicely. A wise defender of manners must admit that they can be weapons as well as shields.

But the remedy for abused courtesy is better courtesy, not none. The real alternative to politeness is not honesty but friction, and friction wears people down. A workplace where no one troubles to express thanks, a household where every request is a command, a public square where each person treats the next as a threat: these are not freer places. They are merely colder.

The philosopher might say that manners are the smallest unit of ethics, the point at which a general principle of respect becomes a concrete act. If so, they deserve more attention than they receive. Anyone can profess to love humanity; it takes training to be patient with the person in front of you in line. Seen this way, politeness is not the opposite of authenticity. It is how goodwill learns to behave in public.

parts.title: The Archive and the Art of Forgetting
parts.intro: An essay on what we keep, what we lose, and who decides.
paragraphs: We tend to think of an archive as a defense against forgetting: a place where the past is stored against the erosion of time. The image is comforting, and partly true. But every archive is also, necessarily, an act of selection, and what it preserves is only a thin fraction of what once existed. Behind each collection lies a series of decisions, often invisible, about what was worth keeping and what could be allowed to vanish.

Consider the sheer scale of loss. Most of the documents that have ever been written have disappeared: burned, flooded, discarded in a clearing of attics, or simply never thought important enough to save. What survives is shaped by accident and by power. Official records outlast private letters; the possessions of the wealthy outlast those of the poor; the languages of institutions outlast the speech of those who spoke only to each other. Historians learn early that their sources speak mostly for the people who could afford to be recorded.

Silence, therefore, is itself evidence, though of a difficult kind. When a historian discovers that an entire group is almost absent from the surviving papers, the absence does not prove that the group was unimportant. It more often indicates that someone else controlled the pen. Much recent scholarship has been devoted to reading against the grain of such documents, recovering fragments of lives from court records, tax lists, and the occasional margin note, treating the archive less as a mirror than as a carefully arranged stage.

The digital age has complicated the picture in unexpected ways. We now produce more records than any civilization before us, and the common assumption is that nothing will ever be lost again. The reality is more fragile. Formats become obsolete, platforms close, and files stored on devices that nobody can read are, for practical purposes, gone. A parchment can survive a thousand years in a dry cellar; a digital photograph may not survive two decades without constant maintenance. Abundance, it turns out, does not guarantee memory. It may even undermine it, since the effort of selection is replaced by the habit of keeping everything and finding nothing.

There is also the question of whether forgetting is always a failure. Individuals know that it is not. A mind that retained every detail would be crippled by it, unable to generalize, forgive, or move on. Societies, too, sometimes need to let certain things recede: a bitter grievance, a humiliating episode, a quarrel that serves no one. Reconciliation after conflict often depends on an agreement to leave some wounds unexamined, at least for a time. Yet this tolerance for oblivion is dangerous when it is imposed by the perpetrators, who have every reason to prefer a short memory.

The ethical question, then, is not whether to remember or forget, but who has the authority to decide and on what terms. An archive that is open to scrutiny, that admits its gaps and accepts the contributions of those who were once ignored, is a more honest instrument than one that presents itself as complete. Its honesty lies precisely in the visible seams.

In the end, memory is not a stockpile but a practice, continually renewed by those who consult, question, and reinterpret what has been kept. The archive does not hold the past; it holds the materials from which the present assembles an account of it. That account will always be partial. The obligation is to keep it open to correction, and to remember that behind every neat catalogue lies a larger, silent territory of things that were never written down at all.

parts.title: In Praise of the Committee on Committees
parts.intro: A satirical newspaper editorial reacts to a new body created by the city council.
paragraphs: It is with a sense of civic pride, tempered only by mild vertigo, that we welcome the news that our City Council has voted, eleven to nine with two abstentions and one member lost in the car park, to establish a Committee on Committees. The new body, which will meet monthly in a room yet to be identified, is charged with reviewing the work of the forty-three existing committees and determining which of them might, in the fullness of time, be reviewed.

Critics have been quick to call the measure redundant. They are mistaken. Redundancy implies that something is already being done, and no one familiar with the Council’s record on the Harbour Road resurfacing project, now in its ninth year of consultation, could level that charge. The road, residents will be relieved to learn, remains fully intact in its original condition of disrepair, preserved with a devotion that any heritage society would envy.

The Council’s chair, Councillor Hargreave, defended the proposal with characteristic economy of language, which is to say that she spoke for fifty minutes and said, in effect, that more oversight is better than less. “Oversight,” she observed, “is the quiet engine of democracy.” It is an arresting image, though one wonders whether an engine so quiet has ever been observed to move anything.

Nor should we overlook the budget. The committee will cost taxpayers a modest £212,000 a year, a sum that supporters insist will be recouped through efficiencies identified by the committee itself. This is the kind of reasoning that lets a man buy a second umbrella to find out whether the first one is working. We admire its elegance even as we check our wallets.

A word, too, on transparency, that most fashionable of civic virtues. The Council has promised that every deliberation of the new committee will be open to the public, recorded in full, and published online within a reasonable period, a phrase which, in the municipal dictionary, is defined as “eventually, and in a format no one can open”. Residents wishing to observe proceedings are advised to apply in writing, at least six weeks in advance, to an office that has been closed since March.

There is, to be fair, a case to be made on the other side, and it is this: that a city which cannot decide what to do about a pothole may at least be trusted to decide how to decide. Procedure, after all, is the one product the Council manufactures at scale. Its minutes alone, printed and stacked, would rise higher than the clock tower, a monument of sorts, though one that no tourist has yet asked to photograph.

We therefore propose a modest amendment. Let the Committee on Committees be given, as its first task, a deadline. Not a long one: say, the end of the financial year. Should it fail to report by then, it will be dissolved automatically, and its dissolution referred to a sub-committee for review. If this seems a cruel joke at the Council’s expense, we can only reply that the Council has been supplying the jokes for years; we merely write them down.

Until then, we wish the new committee every success, and we hope it will find its room. The first meeting, we are told, will be held “at a time convenient to all members”, which suggests, correctly, that it will not be held at all.

parts.title: An Open Letter on the Number 9 Bus
parts.intro: Residents of a village write publicly to a transport company that plans to end their bus service.
paragraphs: Dear Mr Penhale, We write to you not as customers, a word that implies a choice, but as residents of Thornby Edge, a village of some six hundred souls which has, until this month, been connected to the rest of the world by the Number 9 bus. Your company’s announcement that the service will be withdrawn from the first of January, citing “sustained under-performance against commercial targets”, reached us on a Friday, which we assume was chosen to ensure that no one could respond before Monday.

We should like, with respect, to dispute the premise. A bus is not a product whose success is measured in margins; it is a thread, and a village is a garment that holds together only so long as its threads do. Consider those who depend on the Number 9: Mrs Okafor, eighty-one, who travels to the hospital for dialysis three times a week; the sixth-formers who reach college by a quarter to nine; the café owner, who has no car and no wish for one; and the many who, being neither old nor young, simply need to be somewhere else for a few hours each day and to come back again.

Your figures, we note, record the number of passengers, but not their reasons. They cannot show that the 7.42 is, for a dozen people, the difference between independence and isolation. Nor do they capture the quiet fact that the early service is filled largely by cleaners and care workers, the very people whose labour your own city depends on and whose wages leave little room for taxis.

We are not naive. We understand that fuel prices have risen, that drivers are hard to retain, and that a route which loses money is, to a shareholder, an affront. But a company that has accepted public subsidy for the last decade, as yours has to the sum of £1.4 million, cannot entirely disown the public it served. If the arithmetic no longer works, we invite you to show it to us; we have among our number an accountant, a retired transport planner, and a woman who has, for forty years, reconciled the parish accounts to the penny.

We therefore make three requests. First, that the withdrawal be postponed by six months, so that alternatives may be explored in good faith. Second, that you meet us here, in the village hall, rather than in a conference room forty miles away where our voices must travel by speakerphone. Third, that you consider a reduced service, even two journeys a day, rather than none, since the difference between something and nothing is greater than any spreadsheet will admit.

We say all this without rancour, though not without feeling. It would be easy to write in anger, and some of our neighbours urged us to. We have preferred to assume that you are a reasonable man in an unreasonable market, and that a reasonable man, shown what is at stake, may yet reconsider. Should we be mistaken, we shall of course continue to make our case, in the press, at the council and, if necessary, on foot, a mode of travel to which, thanks to you, we are about to become reaccustomed. We would, however, much prefer to ride, and to thank you for the privilege in the village newsletter, which we should be delighted to publish.
Yours faithfully, on behalf of the residents of Thornby Edge, Margaret Ellison, Chair, Thornby Edge Parish Council.

parts.title: Salt & Ember: A Restaurant Review
parts.intro: A critic reviews a small fictional seafood restaurant with a very clear point of view.
paragraphs: There is a particular kind of restaurant that announces itself with a hand-lettered sign, a short menu and a refusal to explain anything. Salt & Ember, which opened in the spring in a converted net loft on Harbour Street, is such a place, and I went in prepared to be irritated. I left, three hours later, irritated only that I could not decently order the whole menu again.

The room is spare: whitewashed brick, a long communal table, and a wood-fired oven that glows at the far end like a small, well-behaved sun. The chef, a taciturn woman named Ines Varga, cooks in full view of the diners and speaks to them, as far as I could tell, only through the plate. This is a gamble. It pays off.

Begin with the bread, which arrives blistered and still faintly smoking, accompanied by a cultured butter whipped with burnt-onion ash. It sounds like the sort of thing a restaurant does in order to be photographed. It tastes, instead, like the sort of thing one’s grandmother would have done had she been braver. The crab that follows, dressed with nothing but lemon, a trickle of green oil and a few shavings of fermented radish, is a lesson in restraint; one understands that every ingredient has been asked whether it is truly necessary, and the answers have been honest.

Not everything succeeds. A dish of lamb shoulder, slow-cooked for fourteen hours, is tender to the point of surrender but arrives under a jus so reduced and so salty that it seemed to belong to a different, angrier meal. And the dessert, a burnt-honey custard, is more interesting to describe than to eat; its bitterness, presumably intentional, tipped over into the merely stern.

The wine list is short and intelligent, the work of a sommelier who evidently prefers persuasion to intimidation. There is no vintage here that exists merely to be mentioned. I was steered, with a gentle hand, towards a cloudy white from the cold north that tasted of wet stones and green apples, and I am still thinking about it, which is more than I can say for the bottle I ordered at a considerably grander address last month.

Service is the restaurant’s one real weakness, though even here the failing is of a charming kind. The staff are young, earnest and visibly in love with the food, and they describe each dish with a breathless thoroughness that can add ten minutes to a course. When I asked, merely to be polite, where the salt was harvested, I received a history of the coast. I did not mind; I would simply have preferred to eat the crab while it was cold.

Prices are, by the standards of the neighbourhood, fair rather than cheap. Dinner for two, with wine, comes to about £140. This is not a sum one spends lightly, but nor is it the sort of bill that makes a diner feel mildly robbed, a sensation I have grown to expect, and to resent, in restaurants with considerably grander addresses.

What Salt & Ember offers, in the end, is conviction. Too much of our dining is a form of hedging: the menu that tries to please everyone, the dish that apologises for its own simplicity. Here nobody apologises. The kitchen has decided what it believes about food and cooks accordingly, and one can disagree, as I did about the lamb and the custard, without ever doubting the sincerity of the argument. Go early, book ahead, and bring someone who does not mind being quiet for the first mouthful.

parts.title: The Slow Repair
parts.intro: A personal essay about an impatient person who learns something unexpected from mending an old clock.
paragraphs: When my grandfather died he left me three things: a pair of reading glasses with one arm mended in thread, a drawer of unlabelled keys, and a mantel clock that had not run in thirty years. I wanted, naturally, the glasses. It was the clock that insisted on being dealt with.

I am not a patient person. I answer messages within minutes, I resent lifts that stop at every floor, and I have, on more than one occasion, abandoned a book because the opening chapter declined to hurry. So it was with some embarrassment that, in the January after the funeral, I found myself at a kitchen table with a screwdriver set the size of a pencil case, a jeweller’s loupe, and a video of a Dutch horologist explaining, in a voice of heroic calm, how to remove a mainspring without losing an eye.

The first lesson was humiliating. A clock, once opened, reveals itself to be not a mechanism but an argument: dozens of small wheels, each pressing upon the next, each in a quarrel with gravity and friction that it has been winning, narrowly, for a century. I took it apart in an afternoon and spent the next five weeks failing to put it back. Parts that had fitted perfectly one day refused, with a kind of bland obstinacy, to fit the next.

Somewhere in the third week something shifted. I stopped looking at the clock as a problem to be solved and began to look at it as a conversation to be had. I learned to work in the morning light, when my hands were steadiest. I learned that a tiny bent pivot can be coaxed straight, but not forced. I learned, above all, that the impulse to rush was itself the fault I was meant to repair. Each time I hurried, the clock punished me by dropping a spring into the carpet, where it vanished with the serenity of the truly indifferent.

I will not pretend the transformation was complete. I still check my phone too often, and I suspect I always shall. But there is an hour in the early morning, now, in which I do nothing efficient at all. I clean a wheel. I oil a bearing with a needle dipped in something that costs more per millilitre than champagne. I think about my grandfather, who must have sat at this same sort of table, and who, I now realise, was never idle in the way I had mistaken him for, but attentive, which is a very different thing.

The clock ran on a Sunday in late February. There was no ceremony. I wound it, set the pendulum swinging with one finger, and stepped back, expecting nothing. For a long moment there was only silence, and then the first tick fell into the room, dry and unhurried, like a coin dropped into a well. I found that I was holding my breath, and that my eyes had, rather absurdly, filled.

It keeps poor time, as it happens, losing about four minutes a day. I have decided not to mind. A clock that is always right is merely a servant; one that is a little wrong, and known to be, is a companion. I now set it by hand each Sunday, in a small ritual of forgiveness, and it is the only thing in the house that I never think of as running late, since it has taught me that being late, like being early, is only a matter of what one expects of time.

parts.title: Obituary: Ottilie Marchetti, the Piano Tuner Who Kept a Town in Key
parts.intro: A newspaper obituary of a fictional piano tuner, written with warmth and gentle humour.
paragraphs: Ottilie Marchetti, who for fifty-three years tuned every piano in the valley town of Corrow and, by common consent, improved the moral character of most of them, died on Tuesday at her home above the old tannery. She was ninety-one. The cause was heart failure, though those who knew her insist that she had simply finished the job.

Born in 1934 to a family of cheesemakers with no musical ambitions whatever, she discovered her vocation at nine, when a neighbour’s upright piano, abandoned in a cart outside the chapel, began to produce a sound she described years later as “a choir of cats in mourning”. She asked to be allowed to fix it. Told that she was a child and that pianos were not toys, she fixed it anyway, using a hairpin, a candle stub and a tuning fork borrowed, without permission, from the church.

She trained in the capital under a Czech master known for his temper and his perfect pitch, and returned to Corrow at twenty-two with a leather bag, a bicycle and an opinion on everything. She was never a gentle woman. She told a visiting concert pianist that his Chopin was “a fine performance of the wrong notes”, and informed the mayor, on the occasion of his daughter’s wedding, that the town hall’s grand had “the voice of an elderly accountant”. Both took the criticism to heart; the piano was replaced within the year.

Yet her bluntness was widely understood to be a form of love. She tuned the pianos of the poor for nothing and those of the rich for a good deal, a policy she called “proportional harmony”. During the flood of 1971 she is said to have waded through knee-deep water to carry the school’s piano upstairs, with the help of six boys and a good deal of language that the headmaster chose not to remember. The instrument, remarkably, played in tune the following Monday, which the headmaster attributed to prayer and she attributed to physics, a disagreement that the two maintained, with perfect courtesy, for thirty years.

She never married, a fact she attributed to having found no one whose pitch she could trust. She did, however, adopt, informally and without paperwork, a succession of apprentices, a number of whom went on to careers in concert halls from Vienna to Montreal. They remember her as exacting, impatient and extravagantly generous. “She would stop you mid-note,” one recalled, “and say, ‘Listen. No, really listen.’ And you realised you had been hearing the world as a rough draft.”

In her last years, as arthritis stiffened her hands, she turned to teaching the town’s children to listen. Every Saturday morning she held a class in her front room, where pupils were asked to identify the tones of a kettle, a closing door, a neighbour’s laugh. Some, she admitted, would never learn; she called these “the tone-deaf”, and treated them with particular tenderness, on the grounds that the world had already been unkind enough.

She is survived by her sister, Benedetta, eleven apprentices and, by her own estimate, roughly four hundred pianos that now sing a little more truly than they otherwise might. A memorial will be held at the chapel on Saturday. The organisers ask that mourners refrain from bringing flowers and instead bring any instrument in need of attention. Her tuning fork, the one taken from the church so long ago, will be returned at last, with, we are told, her apologies.

parts.title: Review: A Gazetteer of Absent Places
parts.intro: A literary review of a fictional novel built as an encyclopaedia of vanished towns.
paragraphs: Tomasz Wren’s third novel, A Gazetteer of Absent Places, takes the form of an encyclopaedia of towns that no longer exist, drowned by reservoirs, erased by borders or simply forgotten. It is a conceit that might easily have curdled into mere cleverness, and in the first fifty pages it very nearly does. That it ends up as one of the most quietly devastating books of the year is a tribute to the author’s restraint, and to a patience with his readers that is increasingly rare.

Each entry begins in the neutral register of reference: population, principal industries, notable buildings. Then, almost imperceptibly, the voice acquires a pulse. A paragraph on the vanished mill town of Harrowgate ends with a note on the “unusual acoustic properties” of its square, “where, on certain evenings, a person speaking at one end could be heard, without effort, at the other”. We do not learn until three hundred pages later that the speaker was the narrator’s mother, and that the other end was the last place she was ever seen.

This is Wren’s method, and it is both the book’s chief glory and its occasional burden. The narrator, never named, is compiling the gazetteer in the long aftermath of a family rupture whose nature is only gradually disclosed. Grief is never mentioned directly; it is displaced onto geography, so that a flooded valley becomes the vehicle for a loss too large for grammar. Readers who prefer plot will be frustrated. Readers who relish implication will find themselves, as I did, rereading single sentences with the particular reverence usually reserved for poetry.

The prose is formidable without being showy. Wren has a gift for the exact, unexpected adjective: a village’s church is “apologetic”, a canal “conspicuously patient”. He is also, unusually among contemporary novelists, funny, in a dry, cornered way, as when he records that a certain province was dissolved by treaty in 1921 “to the relief of its inhabitants, who had never been consulted about its creation either”. These flashes of humour do not dilute the sadness; they sharpen it, much as a thin line of light makes the surrounding dark more precise.

The book is not without flaws. The middle section, a sequence of some forty entries on the provinces of a fictional empire, is overlong, and the invented history, while ingenious, lacks the emotional charge of the real places on either side of it. One senses an author enamoured of his own apparatus. A subplot involving a rival cartographer, presumably intended to leaven the elegy with intrigue, is abandoned so abruptly that it feels less like a thread cut than a thread forgotten.

Yet these are the failings of ambition, and they are redeemed by the last hundred pages, in which the form, so long a screen, becomes a window. The final entry, for a town the narrator has never named and which the reader has, by now, quietly identified, runs to a mere eleven lines. It contains no adjective at all. I have seldom read a more affecting paragraph, nor one so dependent on everything that precedes it.

A Gazetteer of Absent Places will not please everyone. It is slow, oblique and unapologetically literary. But for those willing to meet it on its own terms, it offers something that fiction promises more often than it delivers: the experience of having been, quite gently, rearranged. It is a book about what disappears and what, against all reasonable expectation, remains in the telling.

parts.title: Ask Ottoline: Wisdom for the Weary
parts.intro: An ironic advice columnist answers four readers’ letters with dry wit.
paragraphs: Dear readers, this week’s postbag was heavy, as postbags tend to be after a long weekend and a short temper. As ever, I offer advice freely, which is to say you may take it or leave it, and as ever you will do the second and write to me again in March.

Q: My brother-in-law has started “optimising” our family gatherings. Last Sunday he arrived with a spreadsheet allocating each relative a speaking time. Mine was four minutes. How do I respond without causing a scene? — Timed Out in Tewkesbury

A: Dear Timed Out, I am touched that you consider a scene the worst possible outcome. Many a family has been improved by one. That said, I would counsel against open warfare. Instead, accept your four minutes with exaggerated gratitude and then use them, in full, to read aloud from the minutes of the last meeting at which the family agreed to anything. You will find the silence that follows is considerably longer than four minutes and, in my experience, considerably more productive.
Q: I have been invited to a colleague’s leaving party, and I cannot stand her. Must I go? And if I do, what do I say? — Reluctant in Reading

A: Dear Reluctant, You must go, because absence is a statement and you have, I suspect, stated enough. As to what to say, I recommend the phrase “I shall miss the efficiency with which you left every meeting early.” It is technically a compliment, it is demonstrably true, and she will spend the rest of the evening trying to decide. Do not overdo the champagne. Resentment is a poor mixer.
Q: My partner insists that I “never listen”. I have asked him to repeat this several times, and he becomes upset every time. What am I doing wrong? — Baffled in Bath

A: Dear Baffled, I am afraid I have to be gentle here, which does not come naturally. Your partner is not complaining about the quantity of your hearing but about its direction. Listening is not a matter of receiving sound; it is the art of making another person feel that what they said has landed somewhere. Try, as an experiment, repeating back one thing he said, unprompted, at some point in the next week. I promise he will faint. Do keep a chair nearby.
Q: Is it wrong to want to be right all the time? — Certain in Cardiff

A: Dear Certain, Not at all; it is the most natural ambition in the world and, as it happens, the only one I share with the rest of humanity. The difficulty lies in the “all the time”. Those who are right all the time are rarely invited anywhere twice. Might I suggest that you cultivate, as a matter of social survival, the occasional graceful error? Make it a small one, and make it in front of witnesses. Then watch how warmly they forgive you for being, at last, like them.

That is all for this week. Please do keep writing: my fee remains what it has always been, which is the quiet satisfaction of being ignored by people I have never met, and, on rare and thrilling occasions, of being quoted back to me, wrongly, at a dinner party I was not invited to. Until next week, be kind to your relatives, be wary of spreadsheets, and remember that nobody ever won an argument by being the last to leave the room. — Ottoline

parts.title: The Unhurried Manifesto
parts.intro: A fictional collective publishes a playful but serious manifesto in defence of slowness.
paragraphs: We, the undersigned members of the Collective for Deliberate Idleness, assembled in a borrowed barn on the last wet afternoon of October, hold the following truths to be, if not self-evident, then at least inadequately debated. We do not ask to be believed. We ask only to be given, as a matter of common courtesy, a moment in which to consider whether we are right.

First, that speed is not a virtue. It is a habit, acquired in the nineteenth century, perfected in the twentieth, and now so thoroughly woven into the fabric of daily life that we mistake its absence for illness. We reject the proposition that a person who answers immediately is more intelligent than one who answers next week. Indeed, we maintain that the reverse is frequently true, and that the finest ideas in human history were nearly all conceived in an armchair, a bath or a state of mild neglect.

Second, that idleness is not the opposite of work but its soil. The mind, like a field, requires fallow seasons; a field cropped without pause produces, in the end, nothing but dust and an annual report. We therefore demand the restoration of the afternoon, that vast and shameless territory which has been steadily annexed by meetings, notifications and the strange compulsion to be reachable.

Third, that boredom is a natural resource and must be protected like any other. Our children are being denied it, as they are denied mud and unsupervised ponds, and they are poorer for the loss. A child left alone with nothing to do will, given enough time, invent a country. We see no reason why adults should be less ambitious.

Fourth, that the cult of productivity has confused the measurable with the valuable. It has taught us to count what can be counted, hours logged, emails cleared, steps taken, and to treat everything else as decoration. But no one on their deathbed has been heard to wish they had replied to more messages. The things that matter most, friendship, wonder, the long digestion of a good book, resist every metric devised to capture them, and are the first casualties of any regime of efficiency.

Fifth, and lest we be misunderstood, that we are not opposed to effort. We are opposed to hurry, which is effort’s counterfeit. The craftsman who spends a month on a single chair is not idle; he is merely unwilling to lie about how long things take. We commend this honesty and propose that it be adopted generally, beginning with those who set deadlines.

In pursuit of these principles, we resolve as follows: to take one unscheduled hour each day, to be spent on nothing that can be reported; to answer no message within an hour of receiving it, except in cases of fire; to eat, at least once a week, a meal that lasts longer than the television programme that precedes it; and to greet, with equanimity rather than alarm, any silence that threatens to occur.

We are aware that this document will be mocked, and that some will call it a luxury of the comfortable. The charge has merit, and we accept it. But we note that the comfortable are precisely those who have most to lose by never stopping, and that the habit, once learned, may be passed down the ladder, as other luxuries once were, until the eight-hour day and the weekend, which were also called impossible, came to seem merely ordinary.
Adopted unanimously, after a debate of no great length, and ratified the following morning, when no one had yet managed to get up.

parts.title: Cars in the City Centre: An Edited Debate
parts.intro: An edited transcript of a public debate on closing a city centre to private cars.
paragraphs: [Transcript edited for length and clarity.] MODERATOR (Helen Okoye): Good evening, and welcome to the Town Hall Forum. Tonight’s motion is “This house believes that the city centre should be closed to private cars.” Each speaker has four minutes to open, after which I shall do my best to prevent them from interrupting one another. Dr Duarte, you propose the motion.

DR DUARTE: Thank you. I would like to begin with a number: forty-one. That is the percentage of the centre’s surface area currently given over to roads and parking, space that, in any other sector, we would call a land grab. We have been conducting an experiment in prioritising the car for seventy years, and the results are in. The air is worse, the streets are louder and, paradoxically, the journey across town takes longer than it did in 1985. If a medicine had produced those outcomes, it would have been withdrawn decades ago.

MR STRAND: May I? [Laughter] I appreciate the statistics, but I would remind the audience that a city is not a laboratory. It is a place where people earn a living. The independent shops on Mercer Street, which I represent, tell me that nearly a third of their custom arrives by car, often with a boot full of purchases that cannot be carried on a tram. Close the roads, and you will not create a pleasant pedestrian paradise. You will create a very pleasant, very empty one.

DR DUARTE: With respect, that is an assertion rather than an argument. When Almeria closed its old quarter eight years ago, the same fears were expressed, in nearly the same words. Footfall rose by nineteen per cent. Pedestrians, it turns out, spend less per visit than drivers, but they visit far more often, and they linger, which is the one thing a car park is designed to prevent.

MR STRAND: Almeria is a sunny town of forty thousand people, Dr Duarte. We have a climate best described as a rumour of rain. [Laughter] I do not say that nothing can be done. I say that a blanket ban is a blunt instrument, and that blunt instruments, in my experience, rarely fall on those who designed them. They fall on the elderly, the disabled, the tradesman with a van full of tools.
MODERATOR: That is a serious point. Dr Duarte, can you answer it without recourse to the Mediterranean?

DR DUARTE: Gladly. Nobody is proposing to abandon those who genuinely need access. The motion concerns private cars, not ambulances, delivery vehicles or blue-badge holders, and any sensible scheme would exempt them. What we are really debating is whether the convenience of the many drivers who have alternatives should outweigh the health of everyone who breathes. I put it to Mr Strand that when we say a ban is “unfair”, we usually mean that it is inconvenient, and that is not the same thing.

MR STRAND: That is a clever distinction, and I shall concede that it is partly right. But convenience, Dr Duarte, is not a trivial matter to a woman who closes her shop at six and walks to a car park at night. Any scheme must reassure her, in practice, not merely in a brochure, before it asks her to give up the certainty of parking outside her own door. And I would add that a city which wishes to be admired by visitors must first be affordable to the people who work in it.

MODERATOR: I sense we are nearer to agreement than the motion suggests. [Pause] Both of you accept that vulnerable users must be protected, and both accept that the centre must stay alive after dark. Let me take a vote from the floor, and we shall hear the result after the break.

parts.title: Preface to the Second Edition of A Natural History of Waiting
parts.intro: The author of a fictional book looks back on it with wry humour in a preface to a new edition.
paragraphs: When this book first appeared, twelve years ago, it was greeted with the kind of silence reserved for works that have failed to offend anyone. A handful of reviewers called it “charming”, a word that authors learn to read as a polite form of dismissal. Eleven copies, by my publisher’s reckoning, were sold to people who were not related to me. I mention this not to complain, but to explain why, when the invitation arrived to prepare a second edition, my first instinct was to check the date.

My second was to wonder whether I still agreed with myself. It is a disquieting experience to reopen one’s own book after a decade. The author one meets there, confident, a little breathless, fond of the semicolon, seems at once a stranger and a distant relative, someone one would be glad to meet at a wedding and relieved to leave by the second course. I have resisted the temptation to rewrite him. I have corrected errors of fact, of which there were fewer than I feared and more than I would admit, and I have restored a chapter that the first edition’s editor, rightly or wrongly, considered a digression.

The book’s argument, for those who have not read it and do not intend to, is simple. Waiting, I contend, is not an absence of activity but an activity in its own right, with its own species, habitats and rules of conduct. The commuter on the platform, the patient in the surgery, the farmer watching the sky for rain: each performs a distinct form of attention, and none of them is idle. To wait well, I argued, is among the oldest human skills, and the one we are least inclined to teach.

What has changed in twelve years is not the argument but the world to which it is addressed. When I wrote the first edition, waiting was still something that happened to us, at bus stops, in queues, between one letter and the next. It has since become something we are ingeniously equipped to avoid. The enforced pause, once a nuisance, has turned out to have been a kind of public service, an unmanaged interval in which the mind, deprived of occupation, wandered into thoughts it would never have chosen. I did not foresee how much I would come to miss it.

Some readers have written to say that the book made them more patient. I confess I find this slightly alarming, as I am not a patient man, and the thought that my prose has been inducing a virtue its author lacks suggests a kind of fraud. The truth is that I wrote the book in a spirit of envy, studying the waiters of the world, the fishermen, the astronomers, the grandmothers outside the school gates, in the hope that proximity would be contagious. It was not. But the study was, I now believe, its own consolation.

I owe thanks, as before, to the librarians who tolerated my long afternoons, and to my late friend Anselm Rook, who read the first draft and pronounced it “worth waiting for”, a remark whose cruelty I did not appreciate until years later, when I realised that he had meant it kindly. New thanks are due to my present editor, who has waited, with exemplary grace, for this preface to be finished. She would like it known that she has been waiting for three weeks, and that she regards the entire episode as further evidence for my thesis.

The book is now yours. Read it quickly if you must, but I suspect you will find, somewhere in the middle, that it declines to be hurried, and that you have been waiting, without noticing, for the sentence that makes you stop.
